en: Compendium of Essential Passages from the Various Sutras, Volume One. Section One: The Three Jewels.
Subsection One: Reverence for the Buddha. This section is further divided into six topics.

Universal Reverence: An Exposition of Intent. Contemplating the Buddhas of the Ten Directions; Contemplating Śākyamuni Buddha; Contemplating Amitābha Buddha; Contemplating Maitreya Buddha; Contemplating the Buddha-Samādhi. Universal Reverence: An Exposition of Intent, Part One. Now, the Great Sage possesses the mark of equanimity.
Because my disciples possess the virtue of extolling [the Dharma],
the Buddhas of the ten directions have all emerged together from the turbidity of the mud.
The three bodies of perfect enlightenment are seated together upon a lotus throne;
by recollecting whichever form one desires, one shall obtain benefit.
That is to say, from his initial renunciation until his final attainment of perfect enlightenment, throughout that interval:
subduing the māras under the Bodhi tree and preaching the Dharma at the Deer Park.
His primary and secondary marks were perfectly complete and his radiance was brilliantly manifest;
the color of his body was pure and refined like molten gold,
and his countenance was as dignified and serene as the full moon.
His teeth were like white jade or snow;
his hair was like shining conch shells;
and his eyes were like blue lotuses.
Her eyebrows are as green as willow leaves;
her eightfold voice resonates clearly;
her myriad features are dignified and harmonious.
The five eyes were sharp and lucid;
the six supernormal powers soared afar.
His eloquence flowed like a cascading river, pouring forth in continuous succession as it met the needs of the occasion.
The three circles form the body;
the five parts constitute the essence.
Bearing both the provisional and the ultimate, one delivers sentient beings.
Following the true and responding to the responsive,
one should transform sentient beings; at times fanning the vast wind of great compassion,
and at times pouring down the copious rain of the Dharma.
It enables the field of the body to be moistened,
so that the supreme sprouts are immediately emitted;
once the tree of the mind has flourished, [the fruit ripens].
Thus, there are leaves that flourish without withering.
One comes where there is no coming;
one sees where there is no seeing.
For the sake of sentient beings, he manifests in accordance with conditions;
may ten billion [beings] throughout the ten directions all vow to attend him in succession,
and may those within the trichiliocosm all receive his personal instruction.
Planting seeds deeply in the field of merit,
extensively promoting offerings,
and casting out the roots of false and inverted views.
Uproot the roots of greed and anger,
cultivate the causes of mindfulness of the Buddha,
and you shall realize the fruit of beholding the Buddha.
As the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states:
"The Three Jewels possess six meanings;
therefore, they must be revered."
First is the meaning of rarity:
it is like worldly precious objects that cannot be obtained by those who are impoverished.
Such are the Three Jewels;
sentient beings of meager merit cannot encounter them even in hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes.
Therefore, it is called a "jewel.
Second is the meaning of being free from defilement:
just as a genuine worldly jewel has no flaws or impurities in its substance.
The Three Jewels are thus;
because they are free from all outflows (āsrava),
they are called "jewels" (ratna).
Third is the meaning of power:
just as worldly treasures have great power to eliminate poverty and remove poison,
so too do the Three Jewels.
Because they possess the inconceivable power of the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*),
they are called "jewels.
Fourth is the meaning of adornment.
Just as worldly treasures can adorn the head and body, making the person beautiful,
so too are the Three Jewels;
they can adorn the practitioner’s pure body.
Therefore, it is called a "jewel.
Fifth is the sense of being most excellent:
just as worldly treasures are superior among all things, so too is this.
The Three Jewels are thus;
because they are the most preeminent among all things in the world,
they are called "jewels."
Sixth is the meaning of being unchangeable.
Just as genuine gold of the world cannot be altered by burning, grinding, or smelting,
so it is with the Triple Gem.
It is not altered by the eight worldly dharmas;
therefore, it is called a treasure.
Furthermore, it possesses six meanings.
Therefore, one must show reverence.
A single Buddha is able to provide instruction;
the Dharma is a potent medicine.
The Sangha is able to transmit and propagate [the Dharma]; all of them benefit me.
Out of gratitude for this kindness, I revere them.
Second, in this degenerate age of evil times,
it is not easy to transmit the Dharma;
we pray for your majestic protection.
Therefore, one must pay respect.
Third, one pays respect so that sentient beings may give rise to faith and receive [the teachings].
Fourth, one pays respect to demonstrate the proper ritual for monks and nuns to serve with reverence.
Fifth, one pays respect so that the Dharma of joyful offerings may endure for a long time;
sixth, one pays respect to manifest its superior characteristics.
Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
The Three Jewels are most auspicious;
therefore, I place them at the beginning of this sutra.
2. The Contemplation of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions. Second, as stated in the *Buddha-dhyāna-samādhi-sūtra*:
In the distant past, immeasurable eons ago,
there was a Buddha who appeared in the world,
named Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who,
together with nine disciples,
went to a Buddhist stūpa to pay homage to the Buddha’s image.
They saw a precious image, magnificent and beautiful to behold;
having paid homage, they gazed upon it intently and praised it with verses.
Later, when their lives ended, they were all reborn within great lotuses in the eastern buddha-field of the Buddha Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja.
He was born by sudden transformation in the full lotus posture.
From that time forth, he constantly encountered Buddhas and,
in the presence of those Buddhas, purely cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
They attain the ocean-like samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Having attained this samādhi, the Buddhas bestow upon them predictions of enlightenment,
such that they shall each attain Buddhahood in the ten directions.
The Buddha of Good Virtue in the eastern direction is none other than that teacher;
his nine disciples have become the Buddhas of the nine directions.
That is to say: in the southeast is the Buddha Anupama-guṇa;
in the south is the Buddha Candana-guṇa;
and in the southwest is the Buddha Ratnadatta.
In the west is the Buddha Amitābha;
in the northwest is the Buddha Puṣpadeva;
in the north is the Buddha Lakṣmīdeva.
In the northeast is the Buddha of the Practice of the Three Vehicles;
above is the Buddha of Vast Multitude of Virtues;
below is the Buddha of Illustrious Virtue.
Thus, these ten Buddhas,
by virtue of having prostrated before a stupa, gazed upon an image, and offered a single verse of praise in the past,
have each attained Buddhahood in the ten directions today.
Furthermore, the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhi-sūtra* states:
"In the distant past, long ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world,
named King of Emptiness (*Śūnyarāja*)."
After he entered parinirvāṇa, there were four bhikṣus who together practiced as fellow students to learn the Buddha’s true Dharma;
yet their minds were shrouded by afflictions.
Unable to uphold the precious treasury of the Buddha-dharma,
he will fall into the evil realms due to his many unwholesome karmas.
Then, a voice from the sky spoke to the bhikṣu, saying:
Although the Tathāgata Śūnyarāja has entered parinirvāṇa, what you have transgressed is such that you thought there would be no savior.
You should now enter the stupa to behold the image;
it is no different from when the Buddha was still in the world.
Having heard the voice from the void,
he entered the stupa to observe the mark of the white tuft between the eyebrows of the image,
and immediately formed this thought:
When the Tathāgata was in the world,
how did his radiant form-body differ from this? O Buddha,
Great Being with the marks of greatness, I pray that you will remove my transgressions.
Having spoken these words,
they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground like the collapsing of Mount Tai, repenting for all their transgressions.
By virtue of the causal conditions of entering a Buddha stupa, contemplating the image of the Buddha’s *ūrṇā-kośa*, and repenting,
one shall not fall into the evil realms for eighty billion *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas thereafter; in every birth,
one shall constantly behold the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Having received and upheld the profound samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddhas from all the Buddhas,
and having attained this samādhi,
they receive a prophecy of enlightenment manifested before them by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
They have all now attained Buddhahood.
To the east, there is a land named Abhirati.
The Buddha was named Akṣobhya;
he is none other than this foremost bhikṣu.
To the south, there is a land.
His name was Ānanda; the Buddha’s name was Ratnalakṣaṇa.
He was none other than the second bhikṣu.
In the western direction there is a land called Sukhāvatī; the Buddha there is named Amitāyus.
He was none other than the third bhikṣu.
To the north there is a country named Padmavyūha.
The Buddha named Subtle Sound was none other than this fourth bhikṣu. For this reason.
The practitioner should thus aspire to contemplate the Buddha.
Furthermore, the Kāśyapa Sūtra states:
"In the distant past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago..."
There was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Prabhāsa.
After he entered nirvana,
There was a bodhisattva named Mahāvīrya,
sixteen years of age and of Brahmin descent.
He was of incomparable beauty.
There was a bhikṣu who painted an image of the Buddha upon a white cotton cloth.
He took it and applied himself with diligence.
Seeing the image, his heart was filled with great joy,
and he spoke these words:
The form and image of the Tathāgata are so exquisitely beautiful;
how much more so is the Buddha’s own body!
May I, in the future, likewise achieve such a wondrous body.
Having spoken thus, he reflected:
"If I remain at home, this body will be difficult to attain.
He then addressed his parents, entreating them with compassion to allow him to go forth into the religious life.
The parents replied,
"We are now old, and you are our only son.
If you renounce the household life, we shall die."
The son said to his parents:
"If you do not grant me permission,
from this day forward I shall neither drink nor eat, nor shall I rise upon or sit upon my bed."
He did not speak further.
Having made this vow,
he did not eat for one day, and so on, up to six days.
His parents, his kinsmen, and eighty-four thousand court ladies all wept together;
they paid homage to Mahā-vīrya and immediately granted him permission to leave the household life.
Having already left the household life,
he took the image with him into the mountains, gathered grass to serve as a seat,
and sat cross-legged before the painted image.
Contemplate this painted image with single-minded attention as no different from the Tathāgata.
This image of the Tathāgata is neither conscious nor cognizant;
all phenomena are likewise so.
It is signless, detached from signs, and its essential nature is empty and quiescent.
Having performed this contemplation,
he passes through days and nights.
He accomplished the five supernormal powers,
was fully endowed with immeasurable and unimpeded eloquence,
and attained the Samādhi of Universal Radiance.
Possessing great radiance,
with the pure divine eye,
he beholds incalculable buddhas in the eastern direction.
With the pure divine ear, they hear what the Buddha has spoken and are able to receive it all in its entirety;
for seven full months, they take wisdom as their sustenance.
All the devas scattered flowers as an offering;
emerging from the mountain, he came to the village to preach the Dharma for the sake of human beings.
Twenty thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta,
while immeasurable asaṃkhyeya people dwelt in the merits of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Their parents and kinsmen all abide in non-retrogression toward unsurpassed bodhi.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
The one who was formerly Mahā-vīrya is my very self today.
By means of this contemplation of the image, I have now attained Buddhahood.
If there is anyone who can learn to contemplate in this manner, [they shall likewise attain it].
"In the future, he will certainly attain the Unsurpassed Way.
Furthermore, the *Buddhabhāṣita-buddhasamādhi-sūtra* states:
"In the distant past, long ago..."
There was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Śākyamuni.
After his parinirvāṇa, there was a prince.
His name was Suvarṇadhvaja.
He was arrogant, held false views, and lacked faith in the Buddha’s Dharma.
There was a bhikṣu...
Known as Master of Samādhi,
he spoke to the prince, saying,
"In this world, there is a Buddha image adorned with various precious jewels."
However, it was lovely;
one might briefly enter the stupa to behold the image of the Buddha.
The prince then followed him into the stupa.
Seeing the marks and signs of the image, he said to the bhikṣu,
"If even this Buddha image is so majestic and dignified,
how much more so must the Buddha’s true body be!"
The bhikṣu said:
"If you now see the image and are unable to prostrate,
you should join your palms and recite 'Namo Buddha'."
At that time, the prince immediately joined his palms and paid homage, saying, "Namo Buddha.
Returning to the palace, he focused his mindfulness upon the image within the stupa;
consequently, during the final watch of the night, he saw the image of the Buddha in a dream.
Having rejoiced after the dream, he abandoned wrong views and took refuge in the Triple Gem.
By virtue of the roots of goodness from reciting the Buddha’s name while entering a stupa,
at the end of his life, he encountered nine hundred million *nayuta* buddhas.
In the presence of all Buddhas, they attain the profound *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*.
Because they have attained this samādhi,
the Buddhas appear before them and bestow upon them the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
From that time forward, for a hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas,
he did not fall into the evil realms;
and even until today, he has attained the profound Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
The prince of old was none other than the present Bodhisattva Viśeṣacintin.
By this causal connection...
The wise person should train in mindfulness of the Buddha in this manner.
Furthermore, a verse from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"If a person, with a distracted mind, enters a stupa or temple..."
"To recite 'Namo Buddha' even once brings one to the path of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, the *Upamāna-sūtra* (Piyu jing) states:
"In the past, there was a king..."
Having killed his father to establish himself,
there was an arhat who knew that this king’s life would end before long.
He calculated that his remaining life would not exceed seven days;
after his death, he would surely fall into the Avīci Hell to suffer for one kalpa.
This Arhat then went immediately to convert him.
He exhorted him to sincerely recite "Namo Buddha" without interruption for seven days.
As he was about to depart, he again instructed him, "Be careful not to forget this."
The king then joined his palms and recited [the name] with single-minded devotion, never ceasing day or night.
On the seventh day, he passed away;
his spirit immediately headed toward the Avīci Hell.
Carrying forward his previous practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, he arrived at the gate of hell;
recognizing it as hell,
he immediately cried out in a loud voice, "Namo Buddha!"
When the sinners in the hells heard the sound of the name of the Buddha being invoked,
they all simultaneously cried out, "Namo Buddhāya. At that very moment,
the fierce fires of hell were instantly transformed and extinguished.
All those who had committed sins attained liberation and were reborn among human beings.
Later, an Arhat again preached the Dharma for them.
One attains the stage of Srotāpanna.
By this causal condition,
one obtains the merit gained from reciting the name of the Buddha.
It is immeasurable, boundless, and beyond all analogy.
3. The Third Contemplation on the Buddha Śākyamuni. Furthermore, the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states:
Long ago, when the Buddha was in the world,
he preached the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi Sūtra* for his father, the King, and the great assembly.
The Buddha possesses the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
his body is of a true golden color, and his radiance is immeasurable.
At that time, there were five hundred sons of the Śākyas seated in the assembly.
Due to his karmic obstructions,
he saw the Buddha’s physical body as being like a withered Brahmin covered in ash;
having seen this, he wailed and tore out his own hair.
He threw his entire body to the ground, and blood flowed from his nose.
The Buddha comforted him, saying, "Do not wail."
I shall explain this for you.
In the past, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin.
After he had entered parinirvāṇa,
During the period of the Semblance Dharma,
there was an elder named Candravatī who had five hundred disciples.
He was intelligent and possessed great wisdom, thoroughly versed in all things.
His father, a householder, had faith and reverence for the Triple Gem and constantly expounded the meaning of the Buddha-dharma to his sons.
The sons held entirely wrong views and possessed no faith at all.
Later, when the sons were all stricken with a serious illness,
the father went before his children and wept while joining his palms in reverence.
He said to his sons,
"You all hold false views and do not believe in the Buddha-dharma;
now the sword of impermanence cuts through your bodies."
Upon whom can you rely?
There is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Vipaśyin;
you should invoke his name.
Having heard this, the sons,
out of reverence for their father’s words,
exclaimed, "Namo Buddha!"
He further instructed him to recite the name of the Dharma and the name of the Saṅgha.
Having finished the recitation, he passed away;
because he had recited the Buddha’s name, he was reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
When their lifespan in the heavens comes to an end,
they fall back into hell due to their former wrong views. There,
the hell-wardens and rākṣasas...
They pierced and destroyed his eyes with red-hot iron forks.
While undergoing this suffering, he recollected his father’s instruction and, through the causal conditions of recollecting the Buddha,
emerged from hell to be reborn among human beings.
Though poor and lowly,
he later encountered the Buddha Śikhin when he appeared in the world.
They merely heard the names of the Buddhas but did not behold their forms;
subsequently, they followed the Buddha Kāśyapa and the Buddha Krakucchanda.
The Buddhas Kanakamuni and Kāśyapa likewise had their names heard but their forms were not seen;
because they heard the names of these six Buddhas, [they attained liberation].
"Now you have been born into the Śākya clan together with me.
My body is as majestic and beautiful as Jāmbūnada gold,
whereas you see this greyish and emaciated Brahmin because of the wrong views held in your previous lives."
"You should now recite the names of the Buddhas of the past,
as well as the name of your father,
and also my own name and that of Maitreya Buddha."
Having uttered these words, he prostrated himself and,
toward the great assembly and the venerable Sangha,
cast his body down so that all five limbs touched the ground.
They confessed and repented for the sins of their wrong views.
Once the people had finished repenting according to the instructions,
they beheld the Buddha, golden-hued like Mount Sumeru.
Having seen this, he addressed the Buddha:
"I now behold the Buddha’s thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, along with his immeasurable radiance.
Having spoken these words, he attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
Seeking the Buddha, he left the household life and attained arhatship,
possessing the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
After my parinirvāṇa,
if one invokes my name, saying "Namo to all Buddhas," the merit obtained shall be immeasurable and boundless.
Furthermore, the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Observe how the Tathāgata walks upon the road."
It can cause the high places of the great earth to become low,
and the low places to become high;
all such high and low regions are thereby made level and even.
After the Tathāgata passed by, the ground immediately returned to its original state, and all the groves of trees leaned toward the Buddha.
The tree spirits manifested their bodies and bowed their heads in prostration;
once the Tathāgata had passed, the trees immediately returned to their upright positions.
All hills, mounds, ravines, and pits;
latrines and foul impurities;
thickets and heaps of rubble.
Everything was completely swept clean;
it was pure throughout its entirety,
and the ground was strewn with fragrant, intensely aromatic flowers.
When the Tathāgata walked upon them, even insentient objects all leaned and tilted;
how much more so would sentient beings not show reverence? Why is this?
When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path,
I bowed down, humbled myself, and paid respectful homage to all people without exception.
By virtue of these wholesome karmas, I have now attained Buddhahood.
Whether sentient or insentient,
all things incline and bow their heads in prostration whenever the Tathāgata walks by.
In the past, I personally and with my own hands gave pure, exquisite,
and pleasing assets to all sentient beings with a sincere heart;
by the retribution of this karma, [I have attained this].
When the Tathāgata walks, the great earth becomes level and even;
it is swept and sprinkled clean, and free from shards and pebbles. This has occurred whenever I have traveled on the road in the presence of immeasurable noble ones and sages.
I once swept and cleared the roads and plastered the dwellings with mud.
With a mind of equanimity, free from notions of high or low, I swept them clean.
At all times, I have constantly sought awakening for the benefit of sentient beings.
By virtue of these roots of goodness,
wherever the Buddha-Tathāgata may travel,
the path ahead naturally becomes pure.
The ground was as level as the palm of a hand.
Even Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, eighty-four thousand yojanas high,
was likewise submerged in the great ocean to that same depth.
Furthermore, the Cakravāḍa Mountains are sixteen thousand eight hundred yojanas in height and are likewise as firm and solid as adamant.
At the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, [they...]
There is none who does not bow their head in prostration and pay respect;
even if one wished to avoid it by not bowing,
such a thing is impossible.
Furthermore, the *Lalitavistara Sūtra* states:
"Because the Tathāgata’s mind was pure in the past, free from attachment, and did not harm sentient beings,
wherever he traveled..."
The feet remain unstained;
insects and ants do not harm them.
Furthermore, the *Cūḷa-vyūha-sūtra* states:
When the Tathāgata walks, he does not wear sandals.
There are three reasons for this:
first, to cause the practitioner to have few desires.
Second, he manifests the mark of the wheels on the soles of his feet;
third, he causes those who see them to rejoice.
When the Buddha walks, his feet remain four inches above the ground.
There are three causes and conditions:
first, because one sees insects and ants on the ground;
second, because there is growing grass on the ground.
Third, by manifesting supernatural powers,
he also desires to cause people’s minds to become upright;
thus, when the Buddha walks, the ground— whether high or low— is made level.
There are three causes and conditions:
first, practicing the four immeasurable minds (brahmavihāras) fundamentally,
desiring that all beings be at peace and secure.
The earth rests upon the water;
within the water there is a deity.
All insects and ants come into contact with the soles of the Buddha’s feet.
All were at peace, sharing a single mind and resolve.
Therefore, the lowly became high,
and the high became low.
Second, because the devas and spirits performed meritorious deeds to prepare the ground for the Buddha,
they leveled what was high and low.
Third, when the Buddha was a bodhisattva, he cleared and opened roads, paths, bridges, and causeways to ferry people across.
Because one obtains merit from this, the ground becomes high, low, and level;
it is intended that the minds of people should likewise become so.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
The World-Honored One possesses the mark of excellent, fine, and thin skin;
dust and dirt do not adhere to his body,
just as the lotus leaf does not receive dust or water.

If a bodhisattva walks upon a mountain of dry earth, the soil does not adhere to his feet; even when a *laṇa* wind blows and shatters the earthen mountain into dust, not even a single grain of dust adheres to the Buddha’s body.
When a bodhisattva raises food and places it in the mouth,
at that moment, ambrosia flows from two locations on either side of the throat, blending with all flavors.
This flavor is pure;
therefore, it is called "the supreme flavor among flavors.
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
Those who lack a heart of reverence for the Buddha shall be reborn among dragons and snakes;
it is because they have come from such a state in the past.
Even now, there is still no respect;
one is merely drowsy and deluded.
Furthermore, a verse in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* says:
Those who revere their elders and seniors are able to protect the Dharma;
they will gain renown in the present life and be reborn in the happy realms in the future.
The Fourth Inquiry on the Contemplation of Amitābha Buddha. Question: [What is the contemplation of Amitābha Buddha?]
What is called the Pure Land?
The answer is:
the world is bright and pure.
The eye is designated as "purity";
that which purity inhabits is called a "land."
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The land inhabited is free from the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya*),
like crystal and the like."
It is called the Pure Land.
The *Dharmapada-śāstra* states:
"The dwelling place of sentient beings free from afflictions."
It is called the Pure Land.
There are four different types of pure lands.
The first is the Dharma-nature Land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*).
Because its essence is *tathatā* (suchness). The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) of the Liang dynasty states:
"The king of lotuses serves as a metaphor for the basis of the pure land."
Because the *dharmadhātu-tathatā* serves as the foundational substance (*āśraya*) for the Pure Land.
Second is the Land of Real Reward (*sambhoga-kāya*).
Regarding this, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
Taking the two kinds of emptiness as the gateway,
the three types of wisdom as the path of entry and exit,
and śamatha and vipaśyanā as the vehicle.
It takes fundamental non-conceptual wisdom as its function.
These all define its essential substance by way of the merit of retribution.
This concerns the three matters of the pure land.
This refers to the seven sublime treasures,
which are of the nature of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*);
for sound, fragrance, taste, and touch constitute the characteristics of that land.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The Buddha’s pervasive radiance is the locus of the seven treasures.
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
Within the manifestations of the realm of all Buddhas,
there are various interspersed adornments; thus,
the *Jingtu lun* (Treatise on the Pure Land) says:
It is replete with all kinds of rare jewels and possesses perfect, wondrous adornments.
Furthermore, the newly translated *Mahābodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* states:
"Even if there were as many worlds as described above..."
Even if a great fire were blazing intensely and the Tathāgata were in its midst— whether walking,
standing, sitting, or lying down— a natural water endowed with the eight qualities would spontaneously appear from the earth at that spot.
Fourth is the Pure Land of Transformation.
This refers to the fact that the seven treasures and the five sensory objects transformed by the Buddha constitute the substance of the land of transformation.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
Through the Buddha’s spiritual power, the ground became entirely soft and supple;
it was free of mounds, hollows, soil, sand, gravel, or stones,

even causing immeasurable people to die and fall into hell;
such individuals are evil friends to sentient beings.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"There are five kinds of persons to whom one must not preach the Dharma when questioned."
1. Inquiry for the sake of testing;
2. inquiry free from doubt;
3. inquiry not because one has committed an offense and seeks to avoid remorse.
Fourth, because it is speech that is not accepted;
fifth, because it is a difficult objection—
in both cases, one must not provide an answer.
If the person before you truly possesses a good heart and lacks the aforementioned intentions,
acting out of a desire to give rise to goodness and extinguish evil;
The Dharma Master, according to their capacities and through skillful means, speaks with a benevolent heart.
If one’s own understanding is not yet clear,
or if one has doubts regarding the Dharma, [one should seek further clarification].
Then one must not explain it,
for fear that the former person may have committed an error in transmission,
whereby both parties would incur fault.
Furthermore, the Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra states:
The Buddha said,
"As for those who abide in accordance with the Dharma..."
One who is able to benefit both self and others,
yet does not abide in accordance with the Dharma,
cannot be said to achieve self-benefit or the benefit of others.
One who abides in accordance with the Dharma possesses eight knowledges.
What are these eight? First, the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
2. Knowledge of meaning; 3.
Knowledge of the three times;
4. Knowledge of contentment.
Fifth, knowledge of self and others;
sixth, knowledge of the multitudes;
seventh, knowledge of the faculties.
Eighth, the knowledge of the upper and lower realms.
Such a person is fully endowed with these eight knowledges;
whatever they speak possesses sixteen matters.
First, speaking at one time;
second, speaking with a sincere mind;
third, speaking in proper sequence.
Fourth, speaking with harmony;
fifth, speaking in accordance with the meaning;
sixth, speaking with joy.
7. Speaking with the consent of the assembly;
8. Not speaking with contempt for the assembly;
9. Not speaking with reproach toward the assembly.
10. Teaching in accordance with the Dharma;
11. Teaching for the benefit of oneself and others;
12. Teaching without distraction.
Thirteen, the teaching on the meaning of synthesis;
fourteen, the teaching on the ultimate truth;
fifteen, not giving rise to arrogance after having taught.
Having spoken these sixteen [points], one does not seek rewards in future lives.
Such a person is able to listen to others.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* says:
If there are sentient beings who are correctly practicing wholesome deeds,
and one speaks a single verse of Dharma for them to explain to those with wrong views,
causing them to develop pure faith in the Buddha.
At the end of his life, he was reborn in the Śabdavatī Heaven,
where he experienced various pleasures;
subsequently, when he declined from that celestial realm, he wandered according to the flow of karma.
If one preaches the Dharma to others for the sake of wealth and material goods,
not out of a compassionate heart to benefit sentient beings,
but rather to take possession of their wealth and goods.
Or they may drink alcohol;
or they may eat and drink together with women;
or they may seek wealth by selling themselves according to the manner of actors.
The fruit of such giving of the Dharma is very slight:
one is born in the heavens as a wise bird capable of reciting verses.
This is called the inferior grade of the gift of Dharma.
What is called the middling grade of the gift of Dharma? It is that which is done for the sake of fame and reputation.
He preaches the Dharma to others for the sake of defeating them, and for the sake of surpassing other great Dharma masters.
Or, one might preach the Dharma to others with a deceptive mind;
such a gift of Dharma yields little reward,
resulting in a middling retribution when reborn among the devas.
Or they may be born among human beings;
this is called the middle-grade gift of Dharma.
What is called the superior-grade gift of Dharma?
With a pure mind,
desiring to increase the wisdom of sentient beings,
he preaches the Dharma for their sake and not for the sake of wealth or profit.
To cause sentient beings with wrong views to abide in the True Dharma—
such a gift of Dharma benefits both oneself and others,
and is unsurpassed and most supreme.
Even unto nirvana, its merit shall not be exhausted;
this is what is called the superior grade of the gift of Dharma.
Furthermore, in the *Kāśyapa Sūtra*,
at that time the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“If the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were filled with precious jewels,”
The merit obtained by using these for giving is small;
if one were to recite even a single verse of Dharma, the merit would be far greater.
Even if one were to take all the objects of pleasure in the three realms and bestow them entirely upon a single person, [it would not equal the merit of the Dharma].
It is not equal to the merit of giving a single verse, which is the most supreme.
This merit surpasses that [other gift], for it can bring one free from all suffering and affliction—
more so than a world-system as vast as the sands of the Ganges filled with precious jewels.
Giving to all the Tathāgatas is not equal to the gift of a single Dharma teaching;
though the merit of giving jewels be great, it does not equal the merit of a single verse of the Dharma.
How much more so when the gift is vast—its merit is truly inconceivable!
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Householders should practice the giving of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*);
those who have left the household life should practice the giving of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*)."
Why is this? Because the gift of Dharma by a householder does not equal that of one who has left the household life,
for it is the latter who receives and upholds the Dharma.
Because the faith of householders is shallow,
and because householders possess much wealth, whereas those who have left the home life [possess none].
They read, recite, and master all the teachings of the sūtras;
they explain them to others and remain fearless in the midst of the assembly—
qualities that cannot be matched by those who live as householders.
Furthermore, it causes listeners to give rise to a mind of reverence,
which they cannot achieve as easily through leaving the household life;
moreover, it allows one to preach the Dharma to subdue the minds of others.
It was not possible for me to leave the household life.
As it is said in a verse:
"First practice the Dharma yourself; only then teach others."
One may indeed say this: "If you follow my example, yet you yourself practice unwholesome conduct, how can you cause others to be wholesome?
Since you have not attained tranquility for yourself, how can you bring peace to others?"
Furthermore, for one who has gone forth from the household life,
if they practice the giving of material wealth, it will obstruct other virtues and cause them to distance themselves from forest hermitages (*āraṇyaka*).
They will inevitably go to villages and engage extensively in conversation with laypeople,
thereby giving rise to the three poisons.
Their minds become thin toward the six perfections and so forth,
even to the point of craving the five desires;
they abandon the precepts and return to secular life.
Therefore, it is called death. Or,
when one is able to revert from the precepts and give rise to grave offenses,
these are termed the various afflictions and sufferings such as death.
For these reasons, one praises the gift of Dharma for those who have gone forth,
and praises the gift of material wealth for those who live at home.
Furthermore, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states that there are five matters concerning the one who preaches the Dharma.
The first is the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*), which benefits both oneself and others.
The gift of material wealth is not like this.
Second, the gift of Dharma can cause sentient beings to transcend the triple world,
whereas the gift of material wealth does not lead one beyond the realm of desire.
Third, the gift of Dharma benefits the Dharma-body,
whereas the gift of material wealth nourishes the physical body.
Fourth, the gift of Dharma increases without end.
The gift of material wealth is inevitably subject to exhaustion;
fifth, the gift of Dharma can sever ignorance,
whereas the gift of material wealth merely subdues the mind of greed.
Thus, one knows that the gift of material wealth does not equal the gift of the Dharma.
Within the gift of the Dharma itself, there are inherent gradations.
If one has understanding, one need not rely on the knowledge of others.
Fearing that others might surpass him, he keeps [the teaching] secret and does not speak of it;
thus, from the future onward, he will never hear the Dharma.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
If one is stingy with the Dharma,
one will constantly be born in remote borderlands where the Buddha-dharma does not exist;
because of such stinginess regarding the Dharma, one obstructs the wisdom and illumination of others.
This is not as good as selling the Dharma to others, for the latter would rather surpass this.
Furthermore, the *Sarvadharmavīrarāja-sūtra* states:
"Within Jambudvīpa..."
May all sentient beings who move on water, land,
or through the air attain human form;
and may there be one person who instructs all these people.

The merit obtained by causing others to dwell securely in the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions is not equal to that of a person who instructs and exhorts a single individual, enabling them to attain faith and practice.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"There are four dharmas that cause one to fall away from wisdom."
These are what a bodhisattva should distance themselves from. What are the four?
First, disrespect for the Dharma and those who teach the Dharma.
Second, they are secretive and stingy regarding essential teachings;
third, they create obstacles for those who delight in the Dharma and corrupt their resolve to listen;
fourth, they harbor arrogance, exalting themselves and disparaging others.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which one attains wisdom;
these should be constantly cultivated.
What are the four? First, to revere the Dharma and those who preach the Dharma;
second, [to revere] the Dharma as it has been heard and as it has been recited.
He explains it to others with a pure mind, seeking no gain or sustenance.
Third, he knows that wisdom is obtained from extensive learning.
One should seek with tireless diligence as if one's head were on fire.
Fourth, one should receive and uphold the Dharma as it has been heard without forgetting;
one values practice according to the teaching rather than mere verbal discourse.
3. The Conditions for Hearing the Dharma. Third: One who wishes to hear the Dharma must possess a sincere mind, revering the Dharma and honoring the teacher.
With utmost sincerity, they seek liberation;
they do not hope for the conditioned phenomena of the human or celestial realms.
Therefore, a verse spoken by the Buddha in the Āgamas says:
"Listen with a focused mind, like one drinking from thirst; Enter single-mindedly into the meaning of the words.
One who hears the Dharma with a heart leaping with joy and sorrow— To such a person as this, you may preach."
Furthermore, the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states:
"When listening to others, one should possess sixteen matters. First, listen at the proper time."
Second, listening with joy;
third, listening with a sincere mind;
fourth, listening with reverence.
5. Listening without seeking out faults;
6. Listening not for the sake of debate;
7. Listening not for the sake of victory.
Eighth, when listening, one does not disparage the speaker.
Ninth, when listening, one does not disparage the Dharma.
Tenth, when listening, one never disparages oneself.
Eleventh, when listening, one remains far removed from the five hindrances.
Twelfth, when listening, it is for the purpose of receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting [the teachings].
Thirteenth, when listening, it is for the purpose of eliminating the five desires.
Fourteenth, one listens for the sake of possessing faith;
fifteenth, one listens for the sake of all sentient beings;
sixteenth, one listens for the sake of severing the root of darkness.
Good son, one who possesses the eight kinds of wisdom is able both to speak and to listen.
Such a person is able to benefit both self and others;
one who does not possess these qualities cannot be said to benefit either self or others.
Furthermore, the Aśokarāja-sūtra states:
"In the past, King Aśoka commissioned a practitioner of the Way to preach the Dharma.
At that time, he used portable screens to shield the women so that they might listen to the teaching."
At that time, the Dharma Master preached the Dharma for the women,
constantly teaching discourses on generosity, discourses on ethical discipline, and discourses on rebirth in the heavens.
Among them was a woman who had committed an offense against the king’s law.
He lifted the curtain and approached the Dharma Master,
addressing him, saying,
"The Tathāgata, the Great Awakened One..."
When awakening to all dharmas beneath the Bodhi tree,
did you awaken to generosity and ethical discipline,
or did you awaken to other dharmas?
The Dharma Master replied:
"The Buddha realized that all contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma) are suffering,
just like molten iron."
This cause of suffering arises from habitual practice,
like a poisonous tree;
one should cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path to extinguish this accumulation of suffering.
Upon hearing these words, the woman attained the stage of Srotāpanna;
she then fastened a blade around her neck and went to the king's presence.
He then addressed the king, saying,
"Today I have violated the king’s grave law;
I pray that Your Majesty will punish me according to the law."
The king asked,
"What offense have you committed?
He replied:
I have violated the king’s prohibitions to reach the place of the practitioner,
just as a thirsty cow does not avoid death.
I am truly parched with thirst for the Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, Mūka listened to the Dharma.
The King asked him,
"When you listened to the Dharma, did you perhaps attain anything?"
He replied:
"I have seen the Four Noble Truths; having understood the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, as well as the great elements, all as being without self, I have thereby attained the Dharma-eye."
Upon hearing these words, the king leaped for joy and immediately paid them homage. He then issued a proclamation, saying:
"From this day forward, it shall not be permitted to create obstructions."
Those who delight in hearing the Dharma listen until they reach the presence of the Dharma Master and listen to the teaching face-to-face, exclaiming: "How marvelous!
A jewel among men has emerged from within my palace!"
For these reasons, one should know that listening to the Dharma brings great benefit.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-ratnapiṭaka-sūtra* states:
At that time, the kingdom of Pañcāla presented five hundred white geese as an offering to King Prasenajit.
The king ordered them to be sent to the Jetavana Monastery.
When the community of monks was at their mealtime and people were begging for food,
the geese saw the assembly of monks gathering and stood before them.
The Buddha preaches the Dharma with a single voice,
yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind;
at that time, the flock of geese likewise understood the Buddha.
Hearing the Dharma, they rejoiced;
their voices harmonized as they returned to the pond.
Later, as their feathers grew longer, they flew away to other places.
The hunter covered them all with a net and killed them.
One goose let out a cry, and all the other geese joined in harmony,
sounding as if they were listening to the Dharma.
Riding upon this wholesome mind, one is born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Regarding the dharma of being born in heaven,
there are three recollections.
First, contemplate from where one originally came;
second, contemplate where one will certainly be born;
third, contemplate what karma was previously performed to obtain birth in the heavens.
He then reflected within himself and saw that throughout his past lives he had performed no other virtuous deeds,
except for listening to the Dharma in the presence of the Buddha and the Sangha.
Having formed this thought,
five hundred devaputras immediately descended and stood beside the Tathāgata.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they all attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
King Prasenajit happened to visit the Buddha’s dwelling and frequently saw five hundred geese arrayed before the Buddha.
On that day, they did not see them,
so they asked the Buddha,
"Where have all these geese gone?"
The Buddha said,
"Those who wish to see the geese will first see the lead goose fly away to another place."
Having been killed by a hunter, he ended his life and was reborn in the heavens; these five hundred sons of gods,
wearing fine celestial crowns and appearing exceptionally handsome and distinguished, are they.
Today, all who have heard the Dharma have attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The king asked the Buddha,
"By what karmic conditions did these geese come to be so?"
Having fallen among the animals,
he was reborn in heaven at the end of his life and attained the Way today.
The Buddha said:
In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha,
five hundred women all together received the precepts; however,
because their resolve was not firm, they violated the precepts they had undertaken.
Due to the causes and conditions of violating the precepts, he fell among the animals and took this body of a wild goose; yet,
because he had received the precepts, [he was born here].
Having encountered the Tathāgata and heard the Dharma, they attained the Way;
by virtue of the causal conditions of hearing the Dharma while in the body of a goose,
they were reborn in the heavens.
Furthermore, the *Old Miscellaneous Parables Sūtra* (*Xiù zá pìyù jīng*) says:
Once there was a śramaṇa who recited the sūtras day and night.
A dog lay crouching beneath his bed.
With single-minded devotion he listened to the sutras and no longer thought of food.
In this manner, after many years had passed,
when his life ended, he attained a human form.
She was born in the kingdom of Śrāvastī;
having grown up as a woman,
she saw a śramaṇa begging for alms.
She then ran to bring food herself and gave it to the śramaṇa with joy.
Later, she became a bhikṣuṇī and attained the fruit of the Path.
Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-avadāna* (Fu-fa-zang jing) states:
The Buddha said:
"All sentient beings who wish to emerge from the great ocean of birth and death within the triple world..."
One must rely upon the boat of the Dharma to attain liberation.
The Dharma is refreshing, removing the heat of afflictions;
the Dharma is a sublime medicine, capable of healing the disease of the fetters.
The Dharma is the true spiritual friend of sentient beings;
it brings great benefit and delivers them from all suffering and affliction. Why is this so?
The dispositions and natures of all sentient beings are not fixed;
they follow whatever they are habituated to.
If they associate with the good, they become good.
To associate with the wicked leads to wickedness;
if one associates with evil friends,
one will then commit evil deeds.
The cycle of birth and death has no end or limit; yet,
if one draws near to virtuous friends,
gives rise to a mind of faith and reverence, and listens to and receives the sublime Dharma.
It will certainly enable one to leave behind the suffering and afflictions of the three miserable realms,
and through this merit, one shall experience the most supreme bliss.
The King of Pāṭaliputra possessed a white elephant.
It can destroy enemies;
if a person commits a crime, they may be ordered to be trampled to death by an elephant.
Later, the elephant stable was consumed by fire.
The elephant was moved closer to the monastery.
Hearing the bhikṣu reciting a verse from the Dharmapada Sūtra which says, "By doing good,
one is born in heaven," the elephant [was moved].
"Committing evil leads to the abyss.
Having heard this Dharma,
the elephant’s mind immediately became gentle, and he gave rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion.
Later, when criminals were brought before him,
he would merely sniff them with his nose and lick them with his tongue before departing;
he was utterly unwilling to kill them.
Having seen this, the king was greatly terrified in his heart and immediately summoned his ministers to deliberate on this matter.
A wise minister addressed the king:
"This elephant must have heard the sublime Dharma while near the monastery;
that is why he acts thus.
You should now move him and tether him near the slaughterhouse."
The king followed his words.
When the elephant saw it being slaughtered, its malevolence flared up fiercely,
and its cruelty increased even further.
Therefore, one should know that the dispositions and natures of all sentient beings are not fixed.
Even animals are like this: hearing the Dharma gives rise to compassion, while seeing slaughter increases their harm.
How much more so for humans—how could they not be influenced by such habits?
Therefore, the wise should be aware of this:
seeing evil, they must abandon it;
beholding good, they should draw near to it.
Diligently listen to the sūtras and the Dharma.
Furthermore, in the past, there was a brahmin who carried human skulls, the number of which was very great.
He went to the city of Pāṭaliputra and traveled about everywhere offering it for sale,
but after a long time had passed, there was no one at all who would buy it.
At that time, the brahmin became extremely angry.
He shouted with a loud voice,
"The people in this city are foolish and dull-witted;
if they do not come to me to buy skulls,"
"I shall bring him a bad reputation.
At that time, the lay followers (*upāsaka*) in the city,
hearing this and fearing slander, bought [the goods] for money.
He would then pierce their ears with copper skewers;
if they passed completely through, he would give them a high price,
but for those that only partially penetrated, the payment was proportionally less.
To those who could not pass through at all, he gave no payment whatsoever.
The brāhmaṇa said,
"These skulls of mine are all entirely without difference."
"Why is it that the prices paid for them are not equal?
The upāsaka replied,
"The former ones were completely worn out."
When this person was born, they heard and received the sublime Dharma;
their wisdom was lofty and superior,
and they were esteemed for such qualities as being of great value.
As for those who have mastered only half,
although they listen to the sutras and the Dharma, they have not yet attained skillful discernment;
therefore, they are given a small amount.
Regarding those who do not understand at all:
because these individuals did not listen to the Dharma in the past,
they do not pay the price.
At that time, the lay follower took this skull and went outside the city to erect a stupa and make offerings to it;
after his life ended, he was reborn entirely in the heavens.
For these reasons, one should know that the sublime Dharma possesses great merit;
such is this upāsaka.
If one erects a stupa over the skull of a person who heard the Dharma and makes offerings to it,
they will still attain rebirth in heaven.
How much more so for those who, with a sincere heart, listen to and receive the teachings of the sutras,
and who offer worship and respect to those who uphold the sutras;
the karmic reward of such merit is truly difficult to exhaust.
In the future, they will certainly attain the unsurpassed path.
Therefore, a wise person who desires to obtain unsurpassed peace and happiness [should practice this].
One should listen to the sutras and the Dharma with a sincere and diligent mind.
Furthermore, the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish* states:
Long ago, when the Buddha was in the world...
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was the elder Sudatta,
who with faith and reverence served as a patron (*dānapati*) for the Saṃgha,
providing everything that the monks required.
In the house of Sudatta there were two parrots:
one named Lūtī and the other named Śalūtī.
By nature he was clever and wise, and understood the speech of others.
When he saw a bhikṣu approaching,
he would first inform those in his household, instructing them to go out to welcome him.
At a later time, Ānanda went to the house of the elder and saw that the bird was clever and discerning;
he then preached the Four Noble Truths— suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path— to it.
In front of the gate was a tree where two birds heard the Dharma;
they flew up into the tree and joyfully recited it.
That night, while they were roosting in the tree, they were eaten by a wild fox.
By virtue of these roots of goodness, they are born in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings;
when their lifespan in that heaven is exhausted, they are born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
and when their lifespan in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is exhausted, they are born in the Yāma Heaven.
When his lifespan in Yāma is exhausted, he is reborn in Tuṣita;
when his lifespan in Tuṣita is exhausted, he is reborn in Nirmāṇarati;
and when his lifespan in Nirmāṇarati is exhausted, he is reborn in the sixth heaven, Paranirmita-vaśavartin.
When his lifespan in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations is exhausted, he returns to be reborn in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations.
Following this sequence, he descends again as far as the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
When his lifespan in the Four Heavens is exhausted, he ascends once more as far as the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations.
In this manner, they ascend and descend seven times,
being born in the six heavens of the desire realm where they enjoy pleasures at will;
throughout their lives in these six heavens, they do not suffer premature death.
Later, when his life ended, he was reborn among humans;
he left the household life to practice the Way and attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha,
one name of whom was Dharma.
The second was named Śuddhamma.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states:
"Long ago, when the Buddha was in the world..."
There was a bhikṣu reciting a sūtra in a forest;
his voice was elegant and beautiful.
At that time, a bird heard the Dharma and felt reverent affection for it.
While listening while perched in a tree,
he was shot by a hunter and his life ended;
by virtue of this root of goodness, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
His facial features were upright and his radiance was brilliantly manifest,
such that he had no equal;
he possessed the knowledge of his own past lives.
Knowing that he had been born there because he had heard the Dharma while listening to a bhikṣu reciting the sūtras,
he immediately took celestial flowers and went to where the bhikṣu was.
He paid his respects and inquired after [the bhikṣu’s] well-being, making offerings of celestial incense and flowers to the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu questioned him thoroughly and learned the details of the matter.
He immediately commanded him to sit and preached the Dharma for him.
[The man] attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
Having attained this fruit, he returned to the heavens.
If even birds and animals who listen to the Dharma obtain boundless rewards of merit,
how much more so for human beings?
How could those with faith who listen to the Dharma possibly fail to receive a wholesome retribution?
Furthermore, the *Sudarsana-vinaya-śāstra* states:
"In the past, when the Buddha was in the world,
he went to the banks of the Kālaka Pond in the kingdom of Campā."
He was preaching the Dharma to the assembly.
At that time, there was a single frog in that pond who heard the sound of the Buddha preaching the Dharma by the side of the pond.
He immediately emerged from the pond and went beneath the roots of a grassy plant to listen to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.
At that time, there was a man holding a staff who was tending cattle.
Seeing the Buddha seated and preaching the Dharma to the assembly,
he went to where the Buddha was in order to hear the Dharma; thereupon,
he pierced the ground with his staff.
He mistakenly wore the head of a clam and immediately passed away, being reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven by virtue of his karmic reward.
The palace was twelve yojanas in length and breadth;
there he enjoyed himself and took pleasure with the celestial maidens,
and then, mounting the palace, he went to where the Buddha was.
He prostrated at the Buddha's feet.
Knowing this, the Buddha asked:
"Who are you that suddenly pays homage at my feet?"
His supernormal powers, radiance, and marks of excellence were incomparable,
illuminating this entire realm.
The god Śaṅkha then replied with a verse:
In the past, when he had the body of a frog, while seeking food in the water,
he heard the sound of the Buddha preaching the Dharma. Emerging and going beneath the roots of a grass,
he encountered a cowherd who, holding a staff, came there to listen to the Dharma.
A staff and a spear pierced my head; at the end of my life, I was reborn in heaven.
The Buddha, using the verse spoken by the celestial being Śaṅkha, preached the Dharma for the fourfold assembly.
At that time, eighty-four thousand people within the assembly all attained the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpatti),
while the frog-deva attained the fruit of Stream-entry.
He departed with a smile. 4.
The Fourth [Section] on the Conditions for Gradual and Sudden Enlightenment. As stated in the *Sūtra of Hundred Parables*:
"Long ago, there was a village."
Five yojanas from the royal city,
there was a village with excellent and delicious water.
The king issued a command to the villagers.
He constantly required that fine water be sent to him every day;
the villagers grew weary and exhausted,
and all wished to avoid this village and depart from it.
Then the village headman said to the people,
"Do not go. I shall speak to the king on your behalf."
He changed the five yojanas to three yojanas,
so that you might travel back and forth without fatigue;
he then went at once to inform the king.
The King had it reconstructed to three yojanas in size.
When the people heard this, they were filled with great joy.
Someone said: "It is for this reason."

Section Three: Gathering the Mind This section has four parts: the缘 (conditions) for stating the intent, the conditions for the ten recollections, the conditions for the six recollections, and the conditions for making vows. 1. Stating the Intent (Shūì-yì yuán) First, regarding the statement of intent: Alas, the ordinary passions of sentient beings are difficult to restrain.
It is like a mountain monkey that constantly pursues external objects,
resembling a mad elephant.
The three karmas are stirred into motion,
and their conditioned constructions proliferate and manifest;
therefore, the Buddha established the teachings to ensure they are constantly restrained and controlled.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"One should take the mind as one's teacher; one should not take the mind as one's teacher. (That is, one should master the mind rather than being mastered by it.)
The actions of body, speech, and mind do not associate with evil; the precepts of the body and the wisdom of the mind are as immovable as mountains.
Furthermore, when the mind is regulated and focused on a single point, there is no task that cannot be accomplished.
Yet, the nature of the mind is deluded and inverted.
With the view of self as the precursor,
afflictions and delusions are difficult to restrain,
and the turbulent impulses constantly operate.
At all times, they are haughty and difficult to subdue;
unless they rely upon a place of tranquility to crush and overcome the three poisons.
The body does not wander;
the mouth remains silent with words restrained;
one sleeps little and stays awake much.
Always sitting in meditation and restricting one's food,
contemplate the True Dharma and realize that it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Straighten the body and rectify the intention;
bind the mindfulness before you.
Such are these instructions.
This is called the gathering of mindfulness.
Second, the object of ten recollections (*daśasmṛtyupasthāna*). As stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama*:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus.

The fourth is mindfulness of ethical discipline;

By practicing a single dharma, one personally attains nirvana;

Regarding the second, mindfulness of phenomena:

Third is mindfulness of the Saṅgha.

Not being separated from mindfulness of the Saṅgha, one immediately attains merit;

Fifth, mindfulness of generosity (*tyāga-smṛti*) refers to being single-mindedly and diligently mindful of giving.

"One should be mindful that there are five matters."
First, one should contemplate the merit of the Buddha;
second, one should contemplate the sūtras and precepts of the Buddha;
third, one should contemplate the wisdom of the Buddha.
Fourth, one should reflect that the Buddha’s kindness is great and difficult to repay.
Fifth, one should reflect on the Buddha’s diligence until his entry into *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, there are five additional matters.
First, one should be mindful of the Sangha of bhikṣus;
second, one should be mindful of the kindness of one's teachers;
third, one should be mindful of the kindness of one's parents.
Fourth, one should be mindful of the kindness of fellow practitioners.
Fifth, one should be mindful of all people,
wishing that they all attain liberation and be freed from all suffering.

Calamities and blessings all have their predetermined places;

The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

The Buddha said,
"Do not speak such words.
Then another bhikṣu said, "He is about thirty years old."
The Buddha said,
"Do not speak such words.

The Buddha said,

Furthermore, the *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states:
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma should constantly maintain mindfulness,
contemplating that the body is suffering, empty, impermanent, non-self, and impure,
ensuring that this contemplation never ceases.
Why is this? Because one shall attain the twelve recollections that constitute the noble Dharma.
What are these twelve recollections?
First, one thought is to accomplish one's own person;
second, one thought is to accomplish others;
third, one thought is the aspiration to obtain a human body.
Fourth, one should be mindful of being born into a noble family.
Fifth, one should be mindful of gaining faith in the Buddha’s Dharma.
Sixth, one should be mindful of attaining all dharmas in whatever place one is born, without needing to exert effort.
Seventh, may I be born with all faculties complete.
Eighth, may I encounter the appearance of a Buddha, a World-Honored One, in the world.
Ninth, may I always be able to hear the preaching of the True Dharma wherever I am born.
Tenth, I vow that the Dharma he has taught shall always endure for a long time.
Eleventh, I vow that as the Dharma endures for a long time, I may practice in accordance with it.
Twelfth, I vow that I shall always possess a heart of compassion for all sentient beings.
Therefore, by attaining these twelve recollections and being fully endowed with them, one will certainly attain the noble Dharma. 4.
The Fourth Section on the Conditions for Making Vows: Now, the fruit of Buddhahood is remote and transcendent.
To ascend it, there are steps;
the Clouds of Dharma reach the highest pinnacle.
To arrive there, there must be a gradual progression.
Therefore, when great sincerity is first manifested,
the profound virtue illuminates the future; when the vast vow is initially established, [it extends throughout all time].
Thus, the wondrous vows pervade the realm of space;
with a single thought, one gives rise to the auspicious flowers of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.
To devote oneself with reverence for even half a kṣaṇa is nectar for the great trichiliocosm;
it is indeed the very foundation of the Mahāyāna.
It is the gateway to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The vows of a bodhisattva, briefly explained, are of five kinds."
First, the vow of initial resolve;
second, the vow of birth;
third, the vow regarding the objective sphere.
The four equal vows and the five great vows:
that Bodhisattva first gives rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.
This is called the vow of generating the aspiration:
"In future lives, for the sake of sentient beings,
may I be born according to the favorable realms."
This is called the vow of birth, which consists of correctly contemplating all dharmas, immeasurable roots of goodness, and so forth,
and reflecting upon their objective spheres;
this is called the vow of the objective sphere.
May all bodhisattvas in future ages skillfully gather [beings] through their activities;
this is called the bodhisattva’s vow of equality.
The great vow is precisely the vow of equality.
The Bodhisattva further speaks of ten kinds of great vows:
first, the vow to make offerings of every kind to immeasurable Buddhas;
second, the vow to protect and uphold the true Dharma of all Buddhas.
Third, the vow to penetrate the true Dharma of all Buddhas;
fourth, the vow to be born in Tuṣita Heaven and so forth until final parinirvāṇa;
fifth, the vow to practice all modes of correct bodhisattva conduct.
Sixth, the vow to bring all sentient beings to maturity.
Seventh, the vow to be able to manifest emanations in all worlds.
Eighth, the vow that all bodhisattvas, through a single-minded application of skillful means, shall deliver others by means of the Mahāyāna.
Ninth, may all correct practices and skillful means be unimpeded.
Tenth, may I attain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
These are the vows of a bodhisattva dwelling in the first stage.
Through skillful means and pure faith, one practices in the present and gives rise to ten great vows regarding future matters.
First, with a pure mind, one constantly vows to make offerings to all Buddhas.
Second, receiving and upholding the true Dharma of all Buddhas;
third, exhorting all Buddhas to turn the wheel of the unprecedented Dharma;
fourth, practicing the correct conduct of a bodhisattva in accordance with the teachings.
Fifth, the complete maturation of all vessel-worlds;
sixth, the ability to manifest transformations throughout all worlds;
seventh, the purification of one's own buddha-field.
Eighth, all bodhisattvas employ the same skillful means to transform others through the Mahāyāna.
Ninth, their benefit for sentient beings is entirely non-empty.
Tenth, they attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in all worlds and perform all Buddha-works.

(7) Section on Explaining the Intent; and (8) Section on Citing Scriptural Evidence. 1. Explaining the Intent. First, explaining the intent: I humbly consider that all things exist provisionally through causes and conditions.
The deluded faculties of sentient beings perceive that phenomena are inherently so; yet this is not the case.
Such is the subtle principle of the Perfected Person.
Therefore, within the three realms and six destinies,
beings create karmic obstructions and delude themselves;
yet [there exist] the eight liberations and the ten knowledges.

thus, the Great Master Śākyamuni taught according to conditions.
