The Second Section on the Conditions for Rejoicing and Loathing. As stated in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
All merits are not equal to the mind of renunciation. Why is this?
Because there are immeasurable faults and afflictions for one who dwells at home.
Because those who have gone forth possess immeasurable merit, while those who dwell at home face obstacles;
those who have gone forth are free from hindrances,
whereas those who dwell at home abide in a place of dust and defilement.
The one who has gone forth dwells in a place free from dust and defilement;
the one who lives at home is submerged in the mire of desire,
whereas the one who has gone forth emerges from that mire of desire.
Those who live as householders follow the ways of fools;
those who have gone forth distance themselves from the ways of fools.
Those who live as householders do not attain right livelihood.
The one who has gone forth attains right livelihood;
the one who dwells at home is in a place of sorrow, lamentation, and affliction,
whereas the one who has gone forth is in a place of joy.
The householder’s life is a place of bondage;
the life of renunciation is a place of liberation.
The householder’s life is a place of injury.
The life of one who has gone forth is not a state of harm;
for those who dwell at home there is the suffering of craving for gain,
whereas for those who have gone forth there is no suffering of craving for gain.
The householder’s life is a place of clamor and bustle;
the life of renunciation is a place of tranquility.
The householder’s life is a lowly state.
The life of one who has gone forth is a sublime and exalted state;
the householder is consumed by the fires of affliction,
whereas the one who has gone forth extinguishes those fires of affliction.
Those who live at home always act for the sake of others;
those who have gone forth always act for their own sake.
Those who live at home take suffering to be pleasure.
For one who has gone forth, renunciation is happiness;
for one who lives at home, thorns increase.
One who has gone forth is able to extinguish those thorns.
Those who live as householders accomplish minor dharmas;
those who have gone forth from the household life accomplish the Great Dharma.
Those who live as householders have no use for the Dharma.
Those who have left the household life possess the application of the Dharma;
those who dwell at home are disparaged by the followers of the Three Vehicles,
whereas those who have left the household life are praised by the followers of the Three Vehicles.
Those who live at home are never satisfied;
those who have left the home life are always content.
Those who live at home are cherished by Māra.
Those who have left the household life cause terror in Māra;
those who dwell at home are full of negligence,
whereas those who have left the household life are free from negligence.
Those who live at home are servants;
those who have gone forth from home are masters of servants.
Those who live at home dwell in darkness.
The life of one who has gone forth is a state of illumination;
the life of one who dwells at home is a state where pride increases, whereas the life of one who has gone forth is a state where pride is extinguished.
The life of one who dwells at home yields little fruit.
Those who have left the household life possess abundant karmic fruit;
those who dwell at home are full of guile and crookedness;
those who have left the household life are sincere and straightforward in heart.
Those who live at home are constantly beset by sorrow and suffering;
those who have gone forth from the household life always harbor joy and happiness.
Living at home is a deceptive way of life.
The life of one who has gone forth is the Dharma of true tranquility;
those who dwell at home are subject to much distraction,
whereas those who have gone forth are free from distraction.
The householder’s life is a place of saṃsāra;
the life of one who has gone forth is not a place of saṃsāra.
The householder’s life is like a poisonous drug.
The one who has gone forth is like nectar;
the one who dwells at home loses internal reflection,
whereas the one who has gone forth attains internal reflection.
Those who live as householders have no place of refuge;
those who have gone forth have a place of refuge.
Those who live as householders abound in anger.
Those who have left the household life practice compassion extensively;
those who dwell at home carry a heavy burden;
those who have left the household life have cast off that heavy burden.
Those who dwell at home have faults;
those who have gone forth from the household life have no faults.
Those who dwell at home transmigrate through birth and death.
Those who have left the household life have their limits;
those who dwell at home take material wealth as their treasure,
while those who have left the household life take merit as their treasure.
Those who live as householders flow with the current of birth and death;
those who have left the home life go against the current of birth and death.
Those who live as householders are like a great ocean of afflictions.
Those who have gone forth are like a great vessel;
those who dwell at home are bound by entanglements,
whereas those who have gone forth are free from such entanglements.
Those who live at home receive the instructions of kings;
those who have gone forth receive the instructions of the Buddha and the Dharma.
For those who live at home, companions are easy to find.
For one who has gone forth from the household life, it is difficult for companions to remain;
for the householder, injury is predominant,
whereas for the one who has gone forth, gathering [virtue] is predominant.
Those who live at home increase afflictions;
those who go forth leave afflictions behind.
Those who live at home dwell as if in a forest of thorns;
those who have left the home life have emerged from the forest of thorns, Mañjuśrī.
If I were to disparage the life of a householder and praise the life of renunciation,
my words would fill the entirety of space and still not reach their end.
This refers to the faults of living as a householder and the merits of renouncing the household life.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Living at home is constricting, like a prison."
All afflictions arise because of it;
renunciation is vast and expansive like space,
and all wholesome dharmas increase because of it.
Those who live as householders are inwardly anxious for their wives and children,
and outwardly driven by royal service and labor;
if they are wealthy, noble, or high-ranking, they become indulgent and unrestrained in their passions.
Those who are poor, suffering, and lowly are beset by hunger and cold, losing their resolve.
Disturbed by public and private affairs, they toil day and night;
entangled in myriad tasks, what leisure have they to cultivate the Way?
Furthermore, the *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"Householders have many afflictions;
they are bound by the bonds of affection for their parents, wives, and children."
Constantly thinking of wealth and sensual pleasures, one greedily seeks them without satiety;
having acquired little, one must guard it,
resulting in much anxiety and concern.
Wandering through the six realms of existence and turning away from the Buddha-dharma,
one should regard them as enemies and evil associates;
one should cultivate weariness with domestic life and give rise to the mind of renunciation.
There is no way for those living at home to cultivate and accumulate the path to unsurpassed bodhi;
all attain the unsurpassed path by virtue of leaving the home life.
Furthermore, the *Sutra on the Merits of Leaving Home* states:
If one allows men, women, slaves, or commoners to leave the household life,
the merit is immeasurable;
it is like making offerings for a hundred years to as many Arhats as would fill the entire world.
It is not equal to the immeasurable merit of someone who, for the sake of nirvana,
leaves the household life and receives the precepts for a single day and night;
nor is it equal to the merit of erecting a stupa made of the seven precious jewels reaching as high as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
It is not equal to the merit of leaving the household life.
Furthermore, the *Dayuan jing* (Sūtra on Great Causes) says:
"By virtue of leaving the household life for even one day and one night..."
For twenty kalpas, one shall not fall into the three evil realms.
Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"By practicing the holy life as a renunciant for even a single day and night..."
One will be freed from the sufferings of the three miserable realms for six hundred and sixty thousand and sixty years.
Furthermore, the *Chujia Gongde Jing* (Sutra on the Merit of Leaving Home) states:
"If one [aspires] to leave home..."
They laboriously create obstacles and suppress this person,
thereby severing the seed of the Buddha and accumulating all manner of evils within their own bodies, like a vast ocean.
One will presently contract leprosy and,
upon death, enter the Black Darkness Hell (Kālasūtra-naraka) with no prospect of escape.
Furthermore, the Kāśyapa Sūtra states:
At that time, having heard that the merit of leaving the household life was exceedingly profound,
the king’s sons all resolved to renounce the world. Consequently,
among the four continents, there was not a single sentient being remaining at home.
They all resolve their minds and vow to seek renunciation.
Once those sentient beings have left the household life,
there is no need to cultivate that land.
Husked rice appeared spontaneously;
garments grew naturally upon the trees;
and all the devas attended, served, and provided for them.
Furthermore, the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states:
"One should practice the Way with a single mind, following the practice of the Dharma;
do not concern yourself with food or clothing."
Should there be any need,
a single portion from within the Tathāgata’s ūrṇā-kośa (white tuft between the eyebrows) shall provide for all monastic disciples of the final age.
Nor can it be fully exhausted.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* says:
"Suppose there were a hundred blind people and a single skilled physician."
One is able to arrange their eyes so that they see clearly all at once.
Furthermore, there may be a hundred people whose crimes warrant having their eyes gouged out,
yet one person possesses the power to save them from that punishment.
To ensure they do not lose their sight—
though the merit of these two persons is immeasurable—
it still does not equal that of one who listens to [the teaching on] renunciation.
Furthermore, since his own renunciation, his virtue has been vast and great.
3. The Circumstances of Renunciation, Part Three. First, regarding the desire to renounce:
according to the Vinaya, one first requests two preceptors.
First is the *upādhyāya* (preceptor);
second is the *ācārya* (teacher). Regarding the request for the Dharma according to the Vinaya, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"If one first requests an *upādhyāya*..."
When receiving the ten precepts,
if the preceptor (upādhyāya) is not present before one, one does not obtain the ten precepts.
Likewise, if one hears that [the preceptor] has died, the reception of the precepts is not valid.

Section Seven: On Accepting Invitations. This section contains eight topics:

the topic of explaining the intent, the topic of making offerings, the topic of distinguishing the false, the topic of the noble Sangha, the topic of offering food, the topic of the time for eating, the topic of the method of eating, and the topic of having finished eating. 1. Explaining the Intent. First, the Three Jewels are equal.
Vast as empty space,
it is without enmity or kinship;

Without preference for one thing over another,

It reaches its limit with the expanse of space;
acting according to time and following conditions,
it is equal in measure to the dharma-realm.
Since the cause is inexhaustible,
the fruit is likewise endless; thus,
even if one's worldly wealth is meager and poverty imposes strict limitations, one should still practice giving.
Since objects are finite, the mind is likewise narrow and biased;
it may calculate by selecting people for their virtue,
or it may discriminate against the turbid based on their conduct.
Some grasp at appearances to distinguish forms;
others observe countenances to dispel ugliness.
Thus it is according to persons and according to wealth.
A narrow mind is difficult to enlighten;
those with limited merit do not believe,
yet they nonetheless receive a portion of the boundless retribution.
Therefore, in the past, there was the mother of Viśākhā who separately invited five hundred arhats;
the Tathāgata rebuked her for this.
It is better to invite a single ordinary monk according to the monastic order;
one will obtain immeasurable merit.
Thus, one knows that the mind has no limit.
Thus, merit pervades the ten directions;
regardless of whether wealth is much or little,
the mind encompasses the entire Dharma-realm.
2. The Section on the Conditions for Making Offerings (Pūjā-pratyaya). Second:
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, there are briefly ten kinds of offerings that a bodhisattva makes to the Tathāgata.
First, making offerings with one's whole body;
second, making offerings with one's limbs;
third, making offerings in person.
Fourth, worship not performed in person; fifth, worship performed by oneself;
sixth, worship performed by others;
seventh, worship with material goods.
8. The offering of superior excellence; 9. The undefiled offering;
10. The offering of the path leading to the destination.

and the meal at noon during the time of the Dharma.
At dusk is the time for the eating of animals;
at night is the time for the eating of ghosts and spirits.
The Buddha has severed the causes for the six realms of existence.
This causes one to be equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time; therefore, noon is the time for the Dharma-meal.
After this has passed, [one should not eat].
Because it is the same as the lower realms and not the time for superior food,
it is called "improper time.
The *Śāriputra Vinaya* states:
Only a deva may eat past midday without incurring an offense.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"There was a bhikṣu in Jambudvīpa..."
When he arrived in Aparagoyānī,
he used the time reckoned by Jambudvīpa;
the bhikṣus of Aparagoyānī [did likewise].
The same applies to the other three directions.
If one stays in this region, one should use the time of this region.
If one stays overnight there, one uses the time-measure of that particular region;
the same applies to the other three directions.
Therefore, the Mahāvaibhāṣika-śāstra asks:
"Is there any case where eating at an improper time does not constitute an offense?
He replied, "There is.
For example, if one resides in Uttarakuru."
If one uses that food at the proper time, there is no offense;
the same applies in other regions as well,
provided one is in Jambudvīpa.
When it is midday in the south,
it is midnight in the north and sunset in the east.
The sun rises in the west;
the other directions may be understood by applying this logic accordingly.
Furthermore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
There are four periods of release.
First, from sunrise until midday,
its brilliance grows increasingly intense.
This is designated as "time.
From this point until the latter part of the night,
the light diminishes and disappears.
Therefore, it is called "the improper time.
Second, from dawn until midday is the time for preparing food;
begging at this time does not give rise to stinginess.
Therefore, it is called "the time.
From that point onward until the nightfall is the time for the gatherings,
feasts, and diversions of worldly people.
When entering a village to beg for alms,
there is much physical contact and provocation;
therefore, it is called "improper time."
Third, from dawn until midday,
when laypeople are engaged in their work and sexual misconduct has not yet arisen,
one should beg so as not to cause them distress.
Therefore it is called "time.
From that point onward, all affairs are brought to rest,
as are amorous play, speech, and laughter.
Entering a village to beg for alms, one is prone to being slandered;
therefore, it is called "improper time.
Fourth, from dawn until midday.
This is the time for alms-seeking;
having obtained food to sustain the body,
one may settle the mind and cultivate the Way.
Because the matter accords with the Dharma,
it is called "the proper time.
From this point onward...
One should rely on the path of cultivation;
since it is not the time for alms-seeking,
it is therefore called "non-time."
7. The Conditions for the Method of Eating. Regarding the seventh section on the conditions for the method of eating, as stated in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*:
"When a bhikṣu wishes to eat, he should burn incense and perform three *bhaiṣajya* chants for the sake of the donor (*dānapati*)."
He praised the offering of delicious food fit for consumption.
Furthermore, following the instructions of the Elder,
each of the practitioners emerged from their quarters, washed their hands, and rinsed their mouths.
They each returned to their seats and sat down;
each spoke a verse and then rose in turn according to the sequence.
One must not overstep [this rule].
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"If there is one who makes offerings..."
Holding a censer in his hand, he proclaimed, "The time has come.
The Buddha said,
"Incense is the messenger of the Buddha."
Therefore, one must burn incense to universally invite [the Buddhas] of the ten directions.

Since it is known that burning incense is originally intended to invite the Buddhas, yet ordinary beings, being obstructed by their own vision, do not perceive them, the Buddha commanded that incense be burned to universally invite all ordinary and saintly beings of the ten directions, so that they may manifest for the presentation of meritorious matters and arrive everywhere from the void. When performing the formal practice of burning incense and chanting *geya*, all monastics and laypeople recite one verse each according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, saying:

The fragrance of precepts, the fragrance of meditative concentration, and the fragrance of liberation—clouds of radiant light pervade the world to make offerings to the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions;
those who see or hear them are universally perfumed and realize quiescent extinction.
Furthermore, the *Sānqiānwēiyí jīng* (Sūtra on the Three Thousand Dignified Manners) says:
One may also receive incense while seated when offering it to women; this is permitted because one fears that the incense might soil the hands through contact.

Alternatively, if there is concern regarding public censure or disrespect, one may hold the incense aloft and let it hang down. When men offer incense and women receive it, the procedure is the reverse of the above. Thus it is stated.
If one obtains food and clothing without discriminating between the refined and the coarse,
but simply gains enough to sustain the body and life so as to be able to practice the Way,
this accords with the Buddha’s intention, just as a cart requires oil for its lubrication.
What need is there for refined subtlety? It is already an excellent matter if one can simply ensure that the movement reaches its intended destination.
Thus, the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* states:
The World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"This body is like a chariot; It makes no distinction between the fine and the foul.
Whether it be fragrant oil or stinking fat, They are all equally used for its maintenance."
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Food is for the sake of practicing the Path, not for the sake of benefiting the body;
it is no different from feeding a horse or a pig."
When first obtaining food, one should first offer it to the Triple Gem and subsequently bestow it upon the four classes of sentient beings.
Thus, a verse in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
When obtaining food, one should wish that all sentient beings set their will upon the Buddha-way as an offering of the Dharma.
Furthermore, the Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra says:
"If one personally makes clothing, bowls, or utensils..."
First offer it to the Buddha,
and let one's parents, teachers, elders, and preceptors be the first to enjoy it;
only then should one consume it oneself.
If one offers these to the Buddha, one should redeem them with flowers and incense; as for all that is consumed and eaten [by the Buddha],
[one should likewise offer such things].
One must first give to śramaṇas and brahmins,
and only then eat oneself.
Furthermore, at the very moment of taking the food down, one must form this thought:
When first setting down the first spoonful,
may I vow to sever all evil completely.
When setting down the second spoonful, may I...
I vow that all cultivated roots of goodness may be fulfilled.
When taking the third spoonful below,
[dedicate] the roots of goodness thus cultivated.
Dedicate this to all sentient beings so that they may together attain Buddhahood.
If you are unable to bring this to mind with every morsel,
then when you are about to eat:
It is also permissible to perform this as a single collective recollection.
Thus, the *Madhyamāgama-śāstra* states:
"When receiving food, one should perform the recollection for every morsel."
When obtaining a robe, one should maintain mindfulness at every step;
when entering the room, one should maintain mindfulness at every entry.
For those of dull faculties, they may maintain this as a single, continuous mindfulness.
Therefore, in the sixth fascicle of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
it is stated that a bodhisattva has one hundred and forty vows;
in all their actions, they recite these verses and maintain mindfulness of them.
One who eats in this manner neither possesses afflictions nor is free from afflictions; thus,
principle and phenomena are harmoniously integrated.
It is for the sake of benefiting sentient beings that the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Among all forms of giving, none is superior to the gift of the Dharma."
Among all karmas, none is superior to the karma of the Dharma;
among all acts of kindness, none is superior to the kindness of the Dharma.
If one eats to excess, [it is not true nourishment].
Consequently, the breath will become labored, the body will feel full, and the hundred vessels will be obstructed.
This will cause the mind to become congested, such that one cannot sit in meditation with peace of mind.
If, however, one limits the portions of food consumed, [the situation will improve].
Consequently, the body becomes emaciated and the mind remains in a state of anxious suspension; the vital energy is depleted and lacks stability.
Thus, a verse from the *Ekottarika Āgama* says:
Eating too much leads to suffering; eating too little causes the decline of one’s strength.
One who eats with moderation is like a scale that is neither high nor low.
As stated in the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-putra-sūtra* verse:
For one who eats to excess, the body becomes heavy and slothful;
in both the present and future lives, they lose great benefit for their own person and suffer through sleep, while also causing distress to others.
Confused and distressed, one finds it difficult to wake or sleep. At that time, one should measure out the food;
furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If the person on monthly duty is supervising the food..."

If one wishes to know whether food is raw or cooked, salty or sour, it may be held in the palm and tasted with the tongue; however, the *Cai Fa Jing* (Sutra on the Rules for the Uposatha) prohibits tasting with the mouth, as doing so constitutes an offense due to a lack of pure intention and the presence of a greedy mind.
The commentary states:
Therefore, when those who have left the household life wish to eat, [they must first...]
First, one who receives [food] from another with clean hands is considered superior among those who have left the household life,
for they differ from the common masses.
One must receive [the food] before eating it;
therefore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states that a bhikṣu receives the food.

There are five reasons for this: first, to sever the causes and conditions for theft; if one were to take food for oneself, it would be considered equivalent to the intent of stealing. Second, to serve as a witness; should there be any loss or disappearance, it would not implicate the bhikṣu. Third, to stop slander; to claim that taking food for oneself after leaving the household life is a mark of high excellence is not the case. Fourth, to fulfill the principles of few desires and contentment; if one were not to accept [the food], it would not be consistent with frugality and simplicity. Fifth, to inspire faith and reverence in others; seeing him accept and eat, non-Buddhists will develop faith, just as there was once a bhikṣu in the past.
He was staying together with some non-Buddhists under a tree.
It was nearly time for the meal, and there were fruits upon the tree.
A non-Buddhist said to the bhikṣu,
"Climb the tree and take some fruit.
The bhikṣu replied.
"In my Dharma of the precepts,
one should not climb trees higher than a person.
He further addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Why do you not shake the tree to take the fruit?
The bhikṣu replied,
"In my system of precepts..."
"One must not shake a tree oneself to make the fruit fall.
Having heard this, the non-Buddhists climbed the trees themselves to gather the fruit.
He threw it to the ground and gave it to him,
saying to the bhikṣu,
"Take this fruit and eat."
The bhikṣu said,
"In my system of precepts,
one must not eat without having first received [the food]."
The non-Buddhist practitioner climbed down from the tree, took some fruit,
and offered it to the bhikṣu.
Having witnessed this, the non-Buddhist practitioner [reflected].
If such a functional efficacy exists even for a single mundane fruit,
how much more so for the supramundane Dharma? Thereupon,
the non-Buddhists gave rise to a mind of faith and reverence.
Realizing that the Buddha-dharma is pure and distinct from that of the non-Buddhists,
he then followed the bhikṣus and left the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma.
He then attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Furthermore, the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states that the Buddha said:
Even the non-Buddhist brahmins know how to accept and take [offerings];
how much more so should my disciples not refuse food?
However, it is not that all things must be accepted without exception.
Except for those born with jewels and women;
even so, one who performs the ritual should still bestow upon them the garment worn on their body.
If it is a vessel for storing gold, one may accept it,
provided that its acceptance restricts further giving.
The commentary states:
All food for the Saṃgha must be distributed equally;
regardless of whether one is ordinary or a sage, superior or inferior, it must be shared universally and impartially.
Thus, the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya states:
If a donor provides a large amount of food and gives it all to the senior monk (upādhyāya),
the senior monk should ask:
"Will the entire Sangha receive this same amount?"
Answer: Only the Elder Upasena received them.
One should say that they were given equally to all.
If one says that everyone received them, [it would be incorrect].
One should receive [the food] according to the Dharma of the Sangha's Elder;
one must not eat as soon as it reaches those of lower rank.
After waiting for the universal chanting and other offerings to be completed,
one may then receive food;
this is the rule for the Elder (Upādhyāya).
One should eat slowly;
one must not finish eating quickly and then depart first,
but should instead wait for the water-offering.
Having offered the prayers of auspiciousness in accordance with the occasion, he then departed.
Furthermore, various sutras state:
The Buddha said,
"There are five blessings in not eating after midday."
First, having little sexual desire;
second, sleeping little;
third, attaining single-mindedness.
Fourth, there is no downward wind.
Fifth, the body attains tranquility and does not fall ill.
Therefore, the śramaṇa knows the nature of blessings and does not eat.
The commentary states:
If one harbors excessive greed for food, [one will suffer].
If afflictions increase,
one must contemplate with revulsion and form the perception of impurity.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
Regarding the teaching on the perception of revulsion:
one should contemplate that this food arises from impurity,
just as flesh arises from semen, blood, and the urinary tract.
This is the dwelling place of pus-worms;
it is formed from the transformation of ghee, milk, curd, and blood,
and is no different from putrid pus.
The kitchen is defiled by various kinds of filth;
if this enters the mouth,
there is putrid saliva within the brain that flows down through two channels.
Only after combining with saliva does it become flavor;
its appearance is like vomit,
and it enters through the gate of the abdomen.
The earth supports them while water rots them;
wind agitates them and fire boils them,
like porridge being cooked in a cauldron.
The dregs and turbidity sink to the bottom,
while the clear portion remains above;
it is like the process of brewing wine.
The turbid dregs become excrement;
the clear portion becomes urine.
The throat has three openings.
The wind blows the oily essence,
dispersing it into the hundred vessels where it blends with the pre-existing blood.
The congealed transformation becomes flesh;
from the new flesh, fat and marrow arise;
from within this, the body faculty (kāyendriya) is produced.
From the union of new and old flesh,
the five sense organs arise;
from these five organs, the five consciousnesses arise.
Following the five consciousnesses, the mental consciousness arises;
it discriminates and grasps characteristics, deliberating upon what is beautiful and ugly,
and subsequently gives rise to thoughts such as "I" and "mine."
All afflictions and all sinful karmas.
Furthermore, one should reflect that the labor expended to produce this food is exceedingly great.
He calculated that for a single bowl of rice,
his laborers had sweated until they were exhausted;
he then gathered them together to measure the amount.
One eats little yet perspires profusely;
such is the bitterness of this food that it becomes impure as soon as it enters the mouth.
Within a single night, it transforms into excrement and urine;
what was once a delicious food becomes something so loathsome that one does not even wish to look upon it.
The practitioner reflects to himself:
"If I were to become greedily attached to such inferior food as this..."
One should contemplate food in this way when about to fall into the three miserable realms,
and one should cultivate revulsion for the five desires. For example, there was once a certain brāhmaṇa.
While practicing the dharma of purity, due to certain circumstances,
he arrived in an impure land and thought to himself: "How may I avoid this impurity?"
"One may attain purity only by eating dry food.
He saw an old woman selling cakes of white marrow.
And he said to him:
"I have certain causes and conditions for staying here for one hundred days."
She would regularly prepare cakes and bring them,
giving him a high price for them. Thus,
the old mother prepared cakes every day and sent them to him.
The brahmin was greedily attached to eating his fill and rejoiced.
The old woman made cakes;
at first, they were pure white.
Later, when it had turned colorless and tasteless,
he asked the old woman,
"For what reason has this happened?"
The mother said,
"Because the abscess has healed.
The brahmin asked.
"What does this mean? [He asked.
His mother said, "I am the lady of our great household."
A boil arose in a private part; he treated it by applying flour and ghee.
When the boil had ripened and the pus was discharged, he mixed the ingredients to make a ghee-cake.
Day after day it was thus.
Because I made this cake for you, the cake was excellent.
Now, the lady's abscess has healed.
"Where else shall I obtain it?
When the Brahmin heard this,
he struck his head twice with both hands.
Beating my breast and dry-heaving, I thought: "What shall I do?
I have violated this pure Dharma."
I have finished my business;
having abandoned the matter at hand, I shall hasten back to my native land.
The practitioner is likewise.
Attached to these foods and drinks,
they joyfully delight in eating them without contemplating their impurity;
later, when they receive the retribution of suffering, what can they do to remedy their regret?
8. The Circumstances Regarding the Completion of the Meal. The eighth circumstance regarding the completion of the meal is as stated in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*:
"There was a bhikṣu who, having accepted an invitation for a meal, entered [the donor's house] in silence and departed in silence."
The laypeople rebuked them, saying,
"We do not know whether the food was good or not.
The bhikṣus then informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, during mealtime,
you shall perform *bhāṣaṇa* and offer prayers of blessing for the sake of the donors."
It was not known who had made it.
The Buddha said,
"The Elder made it."
If the Elder is unable, one who is capable according to the order of seniority should be appointed to perform it.
Thus, the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya says:
Venerable Elder, you should know:
for whatever kind of gift the person before you has given,
you should offer a timely blessing accordingly.
Furthermore, the *Upāliparipṛcchā* states:
"When monastics— whether monks or nuns— and laypeople have finished their midday meal,
they should not use powdered soap beans (*yavakṣāra*), *goma*, or similar substances to wash their mouths."
In all such cases, the fast is not accomplished.
For example, in the past there was a bhikṣu named Liandi who observed the fast and precepts for sixty years without fail.
One may observe the fast using only large quantities of bean flour and the like for daily consumption;
if one does not do so, the fast is not accomplished at all.
This scripture lacks clarity on this point.
According to the *Chuyao lüyi* (The Vinaya of Essential Liberation), "gomaya" refers to cow dung.
If one follows this sutra, would one then use cow dung to purify the mouth?
The *Sheshi Fashi Zhuanji* (Biographies of the Dharma Master Sheṣa) states:
"Among the laypeople and non-Buddhists of the West,
they take Brahmā, the ox, and others as their objects of devotion."
By means of these two matters,
they are able to produce all things and nourish the people;
therefore, one uses cow dung to purify the site of practice (maṇḍala).
The Buddha also adopted purity according to worldly conventions;
however, he did not employ the purification of the mouth.
This is as stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and other texts.
One merely maintains the four modes of deportment— walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—
and partakes of the five kinds of formal food;
provided that these four characteristics are not violated, the dharma of the fast (upoṣadha) is accomplished.
Regardless of whether one cleanses the mouth with cleansing powder (zǎodòu) to fulfill the requirements for the fast,
if the prescribed time has passed or if one’s deportment (wēiyí) has been lost,
then even if one uses cleansing powder, the fast is not accomplished.
Furthermore, the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"If, after having finished the fast,
one has vomited food that has not yet passed the throat, swallowing it again constitutes no offense."
If one spits it out and swallows it again, one commits an offense.
Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If, after having finished eating, one becomes thirsty..."
The Buddha permitted that all grains, beans, and wheat be boiled;
if they have not been broken, one may take the juice at improper times and drink it.
This also applies to ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar.
Various fruit juices and the like must be purified with water before they may be drunk;
if the residual water remaining at the bottom of the vessel has been washed away by rain, it is likewise acceptable.
It is also called "pure.
The *Śāsanodbhāvana-śāstra* states:
"The juice of the śaluka fruit."
Clarifying the liquid makes it pure.
It may be drunk at improper times; this refers to lotus-root juice. The *Mahādeva-lakṣaṇa-śāstra* states:
"Sugar-cane syrup."
It may also be drunk at improper times.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"A person has four hundred and four illnesses."
There are one hundred and one [afflictions] caused by the wind element;
they are treated with medicinal oils.
There are one hundred and one fevers caused by the fire element.
Treat it with ghee for the one hundred and one diseases caused by excessive cold water;
treat it with honey.
There are one hundred and one miscellaneous ailments;
treat them according to the application of the three aforementioned medicines.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
Stone honey (śarkarā) must not be consumed at improper times (vikāla).
There are five types of persons who may consume food at improper times:
namely, those traveling on a long journey.
A sick person,
a person who eats little,
or a place where water is distributed.
It may be drunk after being mixed with water.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"It is permitted to drink during the two times of hunger and thirst. From this, one knows that for those who are not ill, even if it is rock honey, ghee, oil, or the like, it must not be consumed at an improper time (*akāla*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
Black pepper, long pepper, ginger, and *harītakī*—
these medicines may be consumed at any time.
The *Andhaka-vinaya* permits the wearing of [robes] at improper times.
Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"All bitter, pungent, salty, and sweet [substances]."
Those that cannot be used as food are permitted to be taken as medicine at non-proper times for the rest of one's life.
The *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*) states:
All trees, as well as their fruits, roots, trunks, branches, leaves, and so forth,
are not fit to be used as food.
All may be prepared as medicines to be taken for the duration of one's life.
Shu said: "Recently, I have observed that various people..."
To eat at the proper time during a time that is not the proper time— what is this?
This refers to monastics and laypeople in frontier regions who,
upon hearing that the Vinaya permits the consumption of fruit juice and syrups,
proceeded to consume the juice of dried dates.
Or one may eat pears, grapes, and pomegranates;
one may drink their juice without crushing them, or consume the fruit along with the seeds.
Even when the juice is crushed, [it is permissible].
It was not that he made the turbid clear;
rather, he took the thick, turbid juice along with the dregs and ate them.
Some have heard it said that he permitted the consumption of *śaluka* fruit juice.
Suffering from a feverish illness,
he then took fresh lotus roots and ate them raw;
or some took clear rice-gruel to drink.
Alternatively, his body may be free from hunger and thirst;
he may consume ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, and so forth at inappropriate times,
or use a thick broth made by boiling almonds.
Such instances of confusion are not limited to these alone and cannot be recounted in full.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, this does not apply to the aforementioned five types of persons, such as those who have traveled a long distance.
One must not eat indiscriminately;
eating [at improper times] breaks the fast.
Those seen violating this rule are many.
Therefore, the verse in the *Bie shuji* says:
"In this month, he observes a pure fast; on this auspicious day, he summons those who are invincible.
The four assemblies gather according to the time; the seven groups of disciples assemble in the hall."
In the desolate stillness, the pure *brahman*-chant rises; Its mournful, elegant tones move through the *gong* and *shang* registers.
Fragrance ascends into the void, Riding the wind to disperse across distant lands.
One sighs in admiration of virtue, investigating its profound depths; The eloquence of the words unfolds the sublime fragrance.
Discarding the mundane, you present wondrous verses; Adapting to the moment, you compose elegant chapters.
The ordained and the laity rely upon you; Through wealth and Dharma, you radiate divine light.
May the field of merit be fulfilled this evening; May your grace and wisdom guide both the living and the deceased.

8. Section on Receiving the Upavāsa Vow (Upavāsopasampadā-varga), the Eighth. This has three sections: Section on Breaking the Vow, the Ninth; Section on Wealth and Nobility, the Tenth;

and Section on Poverty and Low Status, the Eleventh. [The following consists of: The Section on Stating the Intent (Abhiprāya-nirdeśa-varga) and the Section on Citing Scriptural Evidence (Āgama-saṃgraha-varga). 1. The Section on Stating the Intent (Abhiprāya-nirdeśa-varga), the First. Regarding the reason why the True Dharma (Saddharma) is disseminated:
The value lies in honoring the scriptures;
thus the field of merit increases. This achievement stems from the practice of fasting and precepts.
Therefore, by relinquishing the offering of a single meal,
one’s merit continues through surplus grain;
by bestowing the provision of a single coin, one’s blessings endure.
The resulting fruit surpasses celestial retribution;
therefore, the field of merit may be esteemed as weighty,
while the accumulation of wealth may be regarded as light.
Together establish an unrestricted assembly (*anavadya-pariṣad*), equally inviting limitless merit. 2.
Citation of Sources, Part Two. Furthermore, the *Old Miscellaneous Parable Sūtra* (*Jiu za piyu jing*) says:
In the past, when the Buddha was invited for a meal by four castes,
there was a man selling cow's milk whom one of the great clans detained to provide him with food.
She instructed him to observe the fast and precepts,
and after he had received and listened to the sutra, he returned home.
His wife said:
While we were waiting for each other before eating,
he forcibly made his husband eat,
thereby destroying his intention to observe the fast.
"Even so, he will be reborn seven times in the heavens and seven times in the human world," the Master said.
If one observes the fast for a single day,
there will be more than six hundred thousand years' worth of surplus grain;
furthermore, there are five blessings.
First, having little illness;
second, physical well-being and tranquility;
third, having little lustful intent.
Fourth, one sleeps little;
fifth, one is reborn in the heavens and constantly remembers the deeds performed in previous lives.
Furthermore, King Prasenajit wished to reward Queen Mallikā with a fragrant necklace;
he summoned her out of the palace to view it.
On the day of the fast, the lady dressed in plain garments and went forth;
among the sixty thousand ladies,
she was as radiant as the sun and the moon.

Preface: Regarding the first section, the Preface, on the intent of the discourse: Now, as for the revolving of the three realms, it is as follows.
One drifts like a duckweed through the six realms of existence;
yet the divine spirit is imperishable,
while consciousness and deliberation remain obscure and vast.
In the moments of dying and being born,
coming and going, one casts aside the grass of body and life.
It is difficult to deliberate upon this;

and its mountains are nothing other than the dust of my own past.
The currents of the vast blue seas are all the same as my tears and blood;

Who is not a kinsman or friend?
Though humans and ghosts differ,

The sentiments of affection and love occasionally manifest like shadows and echoes;

Failing to distinguish between kin and stranger,

They slaughter and dismember one another,
acting as mutual enemies; thus they harbor enmity toward each other throughout successive kalpas.
The retribution of suffering is difficult to exhaust.
Reflecting quietly on this matter,
how could it not cause one’s heart to ache?

the Buddha said that their wickedness and flattery are even greater than those of men.

Such deceptive illusions are ultimately difficult to describe in full;
ordinary beings remain deluded and intoxicated by them.

It is like a treacherous thief who employs all manner of deceptions;

It is like a high net that causes flocks of birds to fall;

domestic discord likewise stems from women.

sentient beings are thus.

it enables sentient beings to carry heavy burdens as they act;
and it enables sentient beings to shoulder heavy burdens as they travel everywhere.
Because it causes sentient beings to feel anxiety and weariness regarding this heavy burden;
because it causes sentient beings to be tormented and oppressed by this heavy burden;
and because it causes sentient beings to be harmed by this heavy burden.
Śāriputra, for what further reason is she called "wife"?
What is called a "wife" is the place where all sentient beings entrust themselves;
it is the place where those enslaved by craving and attachment are swept away and submerged.
This is the place where the compliant wife pays her tax;
this is the place where the charming wife offers her allure.
The place where one is deluded;
this woman is the supreme one;
the place to which one should take refuge.
This woman who has been humiliated is the one upon whom he relies;
she is the one who holds power over him.
It is a state of negligence;
it is being a slave to a wife;
it is a place of exhaustion and suffering.
Śāriputra, as for those who follow their wives,
wherever they turn their gaze and incline their hearts, [they follow].
For these and other such reasons, these various locations are called "wives.
It is by means of them that one is designated as having a wife.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying,
"There are three kinds of seeds."
What are the three? There is the son who conforms [to his father],
and there is the son who excels [his father].
There is the "inferior son.
What is the "conforming son"?
It refers to the son of one's parents.
Do not kill; do not steal;
do not engage in sexual misconduct; do not speak falsely;
and do not drink intoxicants.
The child also follows in learning non-killing and so forth;
this is called the "child born in accordance.
What is the "superior child born"?
If the parents do not undertake the precepts such as non-killing,
but the child is able to undertake them,
this is called a "superior son."
What is meant by "begetting a son of inferior birth"?
It refers to a case where the parents do not undertake the precepts of non-killing and so forth,
and the son likewise is unable to undertake the precepts of non-killing and so forth.
This is called "the son born of a name.
7. The Seventh Chapter on Exhortation: As stated in the Madhyama Āgama, at that time there was a horse trainer.
His name was Kiṃśuka.
He approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
and withdrew to sit to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
I observe that this world is exceedingly trivial and shallow."
It is like a herd of horses;
in this world, I alone am capable of taming wild and unruly horses.
I shall employ skillful means so that,
in an instant, all their afflictions of pride may manifest; then,
according to those afflictions, I will tame them through skillful means.
The Buddha said to the horse trainer,
"Village headman,
by how many kinds of skillful means do you train and subdue horses?"
The horse trainer said to the Buddha,
"There are three methods for taming a wicked horse."
What are the three? First, softness;
second, coarseness.
"Third, they may be supple or coarse and rough.
The Buddha said to the village headman,
"You train horses by means of these three methods."
"If there are those who remain untamed, what should be done with them?
The horse trainer addressed the Buddha.
If they still do not become disciplined, one must then kill them. Why is this?
"Do not let him bring me to shame.
The horse trainer said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One," and added:
"This is the Unsurpassed Tamer of Men.
By how many kinds of skillful means does he tame men?
The Buddha told the village headman:
I also discipline men of noble character through three kinds of skillful means. What are these three?
The first is being consistently gentle.
Second, those that are exclusively coarse and rough;
third, those that are both soft and coarse.
The Buddha told the village headman:
As for what you have called "exclusively gentle," this refers to what you described as virtuous conduct of the body.
This is the retribution for wholesome conduct of body;
this is wholesome conduct of speech and mind;
this is the retribution for wholesome conduct of speech and mind.
These are called devas;
these are called humans;
these are called those born by transformation in the happy realms.
This is called nirvāṇa;
this is what is meant by "gentle.
As for the second, which is exclusively coarse and harsh:
It is as you have said:
this is bodily misconduct,
and this is the retribution for bodily misconduct.
These are the evil deeds of speech and mind;
these are the retributions for the evil deeds of speech and mind; this is called hell.
These are called animals;
these are called hungry ghosts;
these are called evil destinies.
This is called falling into the evil destinies;
this is called the Tathāgata’s harsh teaching.
Third is that which is both gentle and harsh.
That is to say, at times the Tathāgata speaks of wholesome conduct of body;
at times he speaks of the retribution of wholesome conduct of body;
and at times he speaks of wholesome conduct of speech and mind.
At times, he speaks of the retribution for wholesome verbal and mental conduct;
at times, he speaks of unwholesome bodily conduct;
and at times, he speaks of the retribution for unwholesome bodily conduct.
Sometimes it speaks of the unwholesome conduct of speech and mind;
sometimes it speaks of the retribution for the unwholesome conduct of speech and mind.
Such is called "heaven."
Thus one is called a "person.
Thus one is called a "fortunate destination.
Thus one is called "nirvāṇa."
Thus are named the hells;
thus are named the animals and hungry ghosts;
thus are named the evil destinies.
Thus they are said to fall into the evil destinies;
this is called the Tathāgata’s teaching that is both gentle and harsh.
The horse trainer addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
if one were to tame sentient beings by means of three kinds of skillful methods.
"If there are those who are not disciplined, what should be done with them?
The Buddha told the village headman:
"You should also kill him.
Why? So that he does not bring disgrace upon me."
The horse trainer said to the Buddha,
"If one kills a living being,
it is considered impure within the Dharma of the World-Honored One."
"In the Dharma of the World-Honored One, one does not kill living beings.
Yet now you speak of killing;
what is the meaning of this?"
The Buddha told the village headman:
"In the Dharma of the Tathāgata, one likewise does not kill living beings.
However, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata..."
By means of these three kinds of instruction,
those who are not disciplined are no longer spoken to, nor taught, nor admonished.
"Is this not death?
The horse trainer said to the Buddha,
"It is indeed so, World-Honored One."
No longer conversing with them, and never again instructing or admonishing them—
this is truly death.
"For this reason, from this day forward,
I shall abandon all evil and unwholesome deeds.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, he departed with joy.
Furthermore, the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra* states:
The Buddha asked an elephant trainer,
"How many methods are there for training an elephant?"
He replied:
"There are three.
What are these three?"
First, they use a rigid hook with a curved mouth to pierce through their noses and yoke them.
Second, they reduce their food so that they are constantly hungry and emaciated.
Third, they strike them with whips, inflicting upon them agonizing pain.
Because their mouths are hooked with iron hooks,
their powerful jaws are restrained;
because they are not given food or drink.
One restrains the wildness of the body by means of applying the cane and staff;
one subdues the mind thereby.
The Buddha told the householder:
"I too have three [methods] by which I discipline all beings."
One also attains self-discipline and reaches the unconditioned through the first [method]: by means of sincerity.
First, he controls afflictions of the mouth;
second, because he is compassionate and chaste,
he subdues the rigidity of his body.
Third, by means of wisdom, one extinguishes the veil of delusion regarding the mind.
One upholds these three matters.
They deliver all beings, causing them to leave the three evil realms.
Furthermore, the *Yanluowang Wushi jing* (Sūtra on the Five Messengers of King Yama) states:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
Living in this world,
one fails to be filial toward one's parents and fails to show reverence toward śramaṇas.
Those who do not practice benevolence and righteousness,
do not study the scriptures and precepts,
and do not fear the future life.
When that person dies, they shall fall into hell.
The wardens take them away and report it to King Yama.
One speaks of their transgressions and evils,
saying that this person is unfilial and possesses all manner of faults.
Lacking merit, he does not fear death;
only the king shall receive the punishment.
King Yama always first remains calm and composed, and with upright speech,
manifests the five messengers and asks:
"First, did you not see?"
When people first become infants,
they lie helplessly in excrement and urine, unable to protect themselves;
their mouths do not yet know how to speak, nor do they distinguish between what is good and what is evil.
"Did you see it? The man replied, "I saw it.
The king said:
You may say for yourself that it is not so; yet,
since the human spirit proceeds from that [state],
there will ultimately be birth.
Although you have not yet seen [the results],
you should always do good and rectify your three karmas;
how can you let your mind run wild and your will be unrestrained, thereby committing transgressions?
The sinner replied,
"I was ignorant and did not know.
The King said:
"You are yourself foolish and negligent in committing evil;
it is not the fault of your parents, teachers, rulers, devas, śramaṇas, or practitioners."
"I forgive you your transgressions;
how could you not rejoice? You shall now receive [the fruits of your deeds].
This was the first divine messenger manifested by King Yama.
The second King Yama asked again:
"When you were a human being,
the celestial messengers arrived in succession."
"Are you able to perceive it?
The man replied, "I do not perceive it.
The king said:
Do you not see that among worldly people, when they grow old, their hair turns white and their teeth fall out;
they become emaciated and hunched, walking with a stoop,
and are unable to rise or sit down without the aid of a staff?
The man replied, "It is so.
The King said,
"Do you think that you alone can obtain exemption from aging?"
Once a person has been born,
all phenomena are subject to aging and decay;
one should always do good, rectify one's body, speech, and mind, and practice the sutras and precepts.
"How can you act so wantonly?
The person replied,
"It is because of my ignorance."
The King said:
"It was you yourself who committed evil out of ignorance;
it was not the fault of your parents, your sovereign, the gods, the śramaṇas, or the practitioners."
"I forgive you your transgressions;
how could you not rejoice? You shall now receive [the fruits of your merit].
This was the second divine messenger manifested by King Yama.
The third King Yama asked again:
"When you were a human being,
did you not see the men and women of the world?"
The body is afflicted with disease;
the physical frame suffers from pain;
one finds no peace in sitting or rising.
"Life is near its end and urgent with anxiety;
will the many physicians not treat it?
The person replied, "There are."
The King said,
"Can you avoid being ill? Once a person has grown old,
it is the nature of things that they shall fall ill."
Hearing that your body is strong and healthy,
you ought to strive to do good, practice the sutras and precepts, and rectify your body, speech, and mind.
How can you allow yourself such indulgence?
The man replied,
"It is because of my ignorance and darkness.
The king said:
"You consider yourself foolish for committing evil;
it is not the fault of your parents, your sovereign, the gods, śramaṇas, or practitioners.
The transgression is entirely your own."
"How could one not rejoice? One must now accept this.
This was the third divine messenger manifested by King Yama.
The fourth time, King Yama asked again:
When you were a human being,
did you not see those in the world who had died,
their corpses being hidden away?
Or they may abandon it;
by the seventh day, the flesh and muscles have rotted away,
and foxes, wildcats, and hundreds of birds all come to feed upon it.
When ordinary people have died,
their bodies become foul and rot;
do you not see this?
The man replied, "I have.
The king said,
"Do you think that by claiming this alone, you can avoid death?"
All beings who have been born must die;
this is heard throughout the world.
Constantly perform good deeds;
discipline your body, speech, and mind to practice the sutras and precepts.
How can you allow yourself such license?
The man replied,
"It is because of my ignorance and delusion.
The king said:
"You have committed evil yourself;
it is not the fault of your parents, your sovereign, the gods, śramaṇas, or practitioners of the Way.
Your transgression arises solely from you."
"How could you not find joy? You must accept this.
This was the fourth divine messenger manifested by King Yama.
The fifth, King Yama, asked again:
When you were a person in the world,
did you not see those wicked men and evil sons who were apprehended by the officials?
They were taken to the offices of the magistrates;
punishments according to the penal code were inflicted upon them,
such as the severing of hands and feet.
Some have their ears and noses cut off;
some have their bodies burned;
others have their heads suspended and scorched by the sun.
"Or being slaughtered, dismembered,
and subjected to various kinds of poisonous pain?
The person replied, "Yes."
The king said:
"Do you believe that one who commits evil can escape alone?
The eyes clearly behold the distinctions between sin and merit in this world."
"Why do you not maintain goodness and discipline your body, speech, and mind to practice the sutras and precepts?
When asked, the person replied, "I am foolish and ignorant;
that is why I act thus."
The king said,
"It was you yourself who acted with a lack of loyalty and integrity;
this is not the fault of your parents, your sovereign, the gods, the śramaṇas, or the practitioners."
"Now these calamities and sins must be experienced by oneself.
This is the fifth divine messenger manifested by King Yama. After the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, [the assembly rejoiced and practiced accordingly].
All the disciples received these instructions and admonitions;
each stepped forward and paid their respects.
Rejoicing, they shall practice accordingly.
Furthermore, a verse from the *Mahādhammapada-sūtra* says:
"Though one may recite a thousand words, If one does not practice them, what benefit is there? It is better to hear but one [verse]..."
Diligent cultivation brings benefit: though one may recite a thousand words, if the phrasing and meaning are incorrect, they are not worth even a single essential point.
Hearing that which can extinguish the mind is superior; though one may recite a thousand words of no principle, what benefit is there?
It is not worth even a single principle. By hearing and practicing, one attains liberation.
Though one may recite a thousand words, what benefit is there if one lacks respect? It is better to practice with joyful devotion even a single line.
Though one may recite a thousand words, if my mind is not extinguished, it is not worth even a single verse.
Better than that is to abandon pride and negligence. Though one may recite a thousand words...

Seeking fame becomes increasingly deep; it is not as good as a single teaching. Though one may recite a thousand words while abandoning attachments and leaving behind clinging, if one does not wish to eliminate transgressions, it is not as good as a single phrase that leads to the departure from birth and death.
Though one may recite a thousand words, if the passions and desires become ever more firm, it is not as good as a single word.
It is not as good as a single understanding, wherein one forgets the mind and its objects;

though one may recite a thousand words, if they do not seek transcendence from the world, it is not as good as a single awakening, which brings about the severance and departure from the three realms.
Though one may recite a thousand words, if one does not maintain compassion and wisdom, it is not as good as a single hearing [of the Dharma].
Benefiting both oneself and others; Though one may live for a hundred years, If greed and avarice only increase, It is not as good as a single day Of renouncing wealth and sensual pleasures.
Though one may live for a hundred years, Delighting in failing to uphold the precepts, It is not as good as a single day Of maintaining the precepts with a pure mind.
Though one may live for a hundred years, full of anger and lacking forbearance, it is not as good as living for a single day with joy and without hatred.
Though one may live for a hundred years, indolent and lacking diligence, it is not as good as exerting body and mind for a single day. Though one may live for a hundred years...
Delighting in the pleasures of negligence is not as good as dedicating even a single day to the mind of emptiness and stillness.
Though one’s lifespan may reach a hundred years, with a consciousness clouded and dull, it is not as good as dedicating even a single day to penetratingly awakening to ignorance.
Though one’s lifespan may reach a hundred years, if one is clumsy in governing body and mind, [it is not as good as a single day of diligent practice].
It is not as good as spending a single day skillfully and diligently applying oneself; it is better than living for a hundred years constantly harboring fear and weakness.
It is not as good as spending a single day with the power of courageous wisdom;
it is better than living for a hundred years without giving rise to a virtuous aspiration. It is not as good as spending a single day...
The Four Great Vows were proclaimed; when human life spanned a hundred years, it was better to give rise to a single moment of wisdom than to live for a hundred years without it—
thus the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states that the nature of wisdom is sharp and keen.
The devas spoke in verse:
"When a person is born into this world, an axe is born within their mouth;
it is by means of evil speech that they cut themselves down."
To praise those who deserve condemnation, and to condemn those who deserve praise—this fault is born within the mouth; at death, one falls into the evil realms.
The verse says:
Establishing their resolve and admonishing their minds against folly, they look up with admiration to their enlightened companions;
together they establish a great vow, renouncing the secular world to seek the leisure of the mountain retreats.
Dispersed beyond the realm of men, they shine brightly, freed from the entanglements of worldly ties.
In profound stillness, seek to reach the Truth; With tireless diligence, cultivate a supple and alert mind.
Exhort yourself to refine the three karmas, And with fervent resolve, purify the four torrents.
Arouse the heart of great vows and aspirations, To rescue the drowning by steering the boat of compassion.
The auspicious time returns to wondrous enlightenment;
Skillfully realizing nirvana, one cultivates the mind through the Eightfold Noble Path; Resolving to reach the three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

Section Thirteen: Repaying Kindness (Bao'en bu). This section contains three sub-sections. Section Fourteen: Releasing Living Creatures (Fangsheng bu).

The Fifteenth Section on the Department of Flourishing Merit: Explaining the Intent, Conditions for Repaying Kindness, and Conditions for Betraying Kindness. 1. Explaining the Intent (Shū-i-en), Part One: I have heard that the Three Jewels possess a profound and heavy debt of kindness.
The compassionate father of the four modes of birth transforms and nurtures those throughout the ten directions,
regarding them all equally as his only son.
No capacity was too subtle for him not to attend to;
no wisdom came to him that he did not surely embrace.
Thus, it came to pass that Udayana carved an image.
A radiant light surged upward;
its form was cast in concealment.
Rising, he rose from his mat to pay his respects.
From that time forward,
auspicious omens appeared repeatedly,
and his illustrious reputation spread far and wide.
As withered grass follows the wind,
so too does recollection extinguish transgressions and give rise to blessings;
through reverence, one gains the support of goodness for distant generations.
It is truly because the Tathāgata has nourished my Dharma-body,
whereas my parents have nurtured my physical body;
since their kindness and virtue are so profound, [I must repay them].
The vast heavens are difficult to repay;
how much more so when one violates such profound kindness—
would one not sink forever into the sea of suffering?
Therefore, a woman who administered poison to her husband received a reward from the state.
A woodcutter harmed a beast,
and both his arms fell off;
thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
Gratitude is the root of great compassion and the primary gateway to wholesome karma;
it is that which people love and revere.
Their fame will spread far and wide;
after death, they shall attain rebirth in heaven and ultimately achieve the Way of the Buddha.
One who does not recognize kindness is worse than a beast. 2.
The Second Account on Repaying Kindness: As stated in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*:
There are four kinds of kindness that are extremely difficult to repay. What are these four?
First, one's mother;
second, one's father;
third, the Tathāgata.
Fourth are those who preach the Dharma.
If one makes offerings to these four kinds of persons,
one shall obtain immeasurable merit.
Now they are praised by others, and in future ages they will be able to attain bodhi.
Furthermore, the Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, fascicle 443, states: "If someone should ask:"
Who is it that knows gratitude and is able to repay it?
One should answer correctly:
"The Buddha is the one who knows gratitude and repays it."
Why is this? Because in all the worlds,
none surpasses the Buddha in knowing gratitude and repaying kindness.
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus,
"If there are sentient beings who know how to practice reciprocity..."
This person is worthy of respect;
he does not forget even a small kindness,
let alone a great one.
Even if they were separated from this place by hundreds of thousands of yojanas,
they would still be as close to me as if they were not different;
I constantly praise them.
If there are sentient beings who do not know how to repay kindness,
they do not even remember great favors, let alone small ones.
"He is not near me, nor am I near him;
even if he were wearing his saṃghāṭī robe and standing at my side,
this person would still be far away."
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should mindfully practice reciprocity;
do not learn that which lacks reciprocity.
Furthermore, the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* says:
The Buddha said:
"In receiving the precepts, one may practice giving according to one's own capacity;
it is not limited by whether it is much or little."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Why does the Tathāgata say that the kindness of one's parents is so great that it must not go unrequited?
And why does he further say that the kindness of one's teachers and preceptors is immeasurable?"
"Who is the foremost?
The Buddha said,
"As for those who live as householders..."
Filial service to one's parents occurs while remaining at their side;
it should not be thought that the repayment for their upbringing is equal to the act itself.
It is said to be "great" because the kindness of giving birth and raising one is profound.
If one learns from a teacher to develop insight and knowledge,
that subsequent kindness is great indeed. Now,
as for those who have left the household life:
To abandon the house of birth and death— our parents—
and enter the gateway of the Dharma to receive the subtle and wondrous teaching is due to the power of the Teacher.
It nurtures the Dharma-body,
produces the wealth of merit, and sustains the life-force of wisdom;
no achievement is greater than this.
One merely follows the order of their respective births.
Furthermore, in the *Antarābhava Sūtra*,
the Buddha asked Maitreya:
From the time a child in Jambudvīpa is born and falls to the ground until they reach the age of three,
how much milk does the mother provide while holding them in her arms?
Maitreya replied:
"He drank one hundred and eighty hu of milk,
excluding the four parts consumed while in his mother's womb."
In Pūrvavideha, from the moment a child is born and falls to the ground until they reach the age of three,
they consume one thousand eight hundred *hu* of milk.
In Aparagoyānī, from the moment a child is born and falls to the ground until they reach the age of three,
they drink eight hundred and eighty *hu* of milk.
In Uttarakuru in the north, when a child is born and falls to the ground,
he sits at the crossroads;
passersby take his finger and suck it.
They become full-grown after seven days.
That land has no milk.

Beings in the intermediate state (antarābhava) drink and inhale wind. According to the ancient measure used there, one small *sheng* corresponds to one *sheng* of the present Tang measure; since one Tang *sheng* was equivalent to three *sheng* of the old [Han] measure, the milk appears to be abundant.
Furthermore, the *Nanbao jing* (Sutra on the Difficulty of Repaying Kindness) states:
"Carrying one's father on the left shoulder and one's mother on the right shoulder,
one travels for a thousand years while excreting upon their backs."
Even so, one still cannot repay the kindness of one's parents.
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"The meritorious fruit and retribution resulting from filial piety and making offerings to one's parents [are immeasurable]."
His merit was equal to that of a Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood.
Furthermore, the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya-sūtra* states:
"In the past, the Bodhisattva was a great householder."
He accumulated wealth amounting to billions and constantly venerated the Three Honored Ones while extending compassion toward all sentient beings. Once,
while observing the marketplace, he saw a turtle and felt deep pity for it in his heart.
He asked about the price, high or low.
The turtle-keeper knew that the Bodhisattva possessed the virtue of great compassion.
He replied, "One million.
The Bodhisattva said,
"Excellent!"
Carrying the turtle home, he released it by the water's edge.
Watching it swim away, he was moved by both sorrow and joy, and vowed:
"May all beings be as secure from the multitude of hardships as you are now."
He extensively gave rise to great vows,
which all Buddhas praised as excellent.
Later in the night, a turtle came and gnawed at his door.
Hearing a sound at the gate, he went out to look.
The turtle said to the Bodhisattva,
"I have received profound benefit, and my life has been preserved."
There is no way to repay your kindness.
As creatures dwelling in water know the ebb and flow of the waters,
we know that when the floodwaters approach, they will surely cause great harm.
"I pray that you will quickly prepare your boat to come and meet me at the appointed time.
He replied, "Very well.
The next morning, he went to the gate and informed the king of the matter as it was.
Because the king had long possessed a reputation for goodness,
he trusted the Bodhisattva’s words;
he thus moved from a lower position to a higher one.
"The time has come; the floodwaters are approaching.
You must quickly disembark.
Follow where I go, and you shall find safety."
The boat followed after it,
and a snake approached the vessel.
The Bodhisattva said, "Take it."
The turtle said, "Very well.
Then they saw a floating fox,
and he said, "Take it!"
The turtle said, "That is well.
Then he saw a man being swept away by the current,
who was slapping his cheeks and calling out to Heaven, lamenting for his life and begging for rescue.
The man said, "I will take it. The turtle said, "Be careful not to take it!
For the hearts of men are deceitful; few are those who maintain their trust to the end."
"Gratefulness is forgotten while one pursues power and delights in committing atrocities.
The Bodhisattva said, "To save you, who are but insects,
while treating humans as if they were lowly— is this truly benevolence?"
"I cannot bear to do it.
Thereupon he took it.
The turtle said, "What a pity!"
They eventually arrived at the Land of Abundance.
The Tortoise took his leave, saying,
"My service being completed, I beg to withdraw."
He replied,
"I have attained the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
you shall certainly be delivered by me."
The turtle said, "Excellent.
The turtle withdrew, and the snake and fox each departed.
The fox made its burrow its dwelling.
He discovered an ancient hidden treasure of one hundred *jin* of famous purple-gold (*cāmīkara*),
and with joy he said,
"I shall use this to repay that kindness."
The fox replied,
"This small insect has received your moisture and thus saved its fragile life.
This creature is one that dwells in burrows."
Seeking a hollow to dwell in for his own peace,
he obtained a hundred jin of gold;
this hollow was neither a tomb, nor a house, nor a place of plunder, nor a site of theft.

Question: If giving to a noble person (ārya) yields great merit,

Answer: There are many ways to explain the meaning of this passage.
It clarifies that there is a distinction between the foolish and the wise among those who give, and a difference between compassion and reverence regarding the recipients of the gift.
Compassion is poverty and suffering;

Compassion is a field that is inferior yet possesses a superior mind.

7. Relative Conditions (Pratyaya). Seventh: The commentary states:
There are five types of relative distinctions here.
First, regarding the relative distinction between the field (*kṣetra*) and the material gift (*vastu*), there are four cases.
The first is when the field is superior and the material gift is inferior.
As when a child gives earth to the Buddha and so forth:
the material gift is superior while the field is inferior.
As when one gives jewels to a poor person and so forth: the field is superior while the material gift is inferior.
Third, both the field and the material are superior,
as when one gives precious jewels to the Buddha and others.
Fourth, both the field and the material are inferior.
For example, as when one gives grass to animals and the like.
Second, there are four cases regarding the relative weight of the mind and the object:
first, the mind is heavy while the material object is light.
It is like a poor woman who gives a single bolt of cloth as an offering to the great assembly;
she gains vast merit because her wealth is meager while her mind is heavy with devotion.
For example, if a king’s wife, out of arrogance, gives precious objects to the multitude, she gains little merit; the same applies to the two lower cases.
Third, there is the relative distinction between emptiness and existence:
first, the mind is empty while the object is not empty.
For example, although one may study the contemplation of emptiness, if one begrudges wealth and does not practice giving,
one will still receive the retribution of poverty.
Second, the object is empty while the mind is not empty.
Knowing that the gift of wealth results in constant abundance and joy, one practices relinquishment;
it should be understood that the increase of merit follows from this, as with the two lower [types of giving].
Fourth, there is the relative comparison of quantity.
As stated in the *Dharmapada-avadāna-sūtra*:
"There are four matters regarding giving. What are these four?"
First is giving much but receiving little merit:
such as when foolish people perform sacrifices,
drinking wine, singing, and dancing, thereby squandering their wealth and treasures.
There is no merit or wisdom;
this is called giving much but obtaining little merit.
Second, there is giving little but obtaining much merit.
If one can serve virtuous people with a compassionate heart,
and if the Sangha, having finished their meal, applies themselves diligently to study and recitation,
then although such a gift may be small, its merit is exceedingly great.
This constitutes giving little and obtaining much merit.
Third, regarding giving little and obtaining little merit:
for example, when one who is stingy, greedy, and malicious gives to an outsider of wrong views, both parties are equally deluded.
Therefore, when one gives little, the merit obtained is also little.
As for the fourth case, where one gives much and the merit obtained is also much:
if there is a worthy person.
Realizing that the world is impermanent,
they generously contributed their wealth to establish stupas, monasteries, viharas, and orchards.
To make offerings to the Triple Gem—
providing robes, footwear, bedding, and food—
is a merit as vast as the five great rivers.
Entering the great ocean,
the flow of merit continues thus, uninterrupted from lifetime to lifetime.
This is what is meant by giving much and receiving a great reward.
Fifth, the relative nature of defilement and purity.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"Within the Buddha-dharma, there are four kinds of giving."
First, the giver is pure and the recipient is impure.
Second, the giver is impure and the recipient is pure.
Third, both the giver and the recipient are pure.
In the fourth case, both the giver and the receiver are impure.
For now, I shall explain one phrase in detail;
the others can be understood by analogy.
What is meant by "purity of both"?
It is as when the Buddha himself makes offerings to the Buddha;
this is what is meant by the purity of both.
Just as the flowers produced by the power of the merits of the Buddha Ratnākara in the eastern quarter were entrusted to the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha of the Dharma-body at the tenth stage,

To know that the Buddhas of the ten directions are the foremost field of merit—

whether it be much or little.
Whether coarse or subtle,

yet, being inwardly devoid of faith, one is unable to offer gifts,

Therefore, the wise person observes for themselves that a single morsel of food is sufficient to sustain their own life.
If one must give even when it means death,
one should still give;
how much more so when there is an abundance?
