he then attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
For the sake of the Dharma, the Bodhisattva offered his own body as a lamp;
wrapping it in layers of skin and flesh,
he poured ghee over it and burned it as a wick.
At that time, the bodhisattva undergoes this great suffering;
he reproaches his own mind and speaks these words:
"Such is this suffering."
Compared to the sufferings of hell,
[this] does not even approach one hundred-thousandth part of them.
Throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, you—
To undergo such great suffering and distress is entirely without benefit.
If you cannot endure this slight hardship,
how will you be able to rescue suffering sentient beings within the hells?
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates in this manner,
the body does not perceive suffering.
Their mind does not regress;
it is unshakable and irreversible.
At that time, the bodhisattva should deeply know this for themselves.
"I shall certainly attain unexcelled bodhi.
At that time, the bodhisattva was fully possessed of afflictions and had not yet severed them.
For the sake of the Dharma,
they are able to give their heads, eyes, marrow, brains, hands, feet, blood,
and flesh to sentient beings.
Nailing his body with stakes,
leaping from cliffs, and casting himself into fire—
though the Bodhisattva at that time endured such immeasurable sufferings as these, [he did so].
His mind is non-regressive, immovable, and unswerving.
A bodhisattva should know:
"I now certainly possess a non-regressive mind."
One shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra states:
"For the sake of the meaning of even a single word or a single phrase, a bodhisattva..."
One is able to offer the treasures of the worlds of the ten directions to the Dharma King,
and for the sake of even a single verse, one may sacrifice one's own life.
Though one might practice giving for immeasurable eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
it is not equal to the joy arising in the mind upon hearing even once of the matter of bodhi;
such is the delight in hearing and speaking of the True Dharma.
They will constantly be mindful of by all Buddhas and devas.
By the power of that mindfulness,
they will [master] all the scriptures, treatises, and commentaries existing in the world.
One is able to penetrate all of them thoroughly.
Furthermore, the *Upāyakauśalya-pañcadeva-putra-sūtra* (Great Sūtra on the Requital of Kindness through Skillful Means) states:
"A bodhisattva always diligently seeks out spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*)."
For the sake of hearing the Buddha-dharma—
even a single phrase, a single verse, or a single meaning—
the afflictions of the three realms [will be extinguished].
All [the flowers] withered away.
When the Bodhisattva sought the Buddha’s words with a sincere heart,
his thirst for the Dharma was so profound that he disregarded even his own body and life.
Even if they were to tread upon ground of glowing iron and fierce flames,
they would not regard it as a hardship;
for the sake of a single verse, the Bodhisattva [endures such].
If one does not begrudge even one's own body or life,
how much less so the twelve divisions of the scriptures for the sake of a single verse?
They do not even begrudge their own lives,
let alone other material possessions, because hearing the Dharma brings benefit; through it,
the body attains peace and happiness.
They develop deep faith,
possessing a straightforward mind and right view,
regarding the teacher of the Dharma as they would their own parents.
With a mind free from arrogance,
for the sake of sentient beings,
one listens to the Dharma with a sincere heart and not for the sake of gain or sustenance.
It is for the sake of sentient beings,
not for one's own benefit;
it is for the sake of the True Dharma.
They do not fear royal calamities, hunger, thirst, cold, heat,
tigers, wolves, and other predatory beasts, nor robbers and the like;
they first discipline their own afflictions and sense faculties.
Only then should one listen to the Dharma.
Furthermore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:
"In this manner, the bodhisattva seeks the Dharma through skillful means."
Regarding all precious treasures, there is nothing held dear;
one does not conceive the thought of difficulty toward these things.
Yet, if one should obtain even a single verse of the Dharma never heard before, [one would hold it as most precious].
It is better to hear a single verse than to obtain the precious jewels that fill the three thousandfold world system;
it is better than attaining the rank of a universal monarch (cakravartin), Śakra Devānām Indra, or Brahmā.
The Bodhisattva forms this thought:
"For the sake of receiving even a single phrase of the Dharma,
were the trichiliocosm to be filled with great fire,"
I would cast myself down from the Brahma Heaven;
how much more so by a small fire?
I would endure all the sufferings of every hell rather than [avoid this].
One should still seek the Dharma;
how much more so when faced with the various minor sufferings and afflictions of human life?
For the sake of seeking the Dharma, one should give rise to such a mind.
One’s mind is constantly joyful and delighted regarding the Dharma as it has been heard,
and one is able to contemplate it correctly.
Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
If one does not accomplish six qualities,
one will be unable to distance oneself from dust and leave behind defilement to attain the purity of the Dharma-eye. What are these six?
First, not delighting in hearing the Dharma;
second, although hearing the Dharma, not listening with attentive ears;
third, not seeking knowledge and understanding.
Fourth, not seeking with diligent effort those dharmas not yet attained.
Fifth, not skillfully guarding the dharmas already attained.
Sixth, not accomplishing the patient acceptance that accords with reality (*anulomikī kṣānti*).
By reversing these six types [of views],
one is able to distance oneself from dust and leave behind defilement, thereby attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Furthermore, the *Adbhuta-dharma-sūtra* states:
In the past, on Mount Sītavana in the kingdom of Vimala,
there was a jackal who was being pursued by a lion.
He fell into a wild well on a hillside.
Three days had already passed, and his heart was exposed, on the verge of death.
He spoke this verse himself:
All things are impermanent; it is regrettable that one does not bestow [virtue] upon the Lion-like Teacher.
Alas for this body subject to the calamity of death!
To crave life in vain and to die without merit is already regrettable; furthermore, it defiles the waters of the human realm.
I repent before the Buddhas of the ten directions; May they deign to illuminate my heart.
All evil karma from previous lives, Now being repaid, may it all be exhausted.
From this point on, having encountered an enlightened teacher, I shall practice until all become Buddhas.
When Śakra heard of this,
he went to the side of the well with eighty thousand devas and said:
Having not heard the holy teachings for a long time, we have remained in darkness.
What you have just said was extraordinary;
we pray that you will further proclaim the Dharma.
The jackal replied, "O Lord of Devas,
you lack instruction and do not recognize the propriety of the occasion."
While the Dharma Master remained below, he himself occupied the upper seat;
from the very beginning,
he did not offer salutations, yet proceeded to inquire about the essential points of the Dharma.
Śakra then received him with a celestial robe,
prostrated himself in repentance,
and reflected: "I recall having seen such people in the world in the past."
First the high seat was prepared, and afterwards the Dharma Master was invited;
the various devas immediately each removed their precious robes and piled them up to form the high seat.
The jackal ascended the seat and said:
"There are two great causes and conditions:
first, preaching the Dharma to instruct and transform devas and humans."
Because his merit is immeasurable.
Second, in order to repay the kindness of being provided with food;
because that repayment is immeasurable, the Lord of Devas said:
He has escaped the calamity of the well;
his merit must be great.
Why, then, does his gratitude not extend [to you]?
Answer: Birth and death each have their appropriate place.
There are those who crave life.
There are those who delight in death;
there are foolish people who do not know that after death one is born again.
They will be far removed from the Buddha-dharma and fail to encounter an enlightened teacher;
craving life and fearing death, they shall fall into hell.
A person of wisdom serves the Triple Gem and encounters an enlightened teacher.
Reforming evil and cultivating goodness—
such a person enters into evil with joy at birth and is born in the heavens upon death.
The Heavenly Lord said,
"As Your Reverence has taught,
my life is preserved entirely without merit."
He expressed his aspiration to hear about the giving of food and the giving of the Dharma. He replied,
"I shall give you food and drink."
Giving [merely] sustains life for a single day;
bestowing precious jewels relieves the calamities of an entire lifetime.
It increases birth and death;
however, those who preach the Dharma and transform others can cause sentient beings to enter the supramundane path.
They shall attain the fruits of the three vehicles,
escape the three evil realms,
and enjoy the bliss of humans and devas.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"The merit of giving the Dharma as a gift is immeasurable.
The Heavenly Lord said:
"Master, is this present form of yours the result of karmic retribution,
or is it a manifested transformation?"
He replied,
“This offense is not appropriate.
The Lord of Devas said:
"I considered myself a noble one,
yet only now have I heard of the retribution for my offenses;
I do not know the reason for this."
"I wish to hear the causes and conditions.
He replied, "In the past,
I was born in the city of Padmāvatī in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī."
He was the son of a poor family,
born of the Kṣatriya caste;
from his youth, he possessed brilliant intelligence.
He was exceptionally fond of learning.
By the time he reached the age of twelve, he followed his teacher into the mountains,
where he spent fifty years without missing a single seasonal observance.
There are ninety-six kinds of scriptures;
there is none he does not master—
all of this is due to the grace of his Upādhyāya.
The merit thereof is difficult to repay;
it arises from having previously cultivated wisdom and recognized one's own past lives,
and from having received the royal throne.

Indulging in luxury, lust, and pleasure, when his retribution was exhausted and his life ended, he was reborn in the hells or as an animal; the subsequent details are omitted here. At that time, Śakra, together with eighty thousand devas, [approached].
"From the time we received the ten wholesome precepts until now, we have returned to our celestial palaces.
When will our preceptors cast off this retribution for their offenses and be reborn in the heavens?"
The jackal said,
"Seven days from now,
I shall cast off this body and be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven."
"You may now be born there.
In that heaven, many bodhisattvas preach the Dharma and provide instruction.
When your lives end after seven days, you shall be born in the palace of the Tuṣita King."
Later, he will remember his past lives and practice the ten paths of wholesome action.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* says:
The Buddha was in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī,
within a forest grove,
for the sake of the devas, humans, and the fourfold assembly.
As he clearly proclaimed the sublime Dharma,
a flock of five hundred geese in the sky heard the Buddha’s voice and felt deep affection and joy in their hearts.
As it circled and was about to descend,
a hunter spread his net;
the goose fell into it and was killed by the hunter.
He was born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
resting upon the laps of his parents like an eight-year-old child.
Of incomparable majesty and radiance like a mountain of gold,
he thought to himself:
"For what reason have I been born here?"
Immediately recognizing the karmic fruit of their past lives and their love for the Dharma,
they took the flowers together and descended to Jambudvīpa,
arriving at the place where the World-Honored One was.
Prostrating at his feet, he said:
"Having been graced by your Dharma voice,
I have been reborn in the Sublime Heaven."
"I pray that you will grant me further instruction.
The Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths,
and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
He immediately returned to the heavens. This has been a brief exposition of the merit of praising the Dharma;
if one were to explain in detail the methods for seeking the Dharma, it is fully contained in the second fascicle, within the section on "Venerating the Dharma."
The verse says:
A boat and oars upon the river’s path, A ferry for crossing to the other shore.
To transcend birth and death, one must first rely on merit and wisdom; Like a mirror that penetrates the three spheres, Like a pearl that purifies the six obscurations.
When one masters the yoke and completes the harness, it serves as a whetstone for gold. Raising one's traces above the flowing water, one aligns the bit with the tethered grass.
The five levels of patience must be ascended, and the four right efforts never cease.
The waves of the mind are washed clean through and through, and the dust of the passions is rolled away. Once the path of karma is made level, [liberation is attained].

19. Section on Karmic Causes (Karmahetu-varga), the Nineteenth. This consists of five sections:

the section on the intent, the section on the origination of karma, the section on non-meritorious actions, the section on meritorious actions, and the section on mixed karma. 1. Section on the Intent (Abhiprāya-varga). First: Alas, how tragic!
The deluded followers have heavy obstructions;
they cast aside the three vehicles and do not mount them,
drifting and sinking in the sea of suffering.
They endure being scorched and consumed without weariness,
like gadflies and flies delighting in a putrid corpse,
or like moths throwing themselves into a mass of fire.
This is truly because they are deluded regarding causes and mistaken about effects, failing to recognize good and evil;
thus, they delight in creating the causes of suffering and give rise to karma according to conditions.
Having undergone every kind of hardship and suffering the torments of fire and water,
they continue to this day to be burned and boiled without respite.
The Tathāgata, out of great compassion, cannot bear to abandon them forever;
he demonstrates both suffering and pleasure to cause them to feel joy for the former and revulsion for the latter.

2. The Second Section on the Conditions for Initiating Karma. Question: What is the meaning of "karmic path" (*karmapatha*)? Answer: [As follows: *The Conditions for Initiating Karma, Part Two.* Question: What is the meaning of the term "karmic path"?
Answer: [It is as follows:]
The seven karmas of body and speech are designated as "paths of action" (karmapatha) by virtue of their own essential nature;
the remaining three are associated with the mind.
Furthermore, when that very karma can function as the path to its fruit, it is called a "karmic path" (*karmapatha*). Question: [What is the reason for this?]
If it were the case that whatever is called "action" (karma) is necessarily a "path" (mārga) because all such actions lead to rebirth in hell and so forth,
why then are the other three [mental actions] not considered paths of action?
The answer is:
Just as with those seven karmas,
these three are able to serve as their fundamental basis.
Because it is associated [with the mind],
it cannot be like that karma; therefore,
it is not called a "path of action" (*karmapatha*), as stated in the Abhidharma-śāstra.
Furthermore, there are four types of distinctions among karmas:
namely, black karma with black ripening,
and white karma with white ripening.
There is black-and-white karma with black-and-white ripening,
and there is non-black-and-white karma without ripening that can exhaust all karma.
As for black-and-black karma with black ripening:
That is to say, unwholesome karma;
because it is defiled and because its maturation is undesirable.
Karma with exclusively white maturation refers to wholesome karma of the three realms,
because it is non-defiled.
Because its maturation is desirable.
Regarding karma that is both black and white with a black-and-white maturation:
this refers to mixed karma within the desire realm.
Because it is mixed with both wholesome and unwholesome [factors],
it is not a black-and-white action without fruition that can exhaust all karma;
this refers to the stage of the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) and the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
All untainted (anāsrava) karmas are "not black" because the path of preparation (prayoga-mārga) and the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) serve as their antidotes.
It is "white" because it is free from the stains of affliction and is exclusively pure.
It has no maturation because it is contrary to the cycle of birth and death;
it is that which can exhaust all karma.
This is because, by means of untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*),
one attains the permanent eradication of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the three types of tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*), such as the "black" and so forth,
along with their maturation (*vipāka*). Furthermore, the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* states:
Good son, if there are those who do not understand such karmic conditions,
they will wander through birth and death for immeasurable lifetimes.
Although one may be born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception with a lifespan of eighty thousand kalpas,
when one's merit is exhausted, one will still fall back into the three evil realms;
therefore, the Buddha told the son of good family:
Of all forms of drawing, none surpasses the mind;
the mind draws afflictions,
and afflictions draw karma.
Karma then paints the body.
Furthermore, a verse from the "Chapter on Karma" in the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-vyākhyā* states:
Karma can adorn the world; In each and every realm of rebirth, it resides.
Therefore, one should contemplate karma; seeking liberation from the world, one must understand that the accumulation of karma through body, speech, and mind exists within the realms of existence.
That karma constitutes the various formations (*saṃskāra*) which adorn and fashion the manifold bodies.
One should know that bodily action is twofold: namely, manifest (vijñapti) and non-manifest (avijñapti).
Vocal action is likewise. One should know that mental action is volition (cetanā).
Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva* (*Maitreyaparipṛcchāsūtra-śāstra*) states:
These ten unwholesome courses of action—
indeed, all unwholesome dharmas—
arise from greed, hatred, and delusion.
For example, regarding those who commit killing based on the three poisons:
if it arises from a mind of greed,
it may be for the sake of skin, flesh, money, or wealth.
Taking life and so forth—
these are said to arise based on greed.
If they arise based on a mind of hatred:
Or, if one kills an enemy or the like with a mind of hatred,
this is called arising based on hatred.
If it arises based on a mind of delusion:
Some people say that killing snakes,
scorpions, and the like is permissible because they cause suffering and affliction to living beings.
"Though he has been killed, he is without fault. Or it is said:
"Pārasīka and others [are without fault]."
To say that there is no karmic retribution for killing one's elderly parents or those who are gravely ill is called arising from delusion.
For example, regarding those who commit theft based on the three poisons:
if it arises from a mind of greed,
it may be for one's own sake.
Whether for the sake of another's body,
or for food and drink and so forth,
this is called arising based on greed.
If it arises based on a mind of hatred,
it may be directed toward a person who is hateful,
or toward someone beloved by that hateful person.
Stealing those objects and so forth is called arising based on hatred.
If it arises based on a mind of delusion:
For example, as a certain brāhmaṇa said:
"All things that exist upon the entire earth belong to me alone."
Why is this? Because that king previously gave [the gift] to me,
and because I lacked the power [to accept it].
"Others of different lineages have seized my resources;
therefore, what I take is my own property and does not constitute theft."
This is called arising based on a mind of delusion.
For example, just as one who commits sexual misconduct arises from the three poisons,
if it were to arise based on a mind of greed:
Or, when one gives rise to a mind of lustful attachment toward sentient beings and fails to practice in accordance with reality,
this is called "arising based on greed."
If it arises based on a mind of hatred,
it arises either by depending on the protection of one's own livelihood or by depending on the protection of another's livelihood, due to that mind of hatred.
Or one commits sexual misconduct with the wife or concubine of an enemy, or with someone beloved by an enemy;
this is called arising from hatred.
If it arises based on a deluded mind,
some may say that it is like a pestle and mortar.
Ripe flowers and ripe fruits,
food and drink, river water, roads, and so forth;
for a woman to engage in sexual intercourse [with these] is without fault.
Or, as in the case of those such as King Pārasīka who committed sexual misconduct with their own mothers, these are said to arise based on delusion (*moha*).

Just as false speech arises based on the three poisons—which three being easily understood—so too are divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech likewise [arisen from them]. As for those that arise from a mind of greed (*lobha*): [the following applies].
Arising based on the fetter of greed,
the second moment of mind subsequently manifests;
this is what is meant by "arising based on greed."
That which arises in dependence on the fetter of hatred is called "arising in dependence on hatred.
That which arises in dependence on the fetter of delusion...
It is said to arise based on the fetter of delusion (*moha-saṃyojana*).
One should know that this applies equally to greed, hatred, and wrong view.
Question: Among the paths of action, which are the preliminary attendants and which are the subsequent attendants?
Answer: If one initiates the means for taking life,
such as a butcher tending sheep.
Or they purchase them with goods and lead them to the slaughterhouse;
then, either one stroke is struck,
or two or three strokes.
As long as the life of the sheep has not been severed,
all its evil karma is termed its "preceding retinue."
Whichever blade is applied below to sever their life-faculty,
at that very moment of thought—
All performed actions and non-performed actions—
these are all termed the fundamental paths of action (karmapatha).
Following these, there are the bodily activities that constitute performed actions.
This is called the subsequent karma of the retinue resulting from killing;
this applies likewise to all [unwholesome actions] up to frivolous speech.
One should know that the same holds true for the remaining karmas of greed, hatred, and wrong view.
Without prior associates, the fundamental path of action is accomplished at the very moment the initial thought arises.
Furthermore, this applies to the ten unwholesome paths of action of body, speech, and mind.
All things possess preceding and succeeding attendants.
What is the meaning of this?
It is like a person giving rise to a thought.
Desiring to take the life of this being,
one consequently takes the life of other beings as well,
such as when killing sentient beings for the purpose of sacrificing to the heavens.
He immediately seizes another's property;
desiring to kill that person, he further commits adultery with his wife,
giving rise to such thoughts.
He further causes that wife to take her own life by killing her husband,
and uses various divisive words to destroy his kinsmen.
There is no time when it is not real.
One gives rise to a mind of greed toward that object,
and then immediately gives rise to a mind of anger toward that same person.
For the sake of killing that person,
they give rise to such wrong views;
by increasing these wrong views, they take that life.
Furthermore, he desired to kill his wife, children,
and others. In this manner,
he gradually fulfilled the ten paths of unwholesome action.
Such actions as these are termed the preceding associates of all ten unwholesome courses of action.
All cases should be understood in this same way.
Furthermore, departing from the wholesome paths is not the skillful means;
practicing the wholesome paths of action is the skillful means.
Because they are far removed from the root and far removed from the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
As for what is called "preparatory application":
Just as that śrāmaṇera,
wishing to receive the full precepts,
was about to go to the ordination platform.
He prostrated at the feet of the assembly of monks and immediately requested the Upādhyāya to accept his three robes.
The first announcement is made;
when the second announcement is made,
all such [beings] are likewise designated as the preceding retinue.
From the third proclamation until the conclusion of the formal ritual (karmavācanā),
the karma produced through action and the non-action produced by that mental intention—
these are all termed the fundamental paths of action (maula-karmapatha).
Next, the four reliances are explained:
until one does not abandon the virtuous conduct one has undertaken,
including both bodily and vocal actions, as well as non-actions.
All such [factors] as these are termed the subsequent retinue.
The commentary states:
Although the preceding sections have cited sūtras and śāstras to clarify the various types of karmic causes, [the following shall further elaborate].
When the time came to adjudicate the offense, the gravity of the transgression had not yet been clarified;
therefore, he separately cited the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* to distinguish the differences in karmic retribution.
There are four further categories:
first, there are four types regarding the object relative to the intention;
second, there are eight types based on differences in gravity.
Third, there are eight further distinctions based on the differences between superior, middling,
and inferior; fourth, there are eight further distinctions based on the differences between having a mind and being without a mind, according to the Sarvāstivāda-śāstra.
Temporary judgments of guilt encompass all such cases;
thus, the first chapter of the Sūtra states:
"There are instances where the object is grave but the intention is light."
There are things that are light in substance but heavy in intent; there are things that are heavy in substance and heavy in intent;
and there are things that are light in substance and light in intent.
The first case is when the object is grave but the intention is light,
such as killing one's parents without a malicious intent.
The second case is when the object is light but the intention is grave.
This refers to one who kills an animal with a malicious mind.
Regarding the third case, where both the object and the intention are grave:
this refers to one who kills their own father or mother with an extremely evil mind.
The fourth case, where both the object and the intention are light,
is as when one kills an animal with a light mind;
such is the second kind of evil karma.
Furthermore, there are eight types of varying degrees of gravity.
What are these eight? First, there is that which is grave regarding the preliminary application but light once the fundamental act is completed.
Second, there are cases where the root is heavy while the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) is light once completed;
third, there are cases where it is heavy once completed while the preparatory effort and the root are light;
fourth, there are cases where the preparatory effort and the root are heavy while it is light once completed.

5. There are cases where, once the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is completed, the fundamental act (*maula*) is grave while the preparatory application is light. 6. There are cases where, once the fundamental act is completed, it is grave while the preparatory application is light.
7. There are cases where both the preparatory application and the fundamental act are grave once they are completed.
Eighth, when the root has been established through skillful means, it becomes light;
although the substance is of one kind,
one obtains the fruits of lightness or heaviness by virtue of the power of the mind.
As with the ten paths of wholesome action,
there are three factors: first,
the preliminary application (*prayoga*).
Second, the root;
third, having been accomplished.
Furthermore, if there is another person...
They are able to diligently pay homage and make offerings to their parents, teachers, elders, preceptors, and those of virtuous character;
they inquire after them with a proactive and considerate mind, and their speech is gentle and soft.
This is called skillful means.
Once it has been completed,
one is able to cultivate mindfulness.
To feel joy and have no regret is called "having accomplished it.
To be single-mindedly devoted while performing it is [the practice].
This is called the root.
As it is with the ten wholesome actions,
so it is with the ten unwholesome actions.
The third consists of the ten courses of action.
Furthermore, there are three grades:
namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
Either [the path] is completed in the fundamental [state] while being in the preparatory stage above;
or it is completed in the fundamental state while being in the preparatory stage below;

or it is completed in the fundamental state while being in the lower preparatory stage. These eight permutations, formed by alternating [the stages], may be understood according to the preceding principle.

Fourth, according to the *Sarvāstivāda-śāstra*, once the fundamental basis of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) has been established, there are states with mind and without mind that alternate with one another; these eight cases may be understood by analogy with what precedes. Therefore, when one attains dhyāna, there are the ten wholesome courses of action with form (*rūpa*).
If we discuss this in relation to the gods of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*),
according to the Abhidharma (*Vibhāṣā*):
Deities of the formless realm cannot cultivate or give rise to karma pertaining to the meditative absorptions of the form realm;
this is because, having been born in a higher stage, they have abandoned the lower stages.
According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra*:
Even those born in the formless realm can give rise to karma belonging to the lower form realm.
This clarifies that the bases upon which the meritorious karma of dhyāna-concentration and the ten paths of wholesome action arise within the form realm.
As for the basis of the body upon which the karma of the four formless attainments arises,
it can be cultivated and produced by humans and devas within all three realms.
Thus concludes the preceding explanation regarding the bases of the body upon which various meritorious formations arise.
As for the arising of merit by sages, it is not relevant to ordinary beings because they do not aspire to it; therefore, it is not described here.
5. The Fifth Section on the Conditions of Miscellaneous Karmic Actions. The commentary states:
This course of action is called the "uncertain" in the Noble Teachings;
that is to say, it is a sinful course of action.
In various sūtras, it is sometimes referred to as "black-and-black karma" and "unwholesome karma."
The meritorious conduct of ordinary persons is sometimes referred to in various sūtras as "black-and-white karma" or simply "wholesome karma.
Although these designations differ, there is no difference in the essential nature of the conduct itself.
What is the nature of action?
As stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*,
acts such as killing are unwholesome karma.
Generosity and so forth are wholesome karmas;
this refers to the two courses of action, namely demerit and merit.
As for the mention of "killing" and so forth:
The ten unwholesome actions are collectively termed "actions of transgression.

The phrase "giving and so forth" includes, by way of the term "and so forth," the karmas of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and so on, within the category of actual deeds.
These are both mundane virtues;
both are termed meritorious conduct (*puṇya-karma*).
Within these mundane virtues:
The eight dhyāna concentrations,
when compared to the distracted wholesome states of the desire realm,
are called "unshakable conduct."
If one looks toward supramundane insight-wisdom (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*),
this dwelling upon objects is termed meritorious conduct (*puṇya-karma*).
As it is said, among the first five of the six perfections, all meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is also generally termed merit (*puṇya*). However,
the conduct of those who perform various sinful or meritorious deeds differs.
Some exclusively cultivate merit;
some only commit transgressions;
and yet others there are.
Both sin and merit are practiced together;
that which exclusively cultivates merit is what is called a pure mind.
To practice giving, ethical discipline, and so forth for the benefit of others;
whereas those who commit only offenses are said to lack the moisture of compassion.
To move the body, speech, or mind such that they all cause harm to others;
as for "merit and demerit occurring together," it refers to when one cultivates merit while the inner mind is impure.
Or it may involve harming other beings;
this constitutes mixed karma of the desire realm,
as it is not purely wholesome.
It is also called impure.
If one discusses sinful actions,
they are coarse and manifest, and thus can be known.
If one discusses mixed karma,
it shares both similarities and differences with pure meritorious conduct;
being somewhat obscure, it is difficult to discern.
That is to say, regarding those who cultivate merit, if one relies on their external appearances,
their actions performed with faith and devotion within the ritual context are all the same;
however, if one relies on their inner mind...
The requests made for oneself and for others are distinct;
they differ in being either refined or coarse,
because while the cultivation of merit is outwardly identical, it is inwardly different.
There are two types of karma, the pure and the mixed, which differ from one another.
If one can discipline the mind with compassion and pity for all beings,
then whatever actions one performs will all become great goodness.
If one does not maintain mindfulness,
yet cultivates merit by observing external signs,
it will be coarse within and subtle without.
This results only in mixed karma;
though it accords with the sentiments of those fools and is called "transcending the world," in reality it contradicts the Way and is not pure merit.
Because when cultivating merit one does not contemplate the emptiness of arising,
the inversion of selfhood constantly operates throughout all three natures;
thus, all actions performed are associated with that inversion.
This is a nature of false grasping;
therefore, one is deluded regarding the Path.
Because of this unattached mind, one seeks many worldly rewards.
Furthermore, because they frequently seek fame,
it is not pure merit.
Due to this mixture of the pure and the impure, worldly people are largely deluded.
Now, I shall briefly provide a partial discussion to enable people to recognize their conduct.
First, I will discuss miscellaneous karma, and subsequently clarify pure merit.
Regarding these various types of miscellaneous karma, they themselves possess both coarse and subtle levels.
The coarse [type] is evil and further harms others;
the subtle [type] is for oneself alone, seeking only worldly retribution.
First, I shall discuss the coarse and miscellaneous [types].
If we discuss giving from this perspective,
there may be those who give wealth acquired through unrighteous means,
such as stealing another's property to use for almsgiving.
The retribution received from this will likewise always be subject to decay and exhaustion;
having given, if one feels regret, the resulting fruit will be the same.
Thus, the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* says:
If a person, after having given a gift, gives rise to a mind of regret;
or if they take another's wealth by force and offer it as a gift—
though such a person may obtain wealth in the future, [they will not enjoy it].
It is constantly dissipated and does not accumulate.
Or there may be those who, in practicing giving, simultaneously cause harm to others;
that is to say, when giving, they do not maintain right mindfulness of the wholesome.
One may give rise to anger or conceit,
and shall consequently fall into the evil realms.
Although one may receive a karmic reward among the animals,
it does not lead to rebirth as a human or a deva.
Thus, a verse from the *Vibhaṅga-karma-vipāka-sūtra* says:
Practicing great generosity, yet impulsive and prone to anger,
failing to rely on right mindfulness, one later takes birth as the body of a great nāga;
though able to practice great generosity, one remains arrogant and treats others with contempt.
From such karmic actions, the mighty garuḍa is born.
If one seeks worldly rewards by cultivating merit,
it is like seeking a future retribution for oneself when giving away wealth.
Some may renounce out of fear that their bodies and wealth are impermanent;
others do so for the sake of fame, seeking only their own benefit.
This is not compassion intended to relieve the suffering of the poor.
It is like a commercial transaction;
it is not a purely pure karma.
For this reason, it is called "impure giving" in the sutras.
As stated in the *Śata-śāstra*:
"To give for the sake of repaying a donor is called impure giving."
Because it is like a market transaction,
there are two kinds of retribution. As for immediate retribution (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya):
"Renown, respect, and so forth" refers to [rewards] in this life;
"retribution in a later existence" refers to wealth, nobility, and so forth in future lives.
This is called impure giving.
It is like a merchant who travels far to another land;
although he carries various goods that bring much benefit, [he does so with a defiled mind].
However, because it is not out of compassion for sentient beings but rather for the sake of seeking one's own profit,
this karma is impure.
Seeking a reward through giving is likewise so.
By this it is known that there is no true compassion when one seeks fame for oneself.
Or, if performed for the sake of karmic retribution,
even if one practices extensive giving, it is not a pure karma.
Because the karma is not pure, the resulting retribution will not be refined.
Thus, the *Vibhaṅga-karmavipāka-sūtra* states:
"If one gives for the sake of rebirth in heaven,
or again, seeks fame or to repay a debt of gratitude."
Furthermore, because one practices giving out of a desire for reward or out of fear,
the fruit obtained will be impure,
and what is received will be largely coarse and harsh.
Since this is the case for the practice of giving, it is the same for other wholesome qualities such as ethical discipline (*śīla*) and so forth, which are likewise impure.
Thus, the *Śata-śāstra* states:
Those who maintain the precepts with impurity seek their own pleasant retribution:
either seeking to enjoy themselves with celestial maidens in the heavens,
or seeking wealth and status among humans to experience the pleasures of the five senses.
For the sake of lust,
it is like one who conceals their true nature;
internally they desire the physical form of another.
To outwardly manifest intimacy and friendliness is called impurity; this refers to the external,
subtle mental impurity of maintaining the precepts.
As Ānanda spoke to Nanda,
he uttered this verse:
"Just as two rams butt one another, advancing only to retreat again."
If you wish to uphold the precepts, the matter is likewise so:
open your mind and focus exclusively on benefiting others;
thus you will obtain abundant merit.
Furthermore, regarding the objects of giving, there are those who are poor or ill,
or those who possess knowledge of the Dharma yet lack what they require;
if one gives to them, it will cause them to gain benefit and cultivate their virtues.
When there is appropriateness in what is given, one shall obtain abundant merit.
Thus, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states:
"The Buddha praised five kinds of giving that yield immeasurable merit."
That which is called giving to those who have come from afar,
to those departing for distant lands,
and to those who are sick and emaciated.
Giving food and drink to those who are hungry;
giving to those who know the Dharma—
these are the five kinds of giving.
One obtains blessings in the present life.
This giving is such that one may rightly obtain abundant blessings in the present,
unlike the pursuit of fame.
Giving is not necessarily required in all circumstances;
though one may practice extensive renunciation, pure retribution cannot be attained thereby.
Furthermore, regarding those who rejoice in the giving of others:
If one considers those who commit extremely coarse unwholesome deeds,
even their subtle transgressions may be termed "wholesome."
If one aspires for detachment from desire or acts solely for the sake of others,
such mixed karma constitutes a fault. Therefore,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
Coarse people commit coarse offenses;
subtle people commit subtle offenses.
Therefore, these mixed karmas proceed together as both offenses and merit.
A mind that harbors expectations is not pure; this is impure karma.
Thus concludes the preceding explanation that the simultaneous practice of both sin and merit constitutes the impure, mixed karma of the desire realm.
If one discusses pure karma,
it can be understood by reversing the preceding [explanation].
Thus, the *Śata-śāstra* says:
Regarding pure giving (*śuddhadāna*):
because one who is loved, respected,
and beneficial brings forth even greater merit, a verse from the *Karmaprajñapti-sūtra* says:
If there is a poor person who has no wealth to give,
yet gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy when seeing others practice generosity,
the karmic reward of that sympathetic joy is equal to that of the giver and no different.
Furthermore, a verse from the *Mahāpuruṣa-śāstra* says:
"To give with a compassionate heart to a single person, The merit is as vast as the earth;
To give for one's own sake to all beings, The reward obtained is like a mustard seed."
To rescue a single person from calamity is superior to all other forms of giving.
Though the stars possess light, they do not equal the brilliance of the single moon.
So it is with the sins and merits created by ordinary worldlings.
Not understanding that cause and effect, as well as good and evil, lack intrinsic nature is delusion regarding phenomena;
because one grasps at intrinsic nature, one remains perpetually bound within the three realms of existence.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"For example, a fly alights on everything except that it does not alight on a flame."
The attachment of sentient beings is likewise thus:
they are attached to all these wholesome and unwholesome dharmas,
even unto the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Only by not clinging to the great fire of the emptiness of the nature of the *prajñāpāramitā* can one realize and know this:
that there is no inherent nature of good or evil, yet beings constantly cycle through the five destinies.
This refers precisely to those sentient beings who lack Buddha-nature.

This concludes the brief explanation, based on various sutras and śāstras, regarding how ordinary beings, through their two types of conduct—merit and demerit—are deluded by phenomena and grasp at an inherent nature.
