Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoshi of Ximing Monastery. Section 20:
The Section on the Hindrance of Desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*). This section has three parts. Section 21: The Section on the Three Conditions and Four Births.
Part One: The Exposition of Intent. Regarding the Exposition of Intent, the first part: I have privately examined the sūtras and śāstras.
Practitioners cultivating the Path all say that the five desires are the root obstacle to the Path; if one does not train in their abandonment,
[the Path cannot be realized].
Without this, there is no way to realize the state of a sage.
If you wish to know the root cause,
I shall briefly describe three types.
First, the five internal sense faculties;
second, the five external sense objects;
third, the five consciousnesses produced therefrom.
Because of these three, one is able to give rise to defiled desire.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"O son of good family."
For example, it is like a wild elephant whose mind is not yet tamed;
if someone mounts it, it will not go as desired,
but will leave the city or town and head toward a desolate wilderness.
It is likewise with one who cannot properly restrain these five faculties;
such a person will be led far away from the city of Nirvana.
As for the vast wilderness of birth and death,
good son, it is like a sycophantic minister who instructs a king to commit evil.
The five faculties are like sycophantic ministers;
they likewise constantly instruct sentient beings to commit immeasurable evils,
just like a wicked son.
If one does not receive the instructions of teachers, elders, parents,
or rulers, there is no evil one will not commit;
one fails to discipline the five sense faculties.
It is likewise so:
not accepting the virtuous words and instructions of their teachers,
there is no evil they will not commit.
Good son, ordinary persons do not restrain the five sense faculties;
they are constantly harmed by the marauders of the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts.
They are also like enemies and thieves who harm virtuous people.
Furthermore, the *Śāriputra-parivarta* (The Sutra of Bequeathed Teachings) states:
"The five sense-faculties are thieves."
The calamities will extend through successive generations;
the harm is extremely grave,
and one must not fail to exercise caution.
Therefore, the wise person restrains them and does not follow them,
regarding them as thieves;
even if they were to let them loose.
All of these, too, will not endure long;
one sees their eventual decay and extinction.
Now, as for discussing canopies:
This has the meaning of "shading" or "covering.
That is to say, it obscures and obstructs the practitioner,
causing their mental disposition to become dull and lethargic.
When concentration and wisdom are not clear,
virtuous people are obscured;
this is a direct obstacle to the cultivation of the Path.
Therefore, they are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*).
Thus, the Abhidharma-śāstra states:
"These hindrances prevent the wholesome factors from becoming manifest."
This is the meaning of "canopy" (kaṣāya):
it covers and obscures the mind,
obstructing all categories of wholesome qualities.
Because they prevent [the mind] from turning [toward the wholesome],
they are termed "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*).
The aforementioned five desires arise from the five external sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
These five hindrances arise from the five internal sense-faculties.
Second, regarding the five objects of desire as conditions: this is further divided into three conditions. First, suffering bound by desire.
Now, regarding the five desires, since their roots already exist,
they give rise to the five desires,
which bind sentient beings so that they cannot attain liberation.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Ordinary people are bound by the five desires,
allowing Māra Pāpīyān to take them away at his will."
It is like that hunter who captured a monkey, carried it home on his back,
O son of good family.
For example, it is like a king who dwells securely within his own realm with peace and happiness in body and mind,
yet encounters manifold sufferings when he enters another's realm.
All sentient beings are likewise thus:
if they can abide within their own domain,
they will attain peace and happiness.
If one enters another realm,
one will encounter evil Māras and undergo various sufferings and afflictions; however,
within one's own domain, [this is not so].
This refers to the four foundations of mindfulness.
"The realm of others" refers to the five sensual desires.
The five desires refer to the forms,
sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects found upon the bodies of men and women;
that is, their meaning consists in the longing for these five desires.
Clinging attachment to the five sensory objects is called desire (*kāma*).
Furthermore, the objects perceived through the contact of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are termed mental objects (*dharmadhātu*).
These six sense objects are not only called the domain of Māra;
they further receive the name of "evil bandits.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
Just as six great bandits can plunder all the wealth and treasures of the people,
so too are the six sense-objects like evil bandits.
They are able to plunder the wealth of virtue of all sentient beings,
like six great bandits who have entered a person's house.
It can then plunder all that currently belongs to one's household,
making no distinction between the good and the bad,
causing even the immensely wealthy to suddenly fall into poverty.
These thieves of the six sense objects are likewise;
once they enter the faculties of a person,
they are able to plunder all wholesome dharmas.
When wholesome dharmas are exhausted, one becomes impoverished, destitute, and solitary,
becoming an icchantika;
for this reason, the bodhisattva...
Contemplate the six sense objects as being like six great bandits.
Second, regarding the suffering of the obstacle of desire:
as for discussing the faults of desire—
That is to say, the five desires are the corrupt Māra;
the six sense-objects are the evil bandits;
and the Buddha has judged them to be perverse delusions.
Because they obscure the Buddha-nature.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The five consciousnesses of sentient beings..."
Although it is not a single thought-moment,
it is nevertheless tainted;
furthermore, being a state of perverse inversion, it increases all outflows.
All ordinary worldlings grasp at form, and so on,
up to grasping at consciousness.
Because they grasp at form, a mind of craving arises.
Because they give rise to a mind of craving, they are bound by form,
and so on, up to being bound by consciousness.
Because of this bondage, [they suffer].
Then one cannot escape the great suffering of birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, and lamentation, nor all afflictions.
Furthermore, it says:
"If there is a bodhisattva who claims for himself that his precepts are pure..."
Although he does not associate with women, converse with them, jest with them, or listen to their voices,
he nevertheless sees men pursuing women, or sees women pursuing men.
He then gives rise to greedy attachment.
In this way, the bodhisattva accomplishes the dharma of desire,
thereby violating pure precepts and defiling the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
This causes the precepts to become defiled and impure,
such that they cannot be called "endowment with pure precepts.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
The Bodhisattva contemplates various forms of impurity;
among all forms of ruin, the ruin of women is the most grave,
surpassing even swords, fire, thunderbolts, lightning, enemies, and venomous snakes.
One may still approach them for a short while;
however, women— being stingy, envious, wrathful, deceitful, lewd, quarrelsome, greedy, and jealous—
should not be approached.
Why is this? Because women and those of small mind have shallow hearts and meager wisdom;
they regard only desire as kin.
They do not regard wealth, nobility, wisdom, virtue, or renown;
they exclusively practice desire and evil, destroying the roots of goodness in others,
and are bound by shackles and fetters.
To be confined in prison,
though said to be difficult to escape,
is still relatively easy to open up.
The woman’s fetter binds a person;
its roots of attachment are so deep that one cannot escape it.
It is the most grievous of all maladies.
As the Buddha said in verse:
"Better to roll a red-hot iron ball in one's eyes than, with a defiled mind,
to gaze upon female forms with a smiling air and coquettish gestures, driven by pride and shamelessness."
Turning her face and casting sidelong glances, she speaks with sweet words while harboring jealousy and anger;
her gait is seductive and impure, intended to delude men. With a net of lewd desire, she causes all people—whether sitting, reclining, walking, or standing—to sink into ruin.
She casts back glances with artful coquetry, ensnaring those of meager wisdom and foolish minds.
One who is intoxicated may still be subdued by being struck with a sword;
yet a female thief who harms others cannot be restrained.
A venomous serpent may still be grasped by hand; but the passions of a woman that delude men cannot be touched.
That which a person of wisdom should not look upon—if one wishes to observe it, one should do so as if toward a mother or a sister.
Behold it with clear discernment: it is a mass of impurities piled up, where the fire of lust is never extinguished, and by which one is consumed and destroyed.
Since this is the case for visible forms,
the same applies by analogy to all other objects, such as odors, tastes,
and tangibles. All sentient beings—
That one has been submerged in birth and death since beginningless time and is unable to escape is truly due to the bondage of female form, which is difficult to shed.
Blind and lacking the eye of wisdom,
they see the pit of birth and death and fall into it;
now, both monastics and laypeople alike fail to contemplate the afflictions of desire.
I have been running toward it for so long;
on what day shall I return and escape this transgression?
My mind is constantly defiled and cannot abandon it even for a moment.
If even the precepts do not exist,
how can there be meditative concentration, wisdom, or the contemplation of Buddha-nature?
Thus, a verse in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
Committing evil without immediate repentance is like milk turning instantly into curd;
it is like treading lightly upon embers covered by ashes.
This is the third [warning] on the suffering of censuring desire.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"The practitioner should rebuke the five desires, saying:
'Alas! Sentient beings are constantly tormented by the five desires.'"
If one pursues them without ceasing, one will fall into a great pit;
once obtained, they only intensify the affliction, like roasting a scab with fire.
The five desires are as useless as a dog gnawing on a bone.
The five desires increase contention like crows competing for meat;
the five desires burn people like holding a torch against the wind;
the five desires harm people like treading upon a venomous snake.
The five desires are without reality, like what is obtained in a dream;
the five desires do not endure for long, like a temporary loan for a brief moment.
The people of the world are deluded and ignorant.
Clinging greedily to the five desires until death, they do not abandon them;
for this reason, they will undergo immeasurable suffering in future lives.
These five desires provide only a momentary pleasure when obtained.
To miss the opportune moment is a great suffering.
It is like honey smeared upon a blade;
the one who licks it craves the sweetness, unaware that it will wound his tongue.
As for these five desires,
they are known as form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch.
These five matters are the primary obstacles for those in the Chan school.

If one wishes to cultivate meditative concentration, one should abandon all [desires] as described in the three preceding sections; these three sections provide a general contemplation of the five desires, while the following five sections provide a specific refutation of the five desires.
First is the refutation of the faults of sensual desire for form (*rūpa*).
For example, King Bimbisāra,
for the sake of a woman, entered an enemy country with his own body and stayed alone in the chamber of the courtesan Āmrapālī.
Because King Udayana was stained by lustful passion,
he cut off the hands of five hundred rishis.
Such various causes and conditions as these are called the refutation of the faults of sensual desire.
Second, regarding the refutation of the desire for sound:
just as the characteristic of sound does not abide,
it perishes immediately upon being briefly heard.
Foolish people do not understand that the characteristics of sound are impermanent and subject to change and loss; therefore,
they falsely give rise to attachment and delight within sounds.
One gives rise to attachment by recollecting sounds that have already passed.
For example, there were five hundred sages dwelling in the mountains when a kinnarī was bathing in a pool in the Himalayas.
Upon hearing the sound of their singing, they immediately lose their meditative concentration;
their minds become intoxicated and wild, unable to maintain self-control,
and they forfeit all their meritorious virtues.
Later, they fall into the evil realms.
A person of wisdom contemplates the arising and ceasing of sound;
seeing that the preceding and succeeding moments do not coexist and that there is no mutual reaching between them, [they realize it is empty].
One who possesses such knowledge is not defiled by attachment. For such a person,
even the music of the devas cannot cause distraction.
How much more so with human voices.
Through various causes and conditions such as these,
this is called the fault of censuring the desire for sound.
Therefore, the treatise says:
"For example, when five hundred rishis were flying through the air,
they heard the singing voice of a kinnarī."
Their minds became intoxicated with madness;
they all lost their supernormal powers and fell to the ground at once,
just as when the śrāvakas heard the sound of the kinnara king Tuṇḍurumanta playing the lute and singing.
They praised the Buddha by means of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
At that time, Mount Sumeru and all the trees shook.
Mahākāśyapa and the other great disciples [were moved].
They all began to dance upon their seats,
unable to remain composed.
The Bodhisattva Devamāla asked Mahākāśyapa:
"You are the most senior among us and foremost in the practice of dhūta;
why can you not now restrain your own mind?"
Mahākāśyapa replied,
"My mind is not swayed by the various desires of humans or devas."
This is the sound of the retribution of the Bodhisattva’s immeasurable merit;
furthermore, it is a sound produced through the transformations of wisdom,
which others are unable to endure.
For example, even if winds arise from the eight directions,
they cannot cause Mount Sumeru to move;
yet at the time of the kalpa's end, [it is otherwise].
When the Vairambha wind arrives,
it blows Mount Sumeru until it is like withered grass.
It is like a lute that constantly produces sound on its own,
playing whatever one desires.
When there is no one playing,
this state is likewise neither a distracted mind nor a concentrated mind.
Because this is born of the retribution of merit,
it produces sound according to one's wishes;
the Dharma-body Bodhisattva is also like this.
There is no conceptual discrimination,
nor is there a distracted mind,
nor is there any characteristic of teaching the Dharma.
This is due to the causes and conditions of immeasurable merit and wisdom.
Third, regarding the refutation of the fault of desiring fragrance:
people claim that there is little fault in being attached to fragrance.
Attachment to fragrances opens the gateway to the fetters;
though one may have maintained the precepts for a hundred years,
they can be destroyed in a single moment.
For example, there was an Arhat who frequently entered the dragon palace;
after he had finished eating, he gave his alms bowl to a śrāmaṇera and told him to wash it, though there were still a few grains of leftover rice remaining in the bowl.
The śrāmaṇera smelled it and found it very fragrant;
he ate it and found it exceedingly delicious.
He then devised a stratagem.
He enters beneath the teacher’s rope-couch and grasps the legs of the couch with both hands.
When the time for the teacher to arrive comes...
He entered the dragon palace together with the rope bed.
The dragon said,
"This one has not yet attained the Way."
"Why did you bring it?
The Master said,
"I was not aware."
The śrāmaṇera obtained food and drink.
Furthermore, seeing that the dragon girl’s body was upright and beautiful, with a fragrance and excellence beyond compare,
his heart became deeply attached to her.
He immediately made an evil vow:
"I shall perform meritorious deeds to seize this dragon's dwelling and occupy his palace.
The dragon said:
"From now on, do not bring this śrāmaṇera here.
After the śrāmaṇera had returned,
he single-mindedly practiced giving and upheld the precepts, focusing exclusively on seeking his aspiration.
"I vow to become a dragon soon.
At that time, water gushed from beneath his feet as he circumambulated the temple;
he knew for certain that he would surely become a dragon.
He went directly to the edge of the great pond where his teacher had entered,
covered his head with his *kāṣāya*, and went in;
he died immediately and transformed into a great dragon.
Because his merit was so great,
he immediately slew that dragon,
and the entire pool turned crimson.
Before that had occurred,
the various masters and the Sangha rebuked him.
The śrāmaṇera said:
My mind is already settled; the characteristics of the mind have already emerged.
I shall lead the assembly of monks.
He went to the pond to observe it;
such was the causal condition arising from the fault of attachment to fragrance.
Furthermore, there was another bhikṣu.
While he was walking to and fro beside a lotus pond in the grove, he smelled the fragrance of the lotuses;
his nose perceived it and his mind became attached.
Then the deity of the pond spoke:
Why have you abandoned your place for meditative seclusion beneath that grove to steal my fragrance?
It is because of your attachment to this fragrance.
All those who were lying down, bound by their fetters, arose.
At that time, another person came and entered the pond,
taking many of its flowers.
He dug up and pulled out the roots and stalks, leaving them in disarray before departing.
The deity of the pond remained silent and said nothing.
The bhikṣu spoke:
"This man has destroyed the lotuses in your pond,
yet you say nothing at all;
I have merely been walking along the bank of the pond."
He was immediately seen and reviled, saying, "I have stolen the fragrance.
The deity of the pond said,
"You are an evil man of this world."
They constantly dwell amidst the filth of sinful defilements,
submerged head-deep in impurity;
I do not converse with them.
"You are a good person who practices dhyāna,
yet this attachment to fragrance ruins your virtuous practice;
for this reason, I rebuke you."
It is like a piece of white cotton cloth that is fresh and pure, yet stained by some foreign substance,
which everyone perceives;
such is that evil person.
It is like a black garment with black spots that a person with dark skin does not see;
who would ask about it?
Through various causes and conditions such as these,
this is called the condemnation of the faults of desire for fragrance.
Fourth is the condemnation of the faults of desire for flavor.
One should awaken for oneself:
"It is solely because of my attachment to delicious flavors that I shall undergo the suffering of punishment."
One’s mouth is doused with molten copper and one must swallow glowing iron balls;
if one does not contemplate food,
yet the mind of craving remains firm and attached, one will fall among the impure worms.
For example, there was once a śrāmaṇera who constantly craved curd.
Whenever donors sent curd to the Saṃgha,
the śrāmaṇera would invariably receive the leftovers.
With a mind of attachment, joy, and delight that did not depart,
after his life ended, he was reborn in this jar of residual curd.
His preceptor, the śrāmaṇera, had attained arhatship.
When the monks were dividing the curd, he said,
"Distribute it slowly; do not harm this novice who loves curd."
The people said,
"This is a worm.
Why do you call him the curd-loving śrāmaṇera?"
He replied,
"This insect was originally my śrāmaṇera;
it is solely because he sat [there] out of greed for the leftover curd."
It was born within this jar.
When the teacher received his portion of curd,
the insect came forth from within it.
The teacher said,
"O you who love curd, why have you come?
and he immediately gave him some curd.
Furthermore, there was a king named King Candrabhāga.
He had a crown prince who was deeply attached to delicious flavors.
The king’s gardener daily sent him fine fruits.
In the garden there was a great tree,
upon which a bird had raised its young.
He would constantly fly to Mount Gandhamādana to gather excellent fragrant fruits to nourish his children. Once,
while the children were quarreling over them, one fruit fell to the ground.
The gardener saw him at dawn; marveling at his extraordinary appearance,
he immediately sent him to the king.
The king prized this fruit for its extraordinary fragrance and color.
When the prince saw it, he immediately asked for it;
out of his love for his son, the king gave it to him at once.
The Prince ate the fruit and experienced its flavor;
his mind became stained with deep attachment, and day by day he desired to obtain more.
The king immediately summoned the gardener and asked him about the circumstances. The gardener said:
This fruit has no seeds;
it is obtained from the earth,
and its origin is unknown.
The Crown Prince wept and refused to eat.
The King rebuked the park keeper, saying,
"I rely on you to obtain him."
The gardener went to the place where he had found the fruit and saw a bird's nest;
he knew that the birds had brought it there in their beaks.
He hid his body in a tree to wait for the opportunity to seize it.
When the mother bird arrived,
he immediately snatched the fruit and carried it away.
Day after day it was thus.
The mother bird grew angry with it and went to Mount Gandhamādana to fetch poisonous fruit.
Its fragrance, flavor, and color were made to resemble those of the former;
the gardener seized it and presented it to the king,
who gave it to the crown prince for him to eat.
Before long, his body’s flesh will rot and he will die.
Through various causes and conditions such as these,
the faults and excesses of the desire for flavors are censured.
Fifth, regarding the fault of censuring the desire for touch:
this touch is the cause of the fetters (saṃyojana) and the root of the bondage of the mind.
Why is this? While the other four sense-faculties each pertain to their own respective domains,
this [desire] permeates and adheres to the entire body.
Because it is difficult to relinquish, one constantly commits grave offenses.
At that time, the World-Honored One [spoke] for the sake of the bhikṣus.
He spoke of the causal conditions of a past life: "In times long past,
there was a rishi dwelling among the mountains in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī."
In the eighth month of autumn,
while urinating into a washbasin,
he saw a stag and a doe mating.
His lustful mind was immediately stirred,
and his semen flowed into the basin; a stag drank it.
Immediately she became pregnant;
when the months were complete, she gave birth to a son whose physical form resembled that of a human.
It has only a single horn on its head,
and its feet resemble those of a deer.
When the deer is about to give birth, [it experiences this].
She gave birth beside the hermit’s hut;
seeing that the child was human,
she entrusted him to the hermit and departed.
When the rishi emerged and saw this fawn,
he reflected upon his past causes and conditions and knew it was his own son.
Having taken him in, she raised him;
when he had grown up, she diligently taught him learning until he mastered eighteen kinds of great sūtras.
Furthermore, he practiced seated meditation,
cultivated the four immeasurable minds,
and attained the five supernormal powers.
Once, he went up a mountain and encountered heavy rain; the ground was slippery with mud,
and his feet were unsteady.
He fell to the ground, breaking his water jar and injuring his foot;
he then became greatly incensed with anger.
He filled his *kamaṇḍalu* with water and,
through incantation, caused it not to rain;
such was the merit and power of the rishi.
All the dragons, spirits, and deities failed to send rain.
Because there was no rain,
the five grains and the five fruits were entirely unable to grow.
The people were impoverished and had no further means of survival.
The King of Vārāṇasī was filled with sorrow and distress,
and he commanded his high officials to assemble and deliberate on the matter of the rain.
The wise ones deliberated and said:
"We have heard that on Mount Ṛṣigiri there is a one-horned seer who,
because his feet are infirm,"
While climbing a mountain, he stumbled and injured his foot;
in his anger, he cast a spell to cause this rain not to fall for twelve years.
The king reflected and said:
"If it does not rain for twelve years,
my kingdom will surely come to an end;
there will be no people remaining."
The king immediately issued a proclamation:
"To whoever can cause the seer to lose his five supernormal powers and become my subject,
I shall grant half of the kingdom for him to rule."
In this country there was a courtesan named Śāntā,
who was both beautiful and immensely wealthy.
She came in response to the King's recruitment.
The girl asked the people,
"Is this a human being or not?"
The people said,
"He was born from a rishi.
The courtesan said:
"If it is such a person,
I am able to destroy him.
Having spoken these words, he—
He immediately took a golden tray and filled it with fine treasures,
saying to the king,
"I shall ride upon the neck of this rishi and come here."
The courtesan immediately sought five hundred chariots and loaded them with five hundred beautiful women.
There were five hundred deer-carts laden with various kinds of joy-pills,
all of which were compounded from a multitude of medicinal herbs.
One should have them painted in colors so that they resemble various fruits,
and hold various kinds of potent, fine liquor whose color and flavor are like water.
Wearing garments of tree bark, he moved among the forest trees like a rishi;
he stayed by the side of a rishi’s hermitage.
He constructed a thatched grass hut and dwelt there.
A seer from one corner of the region eventually came along and saw it;
all the women came out to welcome and greet him.
They offered beautiful flowers and exquisite incense to the rishi,
who was greatly delighted.
The women addressed him with gracious and respectful words.
He inquired after the rishi's well-being,
led him into the room, and seated him upon a fine couch with excellent bedding;
he then provided high-quality, pure liquor as his ritual water for purification.
He gave them *modaka* cakes as fruit;
once they had eaten and drunk their fill,
he spoke to the women, saying:
"Since my birth, I have never before obtained such excellent fruit and such excellent water," the women said.
I have practiced goodness with a single-minded devotion;
therefore, the devas have granted me this.
I pray that I may obtain this fine water and fine fruit.
The seer asked the women,
"For what reason is your complexion so full and flourishing?"
They replied,
"We eat these fine fruits and drink this delicious water."
Therefore, he was so fat.
The woman said to the seer,
"Why do you not dwell here?"
He replied, "I may also stay.
The woman said, "Let us bathe together."
He then agreed to this.
As the women’s hands were soft and supple, his heart stirred upon their touch;
he then began to wash with the women, each washing one another.
As lustful thoughts arose within him, he subsequently engaged in sexual intercourse and immediately lost his supernatural powers; then,
the heavens sent down a great rain.
For seven days and seven nights,
they were provided with food and drink to their hearts' content;
after the seventh day, the wine and food were all exhausted.
He was then served mountain water, wood,
and fruit, which were not delicious;
he requested the previous [food] once more.
He replied, "It has already been exhausted.
Now we shall go together;
there is a place not far from here where it can be obtained."
The seer said, "As you wish," and they immediately went out together.
Not far from the city, they arrived.
The woman then lay down on the road and said,
"I am utterly unable to go any further.
The seer said:
"If you are unable to walk,
mount upon my neck;
I shall carry you."
The woman first sent a messenger to inform the king, saying,
"Your Majesty may observe my intellectual skill.
The king ordered his carriage to be prepared and went out to witness it.
He asked, "By what means did you attain this?
The woman replied to the king:
By the power of my skillful means,
I have now rendered him thus incapable of anything further,
so that he may remain within the city.
He was well-honored and venerated;
this fulfilled my desires,
and he was appointed as a high minister.
Having resided in the city for only a few days, his body became increasingly emaciated;
with a mind focused on meditative concentration, he felt weary of worldly desires.
The king questioned the seer.
"Why are you not joyful?
Your body has become increasingly emaciated.
The seer replied to the king.
Although I have obtained the five desires,
I constantly and personally recollect the quiet and secluded forest groves where the various rishis dwell;
they cannot leave my mind.
The king reflected to himself:
"If one forcibly contravenes another's will, it causes suffering;
when suffering reaches its extreme, death follows."
This was originally sought to eliminate the calamity of drought,
and now it has been achieved.
For what reason, then, should one forcibly seize his resolve?
He then dismissed him.
Having returned to the mountains,
he practiced with such diligence that before long he regained the five supernormal powers.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"That one-horned seer was none other than myself."
That courtesan was none other than Yaśodharā;
at that time, she deluded me with a pill of joy.
"I have not yet severed my fetters and am thus deluded by them;
now you wish to further delude me with the 'Joy-Inducing' medicinal pill,
but this shall not be possible."
For this reason, it is known that the quality of subtle and soft touch can move even a rishi.
How much more so for the foolish!
For various reasons such as these,
this is called the censure of the faults of contact with sensual desire.
Thus, by being able to censure the five desires, one eliminates the five hindrances. 3.
The Conditions for the Five Hindrances. Third Question: It is asked—
What are called the five hindrances?
The answer is: first, the hindrance of sensual desire;
second, the hindrance of ill will.
3. The hindrance of sloth and torpor;
4. The hindrance of restlessness and remorse;
5. The hindrance of doubt.
The first hindrance, the hindrance of sensual desire,
refers to when one sits upright practicing dhyāna and the mind gives rise to thoughts of desire,
with deluded thoughts continuing in succession.
Seeking it without ceasing ultimately leads to the arising of afflictions,
as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Śūrpaka, by thinking of the king’s daughter,
allowed a lustful desire to arise within him; it was powerful enough to burn his own body and extend its flames to the temple.
How much more so when the poison of desire arises and blazes fiercely,
failing to burn away all wholesome dharmas;
if the mind is attached to desire, there is no way to draw near to the Path.
Therefore, a verse in the treatise says:
"One who enters the Way with a sense of shame and remorse, Holding the alms bowl to gather in sentient beings—
How could such a person indulge in the dust of desire, Sinking into the five sensory passions?"
Having already abandoned the pleasures of the five desires and cast them away without looking back,
how could one wish to obtain them again? Like a fool who eats his own vomit,
desires bring suffering when sought and much fear when attained.
When lost, there is much heat and affliction; in all places, there is no joy.
Since all such miseries have been described, how can one abandon them?
By attaining the bliss of meritorious meditative concentration, one will no longer be deceived by them.
Regarding the second hindrance, ill will (*vyāpāda*):
anger is the root of losing all wholesome dharmas and the causal condition for falling into the various evil realms.
An enemy of the joy of the Dharma,
a great thief of the virtuous mind,
and a treasury of evil speech.
The axe and hatchet of calamity:
if one reflects while practicing the Path,
[one sees that] this person vexes oneself and vexes one's kin.
They praise my enemies;
their scheming regarding the past and the future is likewise the same.
These are the nine bases of resentment from which anger arises;
because the thought of anger obscures the mind,
it is called a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*).
One should quickly abandon them so that they do not increase.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* records, Śakra questioned the Buddha with a verse:
"By killing what is one at peace? By killing what is there no sorrow?"
"What is the root of poison that swallows up all goodness?
The Buddha answered with this verse:
"To kill anger is peace; to kill anger is freedom from sorrow."
Hatred is the root of poison; it destroys all that is wholesome.
Having understood this, one should cultivate loving-kindness and compassion.
One should eliminate [anger] through patience to purify the mind.
Contemplating that sounds are empty and provisional, one should not give rise to anger.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
The Bodhisattva knows that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished,
and that their nature is entirely empty. Thus,
even if someone should become angry or revile them, [they remain undisturbed].
Whether struck or killed,
it is like a dream or a magical illusion;
contemplate that sound is fundamentally non-existent.
It is merely the sound of wind;
it exists due to conditions.
Why should one feel anger toward it?
Therefore, the treatise says:
"Just as when one wishes to speak,
the wind within the mouth is called *udāna*."
It returns and enters until it reaches the navel;
upon touching the navel, a resonance emerges.
When the resonance emerges, it touches seven locations and arises from them.
This is called speech.
As a verse says:
"The wind named udāna touches the navel and rises upward."
This wind touches seven places: the nape of the neck, the gums, the teeth, the lips, the tongue, the throat, and the chest. Within these, speech arises;
the foolish do not understand this, and being deluded and attached, they give rise to anger and ignorance.
Furthermore, the *Upāsaka-sūtra* states:
"If a wise person encounters harsh abuse,
they should form this thought:"
These syllables of abuse do not arise simultaneously; when the first syllable arises, [the others have not yet arisen].
The subsequent syllable has not yet arisen;
once the subsequent syllable has arisen, the initial syllable has already ceased.
If they do not occur at the same time,
how can it be called reviling?
It is merely the sound of the wind.
"How could I harbor anger?
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings."
Even if one were reviled for hundreds of thousands of kalpas,
they would not give rise to a mind of anger; likewise, even if praised for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they would not give rise to a mind of attachment.
Nor does one feel joy.
One thoroughly understands that sounds arise and perish like dreams and echoes.
Third is the hindrance of sloth and torpor.
That which refers to the inner mind being clouded and confused is called sleep;
it is the obscuration of the five sensory faculties.
When the limbs and joints are relaxed and one lies prostrate with the body fully extended,
this is called sleep.
This hindrance of sloth and torpor can destroy the true happiness of both this life and future lives;
such is this unwholesome dharma.
This is most unwholesome.
Why is that? Because other hindrances and mental afflictions can be removed.
Sleep is like a dead person who has no sensation or perception;
because there is no awareness, it is difficult to eliminate.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
The Bodhisattva instructed his sleeping disciples,
speaking in verse:
"Do not lie down embracing a corpse— This collection of various impurities falsely named 'person'."
As if afflicted by a grave illness with arrows piercing the body, amidst a mass of all manner of agonies, how can one sleep?
As if a person were bound and led away to execution, with disaster about to descend, how can one sleep?
So long as the bandits of the fetters are not destroyed and harm has not been eliminated, it is like sleeping in the same room with a venomous snake.
It is also like standing on the battlefield amidst white blades; how could one sleep at such a time?
Sleep is a great darkness in which nothing is seen; day after day it deceives and robs one of clarity.
When the mind is shrouded by sleep and nothing is seen, such a great loss—how can one sleep?
The fourth hindrance, restlessness and remorse,
has three aspects.
First is verbal restlessness.
That is to say: taking pleasure in composing verses,
disputing over right and wrong,
and engaging in useless frivolous talk.
Worldly speech and the like are called verbal restlessness.
Second, bodily restlessness:
That is to say: taking pleasure in riding vehicles,
racing about with negligence,
and engaging in feats of strength such as wrestling, clasping the wrists, or striking with the palms.
This is called bodily restlessness.
Third, mental restlessness refers to the mind and its emotions being dissolute and unrestrained.
They allow their minds to wander toward objects of perception,
contemplating literature, arts, worldly skills,
and various unwholesome thoughts and reflections.
This is called mental restlessness.
Restlessness as a dharma destroys the mind of one who has gone forth.
Thus, a verse from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"You have already shaved your head and donned dyed robes; Holding an earthen alms-bowl, you go forth to beg for food.
Why do you delight in and cling to frivolous and restless ways? Through negligence and indulgence of the passions, you lose the benefits of the Dharma."
Having lost both the benefit of the Dharma and worldly happiness,
one should recognize these faults and swiftly abandon them.
Regarding what is called remorse:
if there is agitation without remorse, it does not constitute an obscuration. Why is this?
Because one was still amidst the objects of perception at the time of agitation,
one only later regrets what was previously done when wishing to enter meditative concentration.
Because they shroud the mind with distress and affliction,
they are called "hindrances" (nīvaraṇa).
These are of two kinds.
First, one gives rise to remorse after agitation,
as previously described. Second,
one becomes a perpetrator of great and heavy transgressions.
He constantly harbors fear;
a poisonous arrow has entered his heart,
firmly fixed and impossible to extract.
As a verse in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
Doing what should not be done, And failing to do what should be done—
One is consumed by the fire of regret and remorse, And in future lives falls into the evil realms.
If a person can repent for their transgressions, Having repented, they should no longer grieve;
In this way, the mind is peaceful and happy, And one should not harbor constant attachment to it.
There are two kinds of regret: That which arises from failing to do what ought to be done.
To do what should not be done is the mark of a fool; because one does not repent with the heart,
one is unable to undo the evil deeds already committed after having performed them.
The fifth hindrance, the veil of doubt,
refers to the fact that because the mind is shrouded by doubt,
one cannot attain a concentrated mind regarding all phenomena.
Because they lack a concentrated mind,
they obtain nothing at all within the Buddha-dharma,
like a person who enters a mountain of jewels [but finds nothing].
If one has no hands, there is nothing that can be grasped.
Furthermore, pervasive doubt is very abundant,
yet it does not necessarily obstruct meditative concentration.
Now, there are three kinds of doubt that obstruct meditative concentration.
The first is doubt concerning oneself.
Second, doubting the teacher;
third, doubting the Dharma.
First, doubting oneself:
And they formed this thought:
"Our faculties are dull and darkened, and our karmic defilements are deep and heavy;
are we not non-humans?"
One may harbor such self-doubt that concentration and wisdom fail to arise.
If you wish to study the Dharma, do not disparage yourself;
for the roots of goodness from past lives are difficult to fathom.
Second, as for doubting the teacher:
"The person's deportment and appearance are such;
since he himself lacks the Way, how could he possibly teach me?"
To harbor such doubt and arrogance constitutes an obstruction to meditative concentration.
The method for eliminating it is as follows:
It is like gold within a stinking leather bag;
because of one's greed for the gold,
one cannot discard the leather bag.
The practitioner is likewise:
even if the teacher is not pure,
one should still conceive of them as a Buddha.
Regarding the third method for dispelling doubt:
it is like when people of the world mostly cling to their own original minds regarding the teachings they have received.
One cannot immediately accept and practice it with a mind of faith and reverence.
If doubt arises, the mind will not be defiled by the Dharma. Why is this?
As a verse in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"Just as a person at a forked road Is filled with doubt and takes nothing,
So too is it with doubt Regarding the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena."
Because of doubt, one does not diligently seek the true mark of all phenomena.
This doubt arises from delusion; it is the worst among evils within both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, as well as within saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Be certain that these phenomena truly exist; do not give rise to doubt regarding them.
If you harbor such doubts, the wardens of the King of Death will bind you, and like a lion seizing a deer, you shall find no liberation.
