when Pāṇḍu went out on an excursion,
he exhorted his two wives.
"Whoever among you reaches [the destination] first after following behind me shall enjoy a day of supreme pleasure with me;
as for those who follow later, I shall not see them."
After the king had departed,
the two queens adorned themselves most elaborately,
prepared their carriages, and went together to meet him on the road.
Upon seeing a member of the Brahmin caste at a celestial shrine,
he descended from his carriage and paid his respects; having finished his prostrations, he proceeded further.
The king followed his original words and did not go forward.
Thereupon, the lady grew resentful toward the heavenly deity, saying,
"Because of my paying you honor, the king has treated me with contempt."
"If you possess divine power, why do you not protect me?
Thereafter, he destroyed the celestial shrine until it was level with the ground.
The deity who guarded the shrine, overcome with grief and distress, went to his palace.
Desiring to cause harm to the royal palace,
a celestial deity blocked him and would not allow him to enter.
There was a certain rishi dwelling in the mountains.
The king constantly made offerings to him;
every day at mealtime, he would fly into the palace,
not eating the delicacies but partaking only of coarse food and simple provisions.
Once, on a day when the rishi did not come,
a deva, knowing this, manifested his form and sat in his usual place, refusing to partake of the food.
Desiring fish and meat,
he prepared food according to those words and returned;
the next morning, when the former seer arrived, he provided him with meat.
The rishi grew angry with the king and said, "Great Seer,
you commanded me to prepare this food the day before yesterday; why do you not eat it now?"
The seer said, "I was ill yesterday and did not come.
Who told you this?"
It was merely because they treated him with contempt and tested him that the king,
for twelve years thereafter, constantly ate human flesh.
Having finished speaking these words, he flew back to the mountains.
Thereafter, the kitchen supervisor forgot and failed to prepare the meat;
when the time came, he was at a loss for a plan.
He went out to seek meat and saw a dead infant,
plump and white, lying on the ground. He thought to himself,
"This will serve as a meal for my urgent need."
He then carried [the meat], with its head and feet removed, to the kitchen;
having prepared it with various exquisite medicinal herbs, he made food for the king.
When the king ate it, he perceived that its flavor was twice as excellent as usual.
He immediately questioned the kitchen supervisor:
"In all my years of eating meat, I have never encountered such excellence as this.
What kind of meat is this?"
The kitchen supervisor, trembling with fear, struck his chest before the king and said,
"If Your Majesty would pardon my offense,
I would dare to speak the truth."
The king replied to him,
saying, "Simply speak the truth;
I shall not question you regarding your offense."
The kitchen supervisor reported this to the king, recounting the previous events in detail.
The king said,
"This meat is most delicious."
"From this day forward, we shall seek to provide [the food] in this manner.
The kitchen supervisor informed the king:
"Previously, we happened upon a dead child, but seeking another, it could not be found."
The king spoke again, saying:
"You need only take it secretly;
even if there is someone who notices the place where it was cut, that shall be my responsibility."
The kitchen supervisor received these instructions.
Every night he would secretly seize the opportunity to kill him,
providing his flesh to the king day after day.
At that time, the people within the city each wailed as they went about,
crying out that their young children had perished;
they questioned one another in turn, asking how such a thing could have come to pass.
The ministers gathered for consultation,
deciding that they should test him by observing him closely;
they immediately stationed people in various places throughout the streets and neighborhoods.
He saw the king’s kitchen supervisor stealing another man’s child;
he watched him, captured him, bound him, and led him before the king,
reporting the matter in full as it had occurred.
The king said,
"This was my instruction.
The ministers, harboring resentment, each began to discuss the matter among themselves outside.
"The king is a thief who devours our children.
How can we rule together with a king who eats his own people?
We must join forces to eliminate him and remove this calamity."
With one mind, they all deliberated together;
simultaneously uniting, they immediately surrounded the king,
intending to capture and kill him.
When the king saw the assembled troops, he was struck with alarm and fear, and asked,
"For what reason are you surrounding and pressuring me?
The ministers replied:
Now, for one who is a king,
the cultivation of the people is his primary task;
yet you are currently driving them into the kitchen to kill them for food.
Unable to endure such bitter cruelty,
he wished to kill the king.
The king spoke to his ministers.
"From this day forward, we shall never do so again.
We beg only for your compassionate pardon; we shall reform ourselves and exert ourselves.
The ministers said:
"I shall never let you go; there is no need for further words.
When the king heard this, he knew for certain that he would die, and he immediately spoke to his ministers.
"Even though you are about to kill me, please grant me a brief moment's reprieve so that I may hear a single word.
He then made a vow of his own.
The virtuous deeds I have practiced since time immemorial,
my righteous governance as king,
and the merit accumulated through making offerings to sages— [all these I dedicate].
"May this merit cause me to become a flying rākṣasa this very day.
As soon as these words were finished,
he was transformed accordingly and immediately flew into the void.
He addressed his ministers, saying:
"You have all joined your forces in an attempt to kill me by force.
By great good fortune, I was able to extricate myself."
"From this day forward, you must endure well.
I shall eat your beloved wives and children one after another.
Having spoken thus, he flew away.
Dwelling among the mountain forests, they flew about and seized people,
carrying them off as food;
the various classes of people lived in terror, hiding and seeking refuge.
Thereafter, he killed and devoured many people.
Various rākṣasas joined him as his followers,
and as his retinue gradually increased, the scope of those he harmed expanded accordingly.
"Later, we shall serve King Pāṇḍurapāda as our king;
we pray that you will join us for a single assembly."
The king immediately granted his permission,
saying, "I shall summon the various kings so that they number five hundred;
I will hold a gathering for you with them."
Having granted his permission,
[the king] went one by one to seize them and confined them in the deep mountains;
thus he had already captured four hundred and ninety-nine kings.
One person remained missing.
Later, Sudāsa-mi was captured; he was a man of great virtue and high spiritual attainment.
He requested a seven-day leave from the Rākṣasa King;
when the leave expired,
he returned and extensively preached the Dharma to Sutasoma.
He analyzed the crime of killing and its evil retribution,
and further explained the merit of compassionately refraining from killing.
Pāda-lekhana was filled with joy and paid him reverent homage.
Having received and practiced his teaching, they no longer harbored any harmful intent.
They immediately released all the kings, each returning to their own country.
Thus it was with Sudāsa.
Even if the soldiers were to return Pañcapāda to his own country,
once the twelve-year vow undertaken by the former seer was fulfilled,
from that time forward he would no longer eat human beings.
He then returned to the kingdom of Śrāvastī and governed the people as before.
At that time, King Sudāsa was none other than my own self.
The king Pādapāṇi was none other than Aṅgulimāla at present.
At that time, for twelve years, all the people...
Those who were devoured by King Pādapāṇi are these very people now being killed by Aṅgulimāla. These individuals—
"In life after life, he was always killed by Aṅgulimāla;
yet in life after life, I subdued him through goodness.
As for Aṅgulimāla..."
At that time, King Prasenajit again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"As for the bhikṣu Aṅgulimāla..."
"If one kills this person, eats much of their flesh, and attains the Way,
will they still receive retribution?
The Buddha told him:
"Great King,
every action must have its retribution.
This bhikṣu is currently in his cell."
The fires of hell issued forth from his pores;
the extreme suffering and agony were so piercing that they were beyond description.
The Buddha then commanded a bhikṣu.
"Take this door-bolt and go to the cell of Aṅgulimāla; thrust it into the keyhole.
The bhikṣu immediately went and carried out the instruction.
As soon as the bolt entered the interior of the door, it instantly melted away.
The bhikṣu, filled with astonishment, returned and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu,
"Such is the retribution for one's actions."
The king and the entire assembly believed and understood this without exception.
The verse says:
Wealth, sensual pleasure, and wine— These are called the three delusions. If a minister is addicted to them, he ruins his house.
Your Majesty values the preservation of a state; Fleshly obstructions hinder great compassion. Fortunately, this impurity shields pure virtue.
A gentleman who cherishes the Way would not desire such filth.

Section Twenty-Seven: Divination and Physiognomy. This section has three parts: the narrative of the intention, the narrative of observing signs, and the narrative of returning to faith. 1. Narrative of the Intention (First): As for the Great Teaching, it is impartial.
Supreme virtue moves all in common,
yet the karmic actions of ordinary beings and the creative transformations of the cosmos follow divergent paths.
The mind and its objects are mutually opposed,
and the retributions of suffering and pleasure differ,
just as a wax seal is impressed upon clay.
The seals manifest as written characters;
once the signs of karma are distinguished,
the retribution can be discerned.
Therefore, humans and animals are distinguished by their respective sounds;
Hu and Han are differentiated by their physical forms;
and the noble and the humble possess the distinction of honor and subordination.
The noble and the ordinary differ in terms of good and evil.
Second, regarding the contemplation of characteristics and conditions, as stated in the *Sūtra on Right View*:
At that time, within the assembly of the Buddha...
There was a bhikṣu named Samyagdṛṣṭi who,
although he had entered the dharma-robes, harbored a doubtful thought, saying:
The Buddha has taught that there is rebirth in future lives;
yet, when it comes to human death, there is no mutual retribution. How is this known?
Even before this question was asked, the Buddha had already foreknown it.
The Buddha told his disciples:
"It is like the root of a tree."
From a single seed, nurtured by the four great elements,
it naturally attains great growth through sprouts, leaves, stems, and nodes;
undergoing successive transformations, it eventually becomes a great tree.
The tree again produced fruit, and the fruit again became trees;
they increased with the passing of years and months in this manner, beyond measure.
The Buddha told his disciples:
"Suppose one wished to gather together the flowers, fruits, stalks, and nodes and restore them once more to the state of a seed—
would this be possible?"
The disciples said,
"It cannot be obtained;
it has already undergone transformation and is daily decaying."
The rebirth of the seed-nucleus is thus infinite;
yet as it is repeatedly born and repeatedly transformed, it ultimately all returns to decay,
such that it can never again be restored to its original seed-nucleus.
The Buddha told his disciples:
"Birth and death are also like this;
they originally arise from ignorance and are formed through a continuous succession."
The consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna*) transmigrates through the twelve links of dependent origination;
driven by its karma, it encounters further parents and receives another physical form, no longer recognizing its former state.
One must not turn back or report [this].
It is like a householder who smelts ore to make iron,
and casts the iron into vessels.
"Can that which has been fashioned into a vessel be made into stone again? Sajjñā replied,
"Indeed, it is impossible for iron to become stone."
The Buddha said:
"Consciousness transmigrates and dwells in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
just as stone is transformed into iron."
The transformation into the body of another is like iron being fashioned into a vessel;
once its form has dissolved and its substance changed, it cannot be restored to its original state.
Therefore, when consciousness receives a human body, there are further parents.
Once parents have been obtained, there are six obstructions:
first, abiding in the intermediate state (antarābhava), one cannot return;
second, falling into the womb within the body one is to receive.
Third, because of the delusion caused by the pain of birth, there is perception and ideation of consciousness.
Fourth, because of falling to the ground after birth, the perceptions and memories of what was previously known perish,
and new views and perceptions arise once more.
Fifth, because one becomes attached to food as soon as it has been produced, the mindfulness of consciousness is severed.
Sixth, from birth until one grows up, one practices what is new and no longer possesses the consciousness of the past.
The Buddha said:
Disciples, when the consciousness falls into rebirth as good or evil,
what one perceives at the moment of death follows one's past conduct and is not as it was before.
Because the body cannot again return to consciousness,
he answered directly and clearly.
He had not yet conceived the aspiration for the Way, nor did he possess the pure eye.
When the body dies and consciousness departs, it undergoes transformation according to its course;
as it transmigrates to receive another physical form, how could there be mutual retribution?
It is like the moon on a dark night shrouded in shadow.
If objects of five colors are placed in deep darkness,
thousands of millions of people will be unable to see them;
yet if a person holds a torch to illuminate them, they can distinguish all five colors.
Like foolish people,
obscured by darkness on an evil path and lacking the eye of wisdom,
they come and go in mutual retribution like the night of the new moon.
If one wishes to see the five colors, in the end they cannot be seen;
yet if one cultivates the sutras and precepts and restrains the mind,
it will be like holding a torch to distinguish various forms.
It is like one without hands wishing to write,
one without eyes wishing to see,
or threading a needle in the dark of night.
To seek fire within water can never result in its attainment. You, my disciples—
Diligently practicing the sutras and precepts, he deeply contemplates birth and death:
from where does one originally come, and to what place does one ultimately return?
Having attained purity and eliminated his fetters, his doubts were naturally resolved.
Having correctly heard and seen this, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions for Prince Dharmavivardhana of King Aśoka Losing His Eyes* states:
"Each of the six realms of existence has its own distinct characteristics."
Regarding the first appearance of hell:
O people, the root of the faculties wanders through birth and death; drifting and lingering, it rushes about and falls into the five destinies.
That one, having finally passed away there, is born here; all of this has its causes and conditions.
The characteristics of this person’s faculties I shall now explain for you: their gait is unsteady and they are unaware of it;
their vision is dazed and confused; they are constantly prone to forgetfulness, and their movements are light and fickle;
they wander aimlessly through the wilderness—this person has [fallen away] from...
Those from the Reviving Hell come with aching and painful limbs; they wake from sleep in terror, their dreams being of evil portents.
Those from the Black Rope Hell come with coarse hair, distorted eyes, and long teeth;
they are prone to anger, their voices are turbid, and they are violent and impetuous. Those from the Crushing Hell come...
Their voices are loud and high; they lack a sense of shame and remorse.
They delight in quarreling and shouting, unable to distinguish truth from falsehood. While sleeping, they groan and moan, frequently waking in terror with cries.
You should know that such people have come from the Weeping Hell; they constantly take pleasure in lamenting and weeping.
Climbing high to gaze into the distance, they are fond of quarreling with their family members;
they harbor no sense of kinship or intimacy, and words immediately provoke anger. They do not eat for days on end.
This person originally came from a place of great wailing and weeping; their body is large while their feet are thin, and their physical strength is meager.
The speech is choked and the voice is like that of a broken jar;
the consciousness is unsettled and the mind lacks filial piety. One should know that this person has come from the Avīci Hell;
their body is coarse and ugly, they suffer long-term cold and shivering, and they crave heat and delight in thirst.
Stingy, greedy, and envious, seeing others bestow gifts, they give rise to afflictions within themselves.
Such people have come from the Hot Hell; seeing fire, they are terrified yet also rejoice in its warmth.
Their gait is light and nimble, and they pay no heed to the proper timing of things.
Having regretted what was done, they wish to give again. This person comes forth once more from the Great Heat Hell;
having small eyes and being prone to anger, they forget much of what they have received and are narrow-minded in their actions, lacking a vast heart, and feeling terror upon seeing what is great.
Regarding those who indulge in petty pleasures, such persons come from the Utpala Hell;
they have red eyes and an ugly form, always delighting in strife and litigation,
slandering the sages and all who have attained the Way, and observing people day and night for unlawful conduct.
It should be known that this person has come from the Paduma hell;
their eyes are shaped like triangles, they are unfilial toward their two parents, and they are short-lived from birth.
Having come from the Kumuda hell, they are fond of wearing swords and blades, they forcibly incite others to fight, and they will certainly be killed by others.
Having come from the Bhṛtīya hell, his body is covered in sores and wounds; the breath from his mouth is foul-smelling, and he has no intimacy with others.
Having come from the Kānta hell, his physical form is massive yet his gait is feeble and weak;
he has sparse hair and thin skin, and is constantly afflicted by many ailments.
One who becomes angry upon seeing others, who is gluttonous and never satisfied—know that this person has come from the Hell of Blazing Flames.
Their body is pale and their eyes are blue; when they speak, foam flows from their mouth and their words lack coherence.
They delight in playing with dust and soil, and they gaze upon deep, muddy swamps.
Lying upon it, this person follows from the Ash Hell;
with a head wrapped and yellow eyes, he is loathsome for others to behold. Coming from the Sword-Tree Hell, he is terrified when facing matters;
his hands constantly hold a blade, and he rejoices whenever he hears of a fight.
Slain by blades, they come from the Hell of Swords; their bodies are black, their throats are constricted, and they find joy only in dark chambers.
From the Hell of Hot Ashes, they emerge with feeble strength and scant breath, lacking self-mastery regarding what is beneficial or harmful.
First, one has no autonomy. Even if one sees an animal being slaughtered, if one does not leave its side, know that this person has come from the Hell of Flaying. Their anger and joy are unstable;
if they immediately recognize their change of heart and repent, and are able to offer an apology at that moment, they will not remain there for even a day or a night.
His mind is filled with remorse as if he were undergoing punishment. This person has come from the Kumbha hell;
he delights in dwelling in foul-smelling places, prefers coarse and wretched food, and wears ugly clothing.
Having come from the excrement hell, his complexion is hideous.
With coarse and harsh speech, fond of slandering and inciting strife—when you see those who come from the Sūcīla-mukha hell, observe these features;
know the place from which they come and stay far away from them as if avoiding the conflagration at the end of an eon. Such, in brief, are the signs of the hells.
Second, regarding the characteristics of animals:
next, the animals are described. Their physical forms are diverse and distinct;
they contemplate with focused minds and do not create the conditions for rebirth there. Their speech is slow and sluggish, and they do not give rise to anger.
Humble and respectful toward elders; its form originates from the elephant. Its body is large, foul-smelling, and capable of enduring cold and heat;
it is fierce, prone to anger, and difficult to appease. Originating from the camel, it is capable of long journeys and eats voraciously;
it does not avoid dangerous obstacles, remembers past events, and discerns the truth.
Coming from among horses, they are gracious, harmonious, and broad-minded; they can endure cold and heat, and their actions are neutral.
Coming from among oxen, they have loud voices and no sense of shame;
they are full of affectionate thoughts, yet cannot distinguish between right and wrong. Coming from among donkeys, [they are dull-witted].
Fearless among the old and the young, always craving meat, not finding difficulty in various matters—such beings come from lions.
Tall in stature with round eyes, roaming the wilderness while harboring hatred and jealousy toward their wives and children—such beings come from tigers. Having long fur and small eyes.
With little anger, they do not delight in staying in one place; having come from among birds, their nature is fickle.
They take pleasure in killing and sorcery; having come from among foxes, they delight in solitude and dwell in burial mounds.
Their voices are faint and they lack vigor; they are free from lustful desire.
Having no affection for wife or children, one comes from among wolves;
Disliking fine clothing and serving to catch those who commit adultery, one comes from among dogs.
Sleeping little and prone to anger, with a short body and long hair, Greedy for food and fond of sleep, one does not delight in clean places.
Coming from among pigs, their hair is yellow and they are sudden and violent;
they take solitary pleasure in mountains and hills and greedily devour flowers and fruits—these come from among monkeys.
They are full of delusions, have forced smiles, and know no fear or difficulty; they understand how to act with duplicity—these come from among crows.
Abounding in lustful desires and deficient in propriety and righteousness, their minds lack discernment;
they have come from among the pigeons. Their conduct is perverse and contrary, they are eloquent yet endure insults, and they are unfilial toward their parents;
they have come from among the cormorants, and likewise do not know the Dharma.
Furthermore, they do not know what is wrong; day and night they are deluded and confused.
Coming from among sheep, they are fond of idle chatter; they frequently associate with the noble families and are beloved by the masses.
Coming from among parrots, their conduct is impetuous and violent, and they delight in being among crowds of people.
Their speech is verbose and troublesome; they come from among the mynas. Their gait is slow and relaxed, as if their minds were preoccupied with some design;
they cause much harm to living beings. They come from among the cranes;
their bodies are small and they are fond of lust. Their minds are not focused or settled; upon seeing forms, their hearts become deluded.
Coming from among sparrows: their eyes are red and their teeth are short; when they speak, they spit foam, and when they lie down, it entangles their bodies.
Coming from among vipers: when they speak, they are full of rage and do not examine the meaning of what comes;
fire and poison issue from their mouths. Coming from among *viṣa* (poisonous) birds: [the same characteristics as above].
Living alone and greedy for food, making sounds and gasping in the dark; sleeping little at night—these come from among cats.
Breaking through walls to steal, coveting wealth, bold and fearful, showing no distinction between kin and stranger—these come from among rats. Contemplate these characteristics deeply.
The third type of hungry ghost, coming from the realm of animals, is tall and filled with great fear;
they wrap their bodies in their own hair and wear garments soiled with filth.
Coming from the realm of hungry ghosts, they are lewd, dissolute, stingy, and greedy, and they envy what others have obtained.
Having no fondness for giving, they come from among the hungry ghosts;
being unfilial toward their parents and the members of their household, great and small, they engage in strife and litigation whenever they move.
Coming from among the hungry ghosts, they do not believe in ultimate sincerity; whatever they undertake, they possess little strength and meager knowledge.
Coming from the realm of hungry ghosts, their voices are broken and their resonance stifled;

they suddenly give rise to anger, and when eating, their food is always too hot. Coming from the realm of hungry ghosts, they are perpetually lacking wealth and goods, empty, poor, and wretched, held in derision by the wise. Coming from the realm of hungry ghosts.
One who does not serve the Buddha at the gate, nor delights in hearing the Dharma, has forever severed the path to heaven;

such a person comes from among the hungry ghosts. One who fails to instruct their wife, children, brothers, or sisters, and is loathed and envied by others, comes from among the hungry ghosts; such a person is born naked and destitute.
No one looks upon them; in the end, they receive nothing. Not freed from past conditions, their will is narrow and base;
they take no pleasure in honor or adornment. Their conduct is ugly;
having come from the realm of hungry ghosts, what they do brings no gain, and all their actions are fraught with vexation.
Driven away by others, they come from the realm of hungry ghosts (preta). Deluded by affairs and delighting in ruin, they fail to examine the fundamental source.

They do not accept the admonitions of others; coming from the realm of hungry ghosts, they take no pleasure in quietude but delight in dwelling in latrines and cesspools, their countenances foul and filthy.
Coming from the wind deities, their bodies are large and they are fond of pleasure;
they delight in craving meat and enjoy solitary shrines. Coming from the yakṣas, they are fierce in anger and prone to combat;
they are greedy for whatever they see and are devoid of mindfulness or forgetfulness. Coming from the yakṣas, they are devoid of mindfulness or forgetfulness.
Those who see him have their hair stand on end; he strides straight forward, gazing intently. He appears as if he has come from a *rākṣasa* after losing something;
his body is slender and his skin thin, yet his countenance is harmonious and pleasant, and he rejoices upon hearing music.
When a *gandharva* comes, his mind is fond of lightness and his gait is airy.
Anointed with fragrant perfumes, they possess many arts and skills;
the gandharvas come constantly, ever delighting in song and dance. Transmitted from father to son, they speak first and then laugh.
Coming from among the kiṃnaras, their dispositions are gentle and supple, and they understand the proper seasons.
Able to sever the outflows and fetters— The Candra (Gandharva) has arrived.
These characteristics of the hungry ghosts, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and fourthly the asuras:
Round eyes and square faces, Yellow bodies with golden hair, Fully equipped with all arts and skills.
When an asura approaches, he strides straight forward and gazes at the ground;

having no doubts or difficulties, he sees his enemy and strikes him immediately. When an asura approaches—this is a brief description of the characteristics of the fifth type of person among the asuras.
Knowing the destination of rebirth and never forgetting what has been grasped;
understanding that all undertakings come from the human realm; comprehending all illusions and deceptions;
remaining unperturbed by what is done and maintaining equanimity; knowing that both good and evil words come from the human realm.
Never forgetting from the beginning, they do not believe in craftiness or falsehood.
Coming from the human realm, they are characterized by greed, lust, stinginess, and envy; their minds are stubborn and difficult to relinquish.
Only when fully liberated do they understand worldly customs and come from the human realm; with faithful intent they practice generous giving, understanding what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma.
The mind does not lean toward that [other realm]; having come from the human path, one does not miss the proper seasons nor is one indolent. One reveres the worthy and the holy;
having come from the human path, if one encounters a śramaṇa who upholds the precepts and is widely learned, one serves him with a sincere heart.
Coming from the human realm, they serve and attend upon the Buddhas; they hear the True Dharma and the assembly of monks at the proper times.
Coming from the human realm, they are able to understand the Dharma upon hearing it;
hearing of evil, they do not commit it; they swiftly return to Nirvana. Coming from the human realm.
This is the human form; a rough description of its appearance is given.
As for the characteristics of the Sixth Heaven, there are five kinds of deities dwelling upon Mount Sumeru, based on the causal conditions originally created.
Their physical characteristics differ: their waists are slender while their legs are thick; they always delight in smiling.

The wise should observe that those who come from the *Kuru* heaven have refined minds, possess little wealth, and feel fear when witnessing conflict. Those who come from the *Pūrvavideha* heaven [have these traits].
Tall in stature and white of body, with a countenance that is upright and handsome;
not fond of the light of fire, he comes from the realm of Brahmā. Always harboring joy and delight, he is not terrified upon hearing evil;
he does not accept it, having come from the realm of Nanda, where he contemplates and endures suffering.
Though skilled in discerning meanings and filial toward his parents, Vaiśravaṇa came to lodge with him, yet he found no joy in the home.
Delighting in wandering through forests and thickets, his mind was set on the beauty of women;
though his wealth and treasures were vast, he was born into a lowly and humble family.
Delighting in mental purity, he comes from the Heaven of the Three Heavens; though he acts according to his own will, he lacks mastery over himself.
His hopes are severed and his vows are fulfilled as he comes from the Yāma Heaven, finding pleasure in the lust of others and failing to guard his own wife, driven by ghosts.
Coming from the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, he serves his parents; constantly following the principles of the Dharma, he takes upon himself the shortcomings of others.
Coming from the Tuṣita Heaven, he seeks the Way through non-worldly means with a mind free from stinginess; having no delight in the household life, he comes from the Brahma Heaven.
Their dispositions are such that they constantly crave sleep; they do not understand the Dharma and come from the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*).
Among the sentient beings of the six realms of existence, each possesses a fundamental nature and conduct that differs, and their aspirations and characters are distinct.
3. The Third Chapter on the Conditions for Faith. As stated in the *Sūtra of the Questions of King Milinda* concerning the Bhikṣu Nāgasena:
At that time, there was King Milinda, who addressed the Arhat Bhikṣu Nāgasena, saying:
If a person commits evil throughout their life in this world until they reach a hundred years of age,
yet at the moment of death recollects the Buddha,
they will be reborn in heaven after death.
I do not believe these words.
Furthermore, you say that upon killing a single sentient being,
one enters niraya immediately after death.
"I also do not believe this.
The bhikṣu Nāgasena asked the king:
"Suppose a person were to take a small stone and place it upon the water."
"Does the stone float or sink?
The king replied,
"The stone sinks."
Nāgasena said:
"Suppose one were to place a hundred large stones upon a boat;
would that boat sink?"
The king said,
"It does not sink. Nāgasena said:
A hundred large stones in a boat do not sink because of the boat; likewise,
although a person may possess inherent evil,
if they contemplate the Buddha for even a single moment, [they are saved].
Because of this, one does not enter niraya but is instead reborn in the heavens.
Why do you not believe it?
As for those small stones that sank—
Just as a person who commits evil and does not know the Buddhist scriptures enters hell after death,
why do you not believe?
The king said,
"Excellent, excellent!
The bhikṣu Nāgasena said:
It is like two people who both die:
one is reborn in the seventh Brahma-heaven,
while the other is reborn in the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
Although these two individuals differ in their distance [from death],
they will arrive at it simultaneously;
it is like a pair of birds flying together.
One perched upon a high tree,
and one perched upon a low tree;
when both birds flew away at the same time, their shadows reached the ground simultaneously.
The Bhikṣu Nāgasena said:
"Just as when a fool commits an evil deed he incurs great retribution,
whereas when a wise person commits an evil deed he incurs only slight retribution."
It is like a piece of heated iron lying on the ground:
one person knows it is heated iron, while another does not.
Both took [the food],
yet the one who did not know [it was hot] had his hand severely burned,
while the one who knew [it was hot] suffered only slight damage.
The same applies to committing evil;
because the fool cannot repent for himself,
his calamity becomes great.
When a wise person commits an evil deed,
because they know it was improper and repent daily,
their calamity is slight.
Furthermore, the *Fourfold Sutra on Training* states:
"Ordinary worldly people may sometimes be inferior even to animals,
while animals may at times surpass humans."
Why is this? Because people commit sins without ceasing;
upon death, they enter hell.
When their retribution for these sins is completed, they first become hungry ghosts; when their retribution as hungry ghosts is completed, they are reborn as animals;
and when their retribution as animals is completed, they finally return to being human.
Having exhausted their retribution among animals,
they shall then become human beings;
therefore, one should diligently perform wholesome deeds.
By revering the teachings of the Three Honored Ones,
one shall long remain free from the three evil realms and receive the blessings of devas and humans;
thereafter, one shall attain eternal liberation.
Furthermore, the Sutra in Forty-two Sections states:
The Buddha said,
"There are five difficulties in the world."
It is difficult for the poor to practice giving;
it is difficult for the wealthy and noble to study the Way;
it is difficult to master one's life so as not to die.
It is difficult to behold the Buddha’s sutras;
it is difficult to be born during the time of a Buddha.
Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra* says:
There are eighteen things that are extremely difficult to encounter in this world.
First, it is difficult to encounter the era of a Buddha.
Second, even if one encounters a Buddha, it is difficult to obtain a human birth.
Third, even if one becomes a human being, there is the difficulty of being born in a central land.
Fourth, even if one is born in a central land, there is the difficulty of being born into a family of noble lineage.
Fifth, even if one is born into a family of noble lineage...
It is difficult for the four limbs and six sense organs to be fully complete.
It is difficult for the six internal faculties and four limbs to be fully complete.
It is difficult to acquire wealth and property.
Seventh, even if one acquires wealth and property, it is difficult to encounter a virtuous spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
Eighth, even if one encounters a virtuous spiritual friend, it is difficult for them to possess wisdom.
Ninth, even if one possesses wisdom, it is difficult for that wisdom to be endowed with a virtuous mind.
Tenth, even if one succeeds in giving with a virtuous mind,
it is difficult; eleventh, even if one is able to give,
it is difficult to find a person who is worthy, excellent, and endowed with virtue.
Twelfth, even if one happens to meet a worthy and virtuous person,
it is difficult to go before them; thirteenth,
even if one reaches their presence, it is difficult to act with propriety and suitability.
14. Even if one attains what is appropriate and fitting, one may still encounter difficulties in receiving and listening to the teachings.
15. Even if one listens to and hears the teachings...
Sixteenth, even if one attains understanding,
it is difficult to be able to receive the profound sūtras.
Seventeenth, even if one is able to receive the profound sūtras...
It is difficult to practice according to what has been taught.
Even if one were able to receive profound sutras,
it is difficult to practice according to what has been taught.
It is difficult to realize the fruits of the noble path.
These constitute the eighteen difficulties.
Furthermore, a verse from the *Zuìyèbàiyìng jīng* (*Sūtra on the Retribution of Sinful Karma*) says:
The flow of water is never constant; A blazing fire does not burn for long;
The sun sets in an instant; And the full moon soon wanes again.
Even those who are honored, illustrious, and noble— Impermanence exceeds even this.
Therefore, know that a human body is difficult to encounter and easy to lose;
because it is easy to lose, one should not give rise to attachment toward it.
One should know that the human body approaches death with every thought-moment,
like a pig or a sheep being led to the slaughterhouse.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
Observe this life-span:
it is constantly surrounded by immeasurable enemies;
it diminishes with every thought-moment and never increases.
It is like a torrential stream that cannot remain still;
it is like the morning mist whose momentum does not last long;
it is like a prisoner being led to the marketplace, drawing closer to death with every step.
Furthermore, a verse from the Māyā-sūtra says:
"Just as a caṇḍāla driving an ox toward the slaughterhouse approaches the ground of death with every step—
the life of a human being passes even more swiftly than this."
Furthermore, it is said in the Śuka Sūtra:
The brahmin youth Śuka addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that a layperson in white robes can cultivate roots of merit and wholesome roots more excellently than one who has gone forth?"
The Buddha said,
"In this matter, I do not give a definitive answer;
there may be those who have left the household life yet have not cultivated roots of goodness."
"Then it is not as good as remaining at home.

If one can practice while at home, that is superior. This is stated as a judgment; however, because those who have left the home life possess a more profound understanding of the Dharma, they are superior to those at home. Thus, it is said that [the former] is not equal to the person who has left the home life. Furthermore, the *Sāhasrika-vaipulya-vinaya* (Three Thousand Codes of Conduct) states:
The tasks to be performed by those who have left the household life are:
first, sitting in meditation;
second, reciting the scriptures and the Dharma.
Third is the encouragement and transformation of various matters.
If one fully performs these three types of actions,
this accords with the dharma of those who have left the household life.
If one does not practice,
one's life is lived in vain and one dies in vain, possessing nothing but the causes for undergoing retribution.
Furthermore, the *Śatākavavadāna-sūtra* (The Sutra of One Hundred Parables) says:
Once there was a man who required both fire and cold water for his use.
He immediately kept a fire burning and placed a vessel filled with dry water upon the fire.
Later, when he wished to obtain fire, the fire was completely extinguished;
when he wished to obtain cold water, the water became hot again.
Thus, both things—the fire and the cold water—were lost.
People of the world enter into the Buddha-dharma, leave the household life, and seek the Way.
Having already left the household life...
He again thinks of the pleasures of his wife, children, and the five desires;
for this reason, he loses the fire of his merit and simultaneously loses the water of his observance of the precepts.
Those who harbor desires are also like this.
A verse says:
Good and evil differ in nature; The paths of sages and ordinary people converge; Though the five aggregates are the same, [their realization differs].
The six realms deviate from the Dharma; by observing signs and colors, one knows that the various forms of suffering and joy are each the result of prior karma. Who is able to restrain this?
(From the *Compendium of Essential Scriptures*, Volume XVII)
*Compendium of Essential Passages from the Various Sutras*, Volume 18, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoshi of Ximing Monastery.
Section 28: The Hell Division. This section consists of eight parts.

Preface to the Intent; Conditions for Convergence; Conditions for Receiving Retribution; Conditions of Time and Quantity; Conditions of the Master of the Canon; Conditions of the Royal Capital; Conditions of Karmic Causes; Conditions of Admonition. 1. Preface to the Intent (The First Section): Now, regarding those who sustain the current [of the Dharma]:
It is not as good as blocking its source;
and raising boiling water is not as effective as extinguishing the fire.
Why is this? The source originates from water;
as long as the source is not blocked, the water will never be exhausted.
Fire boils within the cauldron;
as long as the fire is not extinguished, how could the boiling cease?
Thus, there are those who seek to block the source.
A flowing stream dries up of its own accord without being dammed;
the guest who extinguishes the fire stops the boiling water of its own accord without having to ladle it out.
By discussing matters in this manner,
one may gain a detailed understanding.
For example, as for those who are weary of their fruits:
It is not as good as drawing upon its causes;
how could it compare to being struck with fear by its suffering?
It is surely not as effective as taking warning from its evils.
Causes depend upon effects;
as long as causes are not severed, effects will never cease.
Evil arises from suffering.
If evil is not punished, how can suffering cease?
Thus, those who have severed the causes do not wait for the fruits to exhaust themselves.
The virtuous who punish evil do not fear suffering but abandon it of their own accord;
may all you gentlemen do likewise.
Is this a record of his admonitions?
Second, regarding the title "Conditions of Convergence": Question:
What is meant by the term "hell" (niraya)?
Answer: According to the *Lokaprajñapti-abhidharma-śāstra*,
the Sanskrit name is *niraya* because there is no playful enjoyment (*nir-līlā*) and no joyous pleasure (*nir-āhlāda*).
Furthermore, because there is no emergence through practice;
furthermore, because there is no merit;
and furthermore, because the causes—the non-removal and non-abandonment of evil karma—persist.
It arises therein.
Furthermore, it is said that this path is the most inferior within the desire realm.
It is called "non-path. Because of this matter, hell is termed *niraya*.
As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*,
they are called "those who lack mastery," referring to those sinful persons.
Because they are constrained and controlled by the hell-warden Ābāng,
and lack autonomy,
it is called "hell" (dīyù).
It is also called "unpleasant" (a-nabhirāma);
therefore it is named hell (naraka).
Furthermore, "earth" (nara) means "bottom" (tala).
This refers to the "bottom.
Among all things, the earth is situated at the very lowest;
therefore, it is called the "bottom."
"Prison" (yù) signifies confinement.
Confinement means being restricted and unable to act with autonomy;
therefore, it is called "hell" (dìyù).
The term "niraya" is a Sanskrit word meaning "non-existence.
This refers to the fact that within those hells, there is no meaningful benefit.
It is called "non-existence. Question:
There are many kinds of hells, some of which are located beneath the earth.
Some are situated upon the ground,
while others dwell in the void;
for what reason are they all collectively called "hells"?
Answer: The old translation for "hell" (dīyù) was "narrow place" (xiàchù),
which refers to a confined location that does not encompass the earth or space.
According to the newly translated sūtras and śāstras,
the correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *naraka*;
it is also transliterated as *naloka*.
This term collectively refers to persons.
Because they dwell within suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*), they are called *naraka*.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
Question: For what reason is that destination called *naraka*?
Answer: Because those sentient beings therein have no joy, no affection, no flavor, no benefit, and no delight.
Therefore it is called *naraka*.
Alternatively, some say it is so named because of what was previously created and accumulated by them.
Because one goes there and causes that continuity [of suffering] due to excessive and violent misconduct of body, speech, and mind, it is called *naraka*.
Some say that this realm is called *naraka* because of falling headlong (*nipatana*) into it.
As a verse says: "Those who fall headlong into hell, with feet above and heads below, Are those who,
delighting in solitude and practicing asceticism, Have slandered the Buddhas."
Some say that *nara* means "human" and *ka* means "evil"; thus,
because evil people are born in that place, it is called Naraka.
It is named *naraka*. Question:
For what reason? Answer:
Because it is the lowest and the greatest.
Is it called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*)?
Answer: Because in that place one constantly experiences suffering and there is no interval of joy or pleasure.
Therefore, it is called "Uninterrupted" (Avīci).
Question: In the other hells, could there possibly be singing, dancing, food, and drink?
Is it not called "immediate" because one experiences the maturation of joy and pleasure?
Answer: In other hells.
Although there is no ripening (*vipāka*) joy or pleasure,
there is concordant outflow (*niṣyanda*) joy and pleasure,
as stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*.
In the Saṃjīva Hell, at times they are blown upon by cool winds so that their flesh and blood are restored;
at other times, they utter cries, shouting, "Saṃjīva! (Revive!).
Those sentient beings suddenly returned to life;
this occurred only at the time when such flesh and blood were produced,
and at the time of their revival.
Because there is an interval of pleasant feeling amidst the suffering, it is not called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*). 3.
The Conditions for Receiving Retribution. Third, as stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*:
Question: Where are the hells located? Answer: [They are] as follows.
It is mostly located beneath this Jambudvīpa.
How is it established? Some say:
From this continent, descending forty thousand yojanas,
one reaches the bottom of the Avīci Hell.
This is the Avīci Hell.
Its length, breadth, height, and depth are each twenty thousand yojanas.
Within the upper nineteen thousand yojanas,
the remaining seven hells are established.
That is to say, above that is the Extremely Hot Hell; above that is the Hot Hell;
and above that is the Great Howling Hell.
Above that is the Raurava Hell; above that is the Saṃghāta Hell;
and above that is the Kālasūtra Hell.
Above this is the Sañjīva (Reviving) Hell.
Each of these seven hells is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
Above that, there remains one thousand yojanas:
five hundred yojanas are white plaster,
and five hundred yojanas are clay.
Some say that below this mud,
in the center, lies the Avīci Hell.
The other seven hells surround it on all sides,
just as villages surround a great city.
It is asked:
If that is so, how should one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*? As it says:
Jambudvīpa is six thousand and three and a half yojanas in circumference.
Each individual hell is vast in extent.
How, then, can they all be accommodated beneath this continent?
The answer is as follows:
This Jambudvīpa is pointed at the top and broad at the bottom, like a heap of grain;
therefore, it is able to contain [the waters].
For this reason, the sūtra states that the four great oceans gradually become deeper as one enters them.
Furthermore, each individual great hell has sixteen subsidiary hells (utsada), each having four gates.
Outside each gate, there are four successive terraces (*utsada*).
The first is the Terrace of Hot Ashes (*kukūla-utsada*),
meaning that within this terrace, hot ashes reach up to one's knees.
Second is the Kṛmibhūyiṣṭha (Corpse-Feces) Hell;
that is to say, within this hell, the ground is filled with the mud of corpses and excrement.
Third is the Śastrabhūyiṣṭha (Sharp-Bladed Weapons) Hell.
That is to say, within this increase there are further three types:
first, the Path of Blades,
which refers to that [place] wherein—
They spread blades upward to form a path.
Second is the Forest of Sword-Leaves;
this means that the trees in this forest have exclusively sharp, saw-like sword-blades for their leaves.
Third is the Forest of Iron Thorns.
This means that upon this forest there are sharp iron thorns,
sixteen finger-widths in length.
Although the three types, such as the Path of Sword Blades, differ from one another, they share the same iron forest;
therefore, this [forest] subsumes the four fierce great rivers.
That is to say, within this increase,
there are four great rivers of hot, salt water.
Including the individual hells,
these constitute seventeen;
thus, there are eight great hells together with their various subsidiary realms.
Thus, there are one hundred and thirty-six locations.
For this reason, the Sūtra states that there are one hundred and thirty-six *naraka*s (hells).
Therefore, the *Dīrgha Āgama* says:
There are eight great hells in total.
Each of these eight hells is surrounded by sixteen minor hells.
Just as there are eighty thousand world-systems surrounding the four great continents,
beyond those eighty thousand world-systems there is again a great ocean.
Beyond the sea lies the Great Vajra Mountain;
beyond that mountain lies yet another mountain, also named the Great Iron Ring (Mahācakravāḍa). As the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states, it is situated between these two mountains.
The majestic light of the deities of the sun and moon does not shine there at all.
As for the eight great hells:
first is Sañjīva (Reviving).
Second, Kālasūtra (Black Rope);
third, Saṃghāta (Crushing);
fourth, Raurava (Crying Out).
The Five Great Screams,
the Sixth Burning and Roasting,
and the Seventh Great Burning and Scorching.

Regarding the eight *anantarya* hells—where the names differ in other scriptures due to variations in translation between the erroneous and the correct—the general meaning is the same. First, the Hell of Perception (*saṃjñā-naraka*) has sixteen [divisions].
The sentient beings therein have iron claws growing from their hands; they harbor mutual resentment and anger,
tearing at one another with these claws so that flesh falls away as soon as it is struck.
They perceive it as death;
therefore, that perception is so named.
Furthermore, the sentient beings therein harbor perceptions of malice and harm.
Holding swords and blades in their hands, they strike and stab one another;
their bodies are flayed, sliced, and hacked until they fall to the ground in pieces,
at which point they imagine themselves to be dead.
A cold wind blew, and he was revived.
He thought to himself,
"I have now come back to life."
Having endured these torments for a long time, they emerge from the Saṃjīva Hell;
in their frantic terror, seeking clemency,
they unknowingly and suddenly arrive at the Kālasūtra Hell.
A hot windstorm arises, blowing hot black sand that strikes their bodies,
burning through the skin and penetrating to the bone;
flames erupt from within their bodies, swirling and circling around them.
Their bodies are scorched and withered,
yet because their retribution is not yet exhausted,
they do not die; thus they endure suffering for a long time.
Emerging from the Black Sand Hell,
they arrive at the Boiling Excrement Hell,
where glowing iron balls of excrement spontaneously fill the space before them.
They drive the sinners to embrace iron balls,
which burn their bodies, hands, and feet;
they are then forced to grasp them and thrust them into their mouths.
From the throat down to the abdomen,
everything is thoroughly penetrated and passes through below, with nothing that is not scorched and rotted;
there are iron-beaked worms that gnaw at the flesh and reach the marrow.
The bitter suffering is immeasurable;
though they have not yet finished undergoing their retribution, they are unwilling to die.
After enduring this suffering for a long time, [they are finally released].
Emerging from the Hell of Boiling Excrement,
they arrive at the Hell of Iron Nails. There,
the hell-wardens throw them down, prostrate upon hot iron.
Stretching out his body, they drove nails into his hands and feet;
until the entire body was covered with five hundred nails,
he wailed in bitter agony.
Yet they do not die;
after suffering for a long time,
they emerge from the Iron Nail Hell.
Upon reaching the Hungry Ghost Hell,
they are immediately cast onto glowing hot iron and molten copper is poured into their mouths;
from the throat down to the belly, it flows through.
The heat penetrates downward, passing through them all without exception, so that they are scorched and withered;
yet, as their remaining karma is not yet exhausted, they do not die.
After enduring suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Hungry Hell.
Upon reaching the Hell of Thirst,
they are immediately cast upon hot iron and iron balls are placed in their mouths, burning their lips and mouths.
Piercing through and passing below, there is no place where they are not scorched, burned, and tormented by bitter poison, wailing in lamentation.
After suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Kṣāranadī (Scorching Ground) Hell and arrive at the Tāmradhātuka (Copper Cauldron) Hell.
The hell-wardens, with eyes blazing with rage,
seize the feet of the offenders and turn them upside down into cauldrons;
they are tossed up and down as the boiling water surges and swirls.
Their bodies become putrid and decayed as myriad sufferings converge upon them;
thus they are made not to die even now.
After enduring suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Hell of Copper Cauldrons.
They reach the Copper Cauldron Hell (Tāmra-sthālī-naraka).
The sinners are seized by their feet and cast headfirst into the cauldrons;
as the boiling water surges and bubbles, they are whirled up and down.
Their entire bodies become festering and ruined;
they are then extracted with iron hooks and placed into other cauldrons.
Because their cries of grief and bitter agony are so intense, they are not allowed to die.
Having long endured suffering, they emerge from the Hell of Many Copper Cauldrons and arrive at the Hell of the Stone Mill,
where they seize those offenders.
They are stretched out upon hot stones with their hands and feet extended;
then they are pressed down upon their bodies by large, scorching stones,
which are rotated and rubbed back and forth until their flesh and bones are ground to powder.
Because of the bitter and excruciating pain, they are not allowed to die.
After suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Stone Mill Hell and arrive at the Pus and Blood Hell.
Pus and blood boil and surge;
within it, the offenders run hither and thither,
their bodies, heads, and faces scorched and putrefied.
Furthermore, they take pus and blood and eat it;
as it passes through their bodies, the bitter poison is so unbearable that it prevents them from dying.
After suffering for a long time, they finally emerge from the Pus-and-Blood Hell and arrive at the Hell of Measured Fire,
where there is a great mass of fire.
Its flames blaze fiercely, driving and pressing upon the sinners;
with hands grasping hot iron scales, they measure the mass of fire,
burning their bodies all over.
Suffering from bitter, burning pain, they groan and wail;
thus they are not allowed to die.
After enduring suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Hell of Measuring Fire.
They arrive at the Hell of the Ash River,
which is five hundred yojanas in length, breadth, and depth;
its caustic ash-water surges and boils, emitting a thick, stench-filled vapor.
The reverberating waves clash together with a terrifying sound;
from the bottom to the surface, iron spikes are strewn in every direction.
Upon the banks of the river stands a forest of sword-trees.
The branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are all swords;
when the sinners enter the river,
they are tossed up and down by the waves, overturned, and submerged.
Iron thorns pierce their bodies, penetrating both inside and out;
pus and blood flow forth, causing myriad forms of suffering,
yet they are not allowed to die.
He then emerged from the River of Ashes and reached its opposite bank;
there he arrived at a place where his body was mangled and destroyed by being sliced and pierced with swords,
and furthermore, there were jackals and wolves.
They come to bite the sinful beings, devouring their flesh raw.
When they run up the sword-trees, the sword-blades point downward;
when they descend from the sword-trees, the swords and knives point upward.
As his hands grasp, his hands snap;
as his feet tread, his feet break.
His skin and flesh fall away, leaving only white bones.
The sinews and veins are interconnected;
at that time, iron-beaked crows atop the sword-trees peck at their heads and devour their brains.
Because they wail in bitter agony, they are not permitted to die;
they return to the Ash River, sinking and bobbing with the waves.
Iron spikes pierce their bodies, subjecting them to ten thousand forms of bitter torment.
The skin and flesh rot and fall away, with pus and blood flowing out;
only the white bones remain, floating on the surface.
When a cold wind blows, they immediately stand up.
Dragged by the pull of past karma,
one is unaware that one has suddenly arrived at the Iron Ball Hell.
There, hell-wardens with hot iron balls drive and seize them as they run.
Their hands and feet are scorched and ruined, and their entire bodies are ablaze;
as ten thousand poisons assail them simultaneously, they are made not to die.
After enduring suffering for a long time, they finally emerge from the Iron Ball Hell.
Upon reaching the Hell of Axes and Hatchets,
they seize these sinners and throw them onto glowing red-hot iron,
using heated iron axes and hatchets.
Their hands, feet, ears, noses, and bodies are hacked away;
they wail in bitter agony yet still do not die.
After enduring these punishments for a long time, they emerge from the Kiln-Fork Hell.
Upon reaching the Hell of Jackals and Wolves,
a pack of jackals and wolves vied with one another to leap upon and bite them;
their flesh fell away, their bones were wounded, and pus and blood flowed out.
Because their sufferings are manifold, they are not permitted to die;
after enduring suffering for a long time, they finally emerge from the prison of tigers and wolves and arrive at the Hell of the Sword-Tree.
Upon entering that forest of swords, a violent wind arises,
blowing sword-shaped leaves down upon their bodies;
there is no part of their heads, faces, or bodies that is not wounded and destroyed.
Iron-beaked crows peck at their two eyes;
though they wail in agony and grief, they are prevented from dying.
After enduring suffering for a long time, they finally emerge from the Sword-Tree Hell.
Upon reaching the Hell of Cold Ice,
a great freezing wind blows upon their bodies;
their entire forms are frozen and wounded, and their skin and flesh fall away.
They cry out in bitter agony,
and only then does their life end;
their bodies have committed unwholesome deeds, and so too have their speech and minds.
They fall into the Saṃjīva Hell,
where their hair stands on end with fear.
Second is the Kālasūtra Great Hell.
There are sixteen minor hells surrounding it on all sides,
each being equal in length and breadth.
It is five hundred yojanas [in extent].
Why is it named Black Rope?
It is because the various hell-wardens seize those sinful beings.
They strike him against a red-hot iron surface and stretch out his body;
they bind it straight with hot iron cords,
and a hot iron axe follows the path of the cords.
They cut the sinner into hundreds and thousands of pieces.
Furthermore, they split him apart with iron ropes and saws.
Moreover, they suspend him amidst countless hot iron ropes crisscrossing in every direction.
They drive and compel the sinners to walk;
between the iron cords, fierce winds suddenly arise,
blowing against their bodies so that the iron cords entwine and crisscross over them.
The skin is burned, the flesh pierced, the bones split, and the marrow boils;
though the myriad forms of bitter torment are endless and the remaining retribution is not yet exhausted,
they do not die, and for this reason it is called the Black Rope Hell.
Having long endured suffering, they finally emerge from the Black Rope Hell and proceed to the Black Sand Hell,
continuing on until the Cold Ice Hell.
Thereafter, their lives come to an end;
it is impossible to describe in full detail the sufferings endured in the remaining sixteen hells.
The same principle as before applies;
however, the suffering experienced is intensified because of the malicious intent directed toward one's parents, the Buddha, and the Śrāvakas.
They immediately fall into the Black Rope Hell,
where their suffering and pain are beyond measure.
Third is the Crushing Great Hell.
There are also sixteen minor hells surrounding it,
each five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
For what reason is it named "The Pressing Mound" (Utpala)?
There are great stone mountains standing in pairs facing one another;

"Why do people weep?

**Preface on the Causes and Conditions** **The Preface on the Causes and Conditions, Number One:** Now, the principle of the spirit (*śruti*) is soundless.
One expresses the intended meaning through words and phrases,
yet words and phrases leave no trace;
one perfects the melodic resonance by relying on written characters.
Therefore, characters are the tracks of speech;
speech is the basket for capturing principles.
When sound and meaning coincide, they form a tally.
One must not be partial or err.
Therefore, the application of written characters encompasses and pervades the universe.
Although his traces in brush and ink are numerous, his principles accord with the divine;
yet because the sūtras and śāstras are so vast and extensive,
it is difficult to record them all completely.
The records and biographies are diverse and extensive; some accounts are detailed while others are concise.
Thus, they serve to guide and reach all quarters of the world.

thus, the conditions and traces for establishing the teachings are brilliantly and completely provided,
and the origins of the matters for instructing the laity are all present in their full abundance.
I have searched through the regulations and articles,
extracted their essential points,
and compiled them here in writing.

As for the remaining miscellaneous matters,
they serve to guide and deliver worldly beings.
Those practices that can be implemented now are annotated below,
in the hope that ignorance and delusion may gradually be dispelled.

The Second Chapter on the Conditions for Enmity and Suffering. As stated in the Madhyama Āgama:
At that time, the World-Honored One...

not knowing the fundamental limit of suffering."
"Monks, what do you think?

If one were to count the parents upon whom you have relied throughout the long night of saṃsāra’s revolving,

"O bhikṣus, in this way,
beings have revolved through the long night of beginningless birth and death,

For a long night, you have been cast away in burial mounds;
the flowing of pus and blood is likewise so.

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Throughout the long night, you have transmigrated through birth and death."
The blood you have shed throughout your lives has been immense and beyond counting,
exceeding the waters of the Ganges River and the four great oceans.
Throughout the long night of saṃsāra, you have even been born among elephants.

their blood being immeasurable;
others take on the forms of horses, camels, donkeys, oxen, birds, beasts, and other such species.

their blood being immeasurable; or,
when their bodies perished and their lives ended, they were cast away in burial grounds.
Pus and blood flow forth in immeasurable quantities;
they may fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts.
When their bodies perish and their lives end, [they suffer].

Or, throughout the long night, they transmigrate through birth and death,
losing their fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, and all six classes of kin and acquaintances.

such tears are exceedingly many and immeasurable,
surpassing the waters of the four great oceans.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"When you see sentient beings dwelling in peace and enjoying various forms of happiness,
you should form this thought:"
We have wandered through birth and death for a long night;
we have also experienced such pleasures as these in immeasurable realms of rebirth.
Or, we have seen various sentient beings undergoing manifold sufferings and afflictions.
One should reflect thus:
"In the long night of my past, as I have wandered through birth and death,
I have likewise experienced such suffering."
Their number was immeasurable.
Some saw various sentient beings and gave rise to fear,
their body hair standing on end.
One should reflect thus:
"In the past, we must have certainly committed killing;
we were those who caused harm."
Associating with evil associates,
they wander through the long night of beginningless birth and death,

one should form this thought:
"In such a way, it was during the past ages."
They must have been our parents, brothers, sisters, wives, children, relatives, teachers, friends, or spiritual mentors. Thus,
throughout the long night of saṃsāra, we have revolved in the cycle of birth and death,
shrouded by ignorance.
Craving binds their necks;
thus they revolve through the long night,
unaware of the ultimate limit of suffering.
Therefore, O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves thus: with diligent application,
sever the roots and do not allow them to increase.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
If the bones of a single person were accumulated over the course of one kalpa,
They would remain constantly heaped up without decaying, Like Mount Vipula.
If the noble disciples, with right knowledge, see the truths—
this suffering and the cause of suffering— and, having abandoned suffering, attain its cessation,
they cultivate the eightfold path that leads directly to parinirvāṇa.
"At most, they will undergo seven more existences;
having been born as gods or humans until all fetters are exhausted, they shall reach the ultimate end of suffering.
Thus the Buddha told the bhikṣus.
Sentient beings have been revolving through the long night of birth and death since beginningless time,
unaware of the ultimate limit of suffering;
there is not a single place where they have not experienced birth and death.
Thus, throughout this long night of beginningless birth and death,
one does not know the fundamental limit of suffering,
nor is there a single place where it is absent.
They have no parents, brothers, wives, children, kinsmen, relatives, teachers, or elders;
they are like drops and bubbles in a heavy rain, arising and ceasing in a single moment.
Thus are sentient beings shrouded by ignorance.
Bound by craving around their necks,
they revolve through the long night,
unaware of the ultimate limit of suffering.
It is like a great rain falling from all quarters of heaven,
pouring down in torrents so that there is no place in the east, west, south, or north where it is interrupted;
likewise, throughout the immeasurable lands of the four directions.
The kalpas of formation and destruction are like a great rain falling from heaven, pouring everywhere across the world without interruption;
thus one revolves through the long night.
One does not know the ultimate limit of suffering;
it is like throwing a staff into the air:
either its head will land on the ground first.
Sometimes the tail falls to the ground;
sometimes the middle falls to the ground.
Thus one revolves through the long night of beginningless birth and death.
Some fall into hell;
some fall among the animals;
some fall among the hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven,
for the sake of the assembly of devas, spoke in brief.
Among gods and humans, there are sixteen kinds of suffering.
What are these sixteen?
They are comprised within the category of those who have attained excellence among gods and humans.
First is the suffering of the intermediate state;
second is the suffering of dwelling in the womb;
third is the suffering of emerging from the womb.
Fourth is the suffering of seeking food;
fifth is the suffering of meeting with those one hates;
sixth is the suffering of separation from those one loves.
Seventh is the suffering of cold, heat, and so forth;
eighth is the suffering of illness;
ninth is the suffering of being employed as a servant by others.
Tenth is the suffering of seeking and laboring;
eleventh is the suffering of associating with evil associates;
twelfth is the suffering of the decline and affliction of wife, children, and kinsmen.
Thirteenth is the suffering of hunger and thirst;
fourteenth is the suffering of being despised and reviled by others;
fifteenth is the suffering of old age.
Sixteenth is the suffering of death.
These are the sixteen great sufferings among human beings in the world of men.
Up until the end of life and through all other sufferings,
[existence] within birth and death is unbearable;
among conditioned phenomena, there is not the slightest happiness.
"All things are impermanent; all things are subject to decay.
At that time, the King of the Yāma Heaven spoke in verse:
In the world of humans, all that has aggregates is suffering;
birth inevitably leads to death, and death is followed by birth again.
If one dwells within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one suffers the afflictions of one's own karma.
The suffering of traveling far through the long night— this suffering is beyond description—
of being submerged in excrement and urine and scorched by the heat;
such is the suffering of dwelling in the womb, which cannot be fully told.
Constantly craving the flavors of food, their minds always longing for tastes lead to great suffering; this suffering is beyond description,
for with small minds they constantly long for more, never knowing satisfaction in their desires.
The various sufferings and afflictions one undergoes—these sufferings are unspeakable:
the meeting with those one hates and dislikes, like a great fire or poison;
the sufferings thus produced are unspeakable.
Upon the separation from those one loves, sentient beings give rise to great suffering,
great evil, and unbearable hardship; this suffering is beyond description—
fearful great suffering of cold and heat— from which immeasurable kinds of pain arise.
One gives rise to immeasurable kinds of evil; this suffering is unspeakable.
The suffering of illness harms human life; illness acts as the messenger of the King of Death.
Sentient beings undergo such suffering; this suffering is unspeakable.
Driven by others, they always lack autonomy;
sentient beings undergo such suffering that it is beyond description.
Scorched by the poison of craving, they pursue objects and endure great misery.
From birth through to death—this suffering is beyond description.
If one associates with evil friends, all manner of sufferings will never cease;
one will constantly undergo the miseries of the evil realms—this suffering is beyond description.
When one's wife and children fall into decline and distress, seeing them gives rise to great suffering that exceeds even that of hell; this pain is beyond description,
as hunger and thirst burn the body like a fierce, blazing fire.
That which can destroy both body and mind—this suffering is beyond description.
Constantly treating others with contempt, one gives rise to grief, sorrow, and pain toward kinsmen and friends; this suffering is beyond description.
When a person is oppressed by old age, the body becomes frail and the mind weak;
hunched over and walking with a staff, this suffering is beyond description.
