The Third [Section] on the Conditions of the Eight Sufferings, as stated in the *Pañcarājopadeśa-sūtra* (Five Kings Sūtra):
The Buddha preached the Dharma for the five kings, saying:
In this life, there are constantly immeasurable sufferings that cut into one's very person.
Now, for your sake, I shall briefly explain the eight types of suffering.
What are the eight sufferings?
First, the suffering of birth;
second, the suffering of old age.
Third, the suffering of illness;
fourth, the suffering of death;
fifth, the suffering of separation from those one loves.
Sixth is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
seventh is the suffering of encountering the hated and disliked;
eighth is the suffering of grief and lamentation.
These are the eight sufferings.
What is meant by the suffering of birth?
When a person is at the point of death...
Not knowing toward which realm the spirit is heading,
and not yet having attained a place of birth,
it universally assumes the form of the intermediate state (antarābhava).
When the twenty-first day arrives, the parents unite,
and [the consciousness] immediately comes to enter the womb.
During the first week, it is like thin curd.
In the second week, it is like thick curd;
in the third week, it is like solidified butter;
in the fourth week, it is like a mass of flesh.
In the fifth week, the fleshy bubbles are fully formed;
the wind of skillfulness enters the abdomen and blows upon the body,
causing the six sense faculties to open and expand.
Within the mother’s womb, situated below the stomach and above the large intestine,
when the mother consumes a cup of hot food,
it drenches his body as if he had entered a cauldron of boiling water.
When the mother drinks a single cup of cold water,
it feels as if freezing ice cuts through her body.
When the mother is full, [she experiences the same].
The body is constricted with pain that is beyond description.
When the mother is hungry,
the fetus feels as though it is being crushed within her womb, like being hung upside down.
He experienced immeasurable suffering until,
at the time of his full-term birth,
he turned his head toward the birth canal.
The birth is as perilous as two rocky cliffs;
when the child is about to be born,
the mother is in danger and the father is filled with fear.
Born and falling upon the grass,
his body was delicate and soft;
yet when the grass touched his body, it felt as if he were treading upon swords and blades.
Suddenly, he lost his voice and cried out in a loud shout: "Is this suffering?
Everyone said: [Yes].
This is great suffering.
What is the suffering of old age?
It refers to when parents have nurtured and raised one until reaching adulthood.
Relying on one's own strength and vigor,
one carries light loads as if they were heavy, failing to exercise self-restraint; thus,
one loses the proper measure regarding cold and heat.
In old age, the hair turns white and the teeth fall out;
the eyesight becomes blurred and dim,
and the hearing grows dull.
Prosperity departs and decline arrives;
the skin slackens and the face wrinkles;
the hundred joints ache with pain.
In walking, his suffering was extreme;
in sitting or rising, he groaned;
his mind was afflicted with grief and sorrow.
As the consciousness-spirit undergoes transformation and extinction, one immediately forgets;
the days of life draw near to their end.
When speaking of this, my tears flow;
I require assistance even to sit or rise.
Is this not suffering?
The answer is: it is great suffering.
What is meant by the suffering of illness?
A person is composed of the combination of the four great elements.
When the four great elements are slightly imbalanced, one hundred and one diseases arise;
when the four great elements are severely imbalanced,
four hundred and four diseases manifest simultaneously.
When the earth element is disturbed, the entire body becomes heavy;
when the water element is disturbed, the entire body becomes swollen;
when the fire element is disturbed, the entire body becomes feverish and hot.
When the wind element is disturbed, the entire body becomes rigid and stiff,
and the hundred joints ache with pain as if one were being flogged with a staff.
The four great elements fluctuate, rendering the hands and feet incapable of function;
his vital strength is utterly exhausted, such that he requires assistance for sitting and rising;
his mouth is parched and his lips are withered.
The tendons snap and the nose collapses;
the eyes no longer perceive forms and the ears no longer hear sounds;
impurities flow forth.
Lying upon it, his heart was filled with anguish,
and his speech was full of sorrow.
The six types of relatives stood by his side, watching and tending to him day and night without ever ceasing; yet,
when fine delicacies and delicious foods entered his mouth, they all tasted bitter.
"Is this suffering? He replied,
"Indeed, it is great suffering."
What is called the suffering of death?
At the time of a person's death,
four hundred and four diseases arise simultaneously.
When the four great elements are about to disperse and the soul and spirit become unsettled,
at the moment of death,
the "sword-wind" (kṣuraka-vāyu) dissolves the physical form, causing pain everywhere.
Cold sweat flows from his body as he reaches into empty space with both hands;
those within and without the household stand at his left and right,
weeping in grief and sorrow until their pain pierces to the very marrow of their bones.
Unable to overcome it,
the dead depart from it; their breath ceases and they vanish like the wind.
The fire is extinguished and the body grows cold;
the vital breaths lose their order,
and the soul departs.
The body remained upright, yet there was no further sensation;
within ten days, the flesh decayed and blood flowed,
becoming bloated, putrid, and foul-smelling such that it was utterly unbearable to approach.
Cast away in the wilderness, it is devoured by various birds;
when the flesh is gone and the bones have dried, the skull lies in a different place. Is this not suffering?
He replied,
"It is indeed a great suffering.
What is meant by the suffering of separation from those one loves?"
That is to say, when members of a household— both those within and without, including brothers, wives, and children—
are bound together by mutual affection,
yet in a single day their home is destroyed and they are plundered by others.
They dispersed in their respective directions:
the father to the east, the son to the west, the mother to the south, and the daughter to the north;
they were no longer in one place.
As slaves to one another, they each wailed in grief;
their hearts were torn asunder,

"Is this suffering?
"It is indeed great suffering," he replied.
What is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks?
It is when one’s household wealth is dissipated through seeking after high officials, commoners, and the populace.
He hoped for wealth and honor;
through unremitting toil and ceaseless seeking, he eventually encountered his opportunity.
Having attained it, he served as a district magistrate on the frontier.
Before long, he greedily seized the property of the people,
and was accused by them.
If one day an emergency arises and they are placed in a cangue to await execution,
their suffering and anxiety at the moment of being about to be killed will be immeasurable.
"I do not know when my life will end or if I shall die; is this not suffering?
He replied:
This is indeed great suffering.
What is meant by the suffering of association with the disliked?
It is that worldly people, driven by vulgar customs, dwell together amidst the midst of craving and desire.
They contend over matters that are not urgent,
further killing and harming one another,
until they eventually form great enmity.
Each avoided the other, finding no place to hide;
they sharpened their blades, notched their arrows, slung their bows, and grasped their staves,
fearing the sight of one another.
They encountered one another on a narrow path;
drawing their bows and loosing their arrows, they faced each other with blades drawn,
not knowing who would emerge victorious.
At that time, there was immeasurable fear.
"Is this suffering?
he asked. He replied:
This is indeed great suffering.
What is meant by sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress?
It refers to human beings living in this world.
Those with long lives may even reach a hundred years;
those with short lives suffer miscarriage or abortion.
As for those with long lives:
Rather than living for a hundred years,
half of which is spent in the night,
one has fifty remaining years.
Due to the illness of alcoholism,
one does not know how to act as a human being; five years are diminished from one's lifespan,
and one remains foolish from childhood.
Until the age of fifteen, he was ignorant of ritual propriety;
by the time he was over eighty,
his faculties were dull and devoid of wisdom.
Deaf and with sight obscured,
lacking all principles of dharma,
they further diminished by twenty.
I am already ninety years old;
with more than ten years remaining,
these final years have been filled with much sorrow and anxiety.
When the world is about to fall into chaos, he is also distressed.
When there is drought throughout the world, he is also distressed.
When there is a great flood throughout the world, he is also distressed.
He is distressed when there is heavy frost throughout the world;
he is distressed when the crops do not ripen throughout the world;
and he is distressed when there are many illnesses both inside and outside his household.
He manages his household wealth and livelihood;
he grieves lest it be lost,
and he grieves that the various taxes and levies of the government have not yet been paid.
When family members are imprisoned by the authorities and one does not know the date of their release, there is sorrow;
when brothers travel far away and have not yet returned, there is also sorrow.
He is distressed that his household is impoverished and cold, lacking both food and clothing;

The family members have died;
having no wealth, they grieve over the lack of means for the funeral rites.

Thus, amidst these various sorrows and lamentations,
there was never a time of joy;
yet on their festival days, they would gather together.
"You ought to rejoice,
yet you instead weep together and face one another; is this not suffering?"
The answer is:
It is indeed great suffering.
Furthermore, the *Suvarṇavarṇa-rāja-sūtra* states:
One day, a goddess spoke this verse to King Suvarṇavarṇa:
"What phenomenon is called suffering? It is said to be poverty."
What suffering is most heavy? It is the suffering of poverty;

4. The Conditioned Arising of the Dwelling Worms, the Fourth. As stated in the *Dhyānaguhya-uttara-sūtra*:
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a practitioner enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*):"
The wind of sensual thought arises from greed and lust;
it moves through four hundred and four channels,
extending from the eyes to the body-faculty.
At that time, they are shaken;
the various sense-faculties are obstructed,
stirring the wind of the mind.
It causes the mind to become deranged;
consequently, one may go mad or be possessed by malevolent spirits,
thinking of sensual desires day and night as if one’s head were on fire.
One should treat this with urgency.
As for the method of treatment,
one instructs this practitioner to contemplate the womb.
The receptacle for the embryo is located below the stomach and above the large intestine,
consisting of ninety-nine layers of membranes.
It is like the carcass of a dead pig;
the four hundred and four channels extend from the uterus like the roots of a tree.
The various sense organs are scattered about like a bag filled with excrement;
it has one thousand nine hundred joints resembling the leaves of a plantain tree,
and is surrounded on all sides by eighty types of worms.
There are one hundred and four vessels,
as well as the womb,
which is like a horse's intestine.
The birth canal extends until it takes the shape of a bracelet for the arm;
it is circular in its overall dimensions,
being round at the top and tapering to a point below.
It resembles the teeth of a shell,
consisting of ninety-nine layers;
within each layer there dwell four hundred and four types of worms.
Each worm has twelve heads and twelve mouths.
When a person drinks water, the water-essence enters the channels and disperses among these worms.
It enters the crown of the *vīra* insect and proceeds directly to the birth canal;
every half-month, it discharges impure water.
The various worms each vomit forth what resembles putrid pus, which enters the mouths of the ninety worms;
it then issues from the six orifices of the twelve worms like a flow of putrid crimson liquid.
Furthermore, there are various insects smaller than the finest autumn hair that sport within it;
this is due to the grave evil karma of those men from their past lives.
The four hundred and four channels spread from the eye-organ in four streams, flowing into the various intestines;
they reach the space below the raw receptacle (āmāśaya) and above the cooked receptacle (pakvāśaya).
On both sides of the vessels of the lungs, spleen, and kidneys,
there are sixty-four worms each.
Each has twelve heads and also twelve mouths;
they are curled and attached to one another, shaped like finger rings.
It is filled with a thick, blue pus like the semen of a wild boar;
its foul stench is unbearable.
Upon reaching the private parts, it divides into three branches.
